articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1705: Starlink speed restored for Ukraine’s troops, Musk says SpaceX simply enforced its terms
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine strikes Russian plant supplying batteries for ballistic missiles and glide bombs with Storm Shadow missiles, OSINT reports – another hit on Russia’s weapons supply chain. The plant is reportedly Russia’s only producer of batteries for glide bomb guidance modules and a key supplier of specialized power sources for missile systems used in attacks on Ukraine.
Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine. AVISMA, a major titanium producer in Russia’s Perm Krai, was reportedly hit by drones early on 25 October. The plant’s titanium alloys are used in military aircraft, engines, missiles, and space technology.
Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight. Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping complex in Belgorod overnight, when it was closed.
Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles. OSINT projects reported that a strike hit the Proton plant in Orel, a facility whose electronic components are used in several Russian weapons systems.
Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia. The Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s coast, with nine crew members rescued and three still missing. The incident adds to a wave of attacks threatening Black Sea shipping and Ukraine’s export routes.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones. Ukrainian pilots are already using the 20-mm ammunition to intercept jet-powered attack drones, as Russia deploys faster targets that challenge Ukraine’s air defenses.
Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says. Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles that will take years to arrive, so it wants partners’ stocks today.
Intelligence and technology
Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal. The warning lands weeks after his company throttled the Starshield service Ukraine’s drones rely on.
A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant. Posing as a Russian military supplier, journalists got a $2.87 million invoice, three bank accounts, and no pushback on military use.
Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns. The agency says Moscow aims to weaken European support for Kyiv by making Russian attacks appear to be the work of Ukraine’s military.
The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show. The firm, co-owned by the bank behind Russia’s defense industry, hides where the money starts before it reaches foreign banks.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays. Ukraine’s military Starlink terminals still lose connection above about 160 km/h, nine days after the limit took effect, and Kyiv has no official explanation of who imposed it.
International
40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote. The tanker loaded at a Baltic port Ukrainian drones struck in March. Trump wants cheaper diesel before the midterms.
Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns. As Russian strikes increasingly threaten civilian vessels and Ukrainian grain exports, Germany’s foreign minister warned that shipping disruptions could leave vulnerable countries without essential food and fertilizers.
Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub. Austrian security authorities raised suspicions of espionage involving four Russian diplomats, prompting Vienna to declare them persona non grata.
Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat. President Maia Sandu condemned the latest incursion as Russia’s war on Ukraine increasingly threatens neighboring Moldova.
Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power. The engines come free from Finland’s state railway, part of a visit that also brought winter energy money and new defense, housing, and satellite deals for Kyiv.
45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect. Poland is Ukraine’s main hub for Western aid, and every new fight over the two nations’ WWII past erodes the trust that role rests on.
Humanitarian and social impact
Pope’s envoy becomes first foreign representative to gain access to Ukrainian POWs held by Russia since 2022. Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, Pope Leo XIV’s special envoy, was allowed to physically visit Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia during his recent visit, Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces. A truce announced by Melania Trump is due to take effect October 29, opening the way for humanitarian supplies and evacuations if Russia and Ukraine implement the agreement.
Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard. The latest exchange returned 261 military personnel and nine civilians. Some had been held since 2018, while many others were captured during the defense of Mariupol in 2022.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution. A captive soldier’s wife says that whenever families find a relative, Russia moves them to another prison and contact is lost again.
Political and legal developments
US midterms could restore Ukraine’s American aid and curb Trump’s Russia deals, if Democrats win Congress. Trump waives sanctions on Moscow that Congress wrote into law. Democrats could fight back after 3 November.
Putin claims Russia is ready for new talks with Ukraine, calls occupied land historical Russia. He also cited unnamed genetic studies to claim Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a day after hosting a US envoy.
Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them. The state budget has paid to keep war-damaged arms plants running. The new model brings private money into the digging.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
Key developments on Oct. 24-25:
- Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
- Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
- Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
- In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
- Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress, senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.
A Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in the city of Vinnytsia overnight on Oct. 25, injuring six people, one of whom was hospitalized, Nataliia Zabolotna, head of the Vinnytsia Oblast Military Administration, said.
The strike caused structural damage between the second and third floors, completely destroying four apartments and damaging nearby parked cars, Zabolotna added.
Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 119 drones, including 64 jet-powered ones. As of 8 a.m., efforts to intercept the remaining drones were ongoing, with at least nine still in Ukrainian airspace.
Some drones evaded Ukrainian air defenses and struck 15 locations, while falling debris was recorded at nine other locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian attacks on the Synelnykove District on Oct. 24 killed three people and injured 14 others, including an 11-year-old girl, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Five of the injured were hospitalized in serious condition.
In the Nikopol District, Russian attacks over the past day killed two women and injured five people, including a 14-year-old boy, Hanzha added.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed a 45-year-old man in the town of Lozova and injured two other men, aged 43 and 26, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kharkiv, a 39-year-old man was injured. Russian attacks also wounded three men, aged 70, 54, and 47, in the town of Derhachi, and a 45-year-old woman in the village of Mala Danylivka, Syniehubov added.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person in the village of Yarova and injured six others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast, a 31-year-old woman was killed in a Russian attack on a farm in the Buryn community, which also injured an 18-year-old man. In the Boromlia community, a Russian drone struck a car, injuring three women aged 68, 56, and 36, according to local authorities.
Russian attacks injured four people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day. Russian forces carried out 832 strikes on 52 settlements across the region using drones, artillery, aircraft, and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), local authorities said.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks targeted 43 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, injuring two people, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, two women suffered acoustic trauma in a Russian strike on the regional capital, Chernihiv, on Oct. 24, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Oct. 24, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.

In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
Russian attacks hit four Epicentr hypermarkets in less than 24 hours, the company said on Oct. 25.
The latest wave of strikes highlights Russia's campaign of terror against civilians, with stores, shopping centers, and other civilian infrastructure among the targets. Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest home improvement and retail chains, has been particularly hard hit.
In a post on Facebook, the company said Russian attacks damaged or destroyed facilities in the cities of Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia, and Poltava on Oct. 24-25, and described the attacks as amounting to "total destruction of the network."
The company did not specify the extent of the damage or when the affected facilities might reopen.
The Poltava Oblast Military Administration said a 52-year-old woman was injured in an attack on a hypermarket on Oct. 25. Authorities in other regions did not report any civilian casualties from attacks on Epicentr stores during the same period.
Founded in 2003, Epicentr operated 72 hypermarkets across Ukraine before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Since the start of the all-out war, ten of the company's shopping centers have been completely destroyed and another 13 have been damaged, Epicentr told the Ukrainian outlet Ekonomichna Pravda in August 2026.
Epicentr's head of public relations, Yuliia Chudnovets, said on Oct. 22 that Russian forces had struck five company sites, including one in Kyiv, in the previous 48 hours.

Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
A massive swarm of Ukrainian drones attacked the Russian border region of Belgorod overnight on Oct. 25, according to local officials and eyewitness footage posted to social media.
The bulk of the drones have concentrated on one area in the Belgorod city center, locals report. According to the monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus, the target was the MegaGRINN shopping complex, Belgorod's largest retail and entertainment center.
MegaGRINN covers an area of more than 163,000 square meters and houses over 200 stores, as well as a supermarket, cinema, and restaurants. The facility was closed and empty of visitors during the overnight attack.
Local residents also reported a fire in the courtyard of a residential complex in the area.
The Belgorod Oblast Operational Headquarters confirmed a "massive UAV attack" against the city and said emergency services had been dispatched to the impacted areas, though they did not name any specific targets.
The attack killed one civilian and injured 14 others, authorities said. At least 30 apartment buildings, 35 vehicles, four houses, three administrative buildings, and eight commercial properties were damaged.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify these reports at the time of publication.
Videos published on social media by eyewitnesses show explosions, fires, and air defense operations over the city of Belgorod. The Operational Headquarters has warned residents to stay indoors as attacks are ongoing in the region.
The city of Belgorod lies just 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia and approximately 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. Its proximity to the front lines makes it a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks, even as Kyiv's expanding long-range capabilities allow its drones to penetrate deep in the Russian interior.
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Belgorod have targeted energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses, including facilities belonging to the Russian retail giant Ozon.
The reported drone blitz on Belgorod comes shortly after Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 24 that its Starshield system had been restored to full speed, allowing troops to more effectively coordinate drone strikes on Russian targets.
Starshield, the military application of the Starlink satellite internet system, had been operating at drastically reduced speed in Ukraine since Oct. 14. The unexplained restriction disrupted key military missions and Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
articles.body:
Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
There has long been talk of “hunter” satellites and an intensifying confrontation in space between Russia and the United States. But this week brought an unprecedented escalation in the new “star wars.” On October 18, a Russian inspector satellite came closer than ever to a spacecraft operated by the Finnish-American company ICEYE. The company openly helps Ukraine, giving its armed forces access to satellite images of Russian military facilities, including airfields, naval ports, and oil refineries. Here’s what we know about the exceptionally close encounter, how Moscow is describing it, and why independent experts are alarmed.
Russian Kosmos satellites have pursued this spacecraft before, but never like this
Overnight into October 18, the Russian satellite Kosmos-2612 approached the radar imaging satellite ICEYE-X36 after a series of maneuvers that began four days earlier. The Ukrainian military uses data from the ICEYE satellite.
This was not their first close encounter. In the spring, four Russian spacecraft were “hunting” this same satellite: Kosmos-2612, 2610, 2611, and 2613 all approached it. Earlier, in February, news outlets reported on maneuvers by Luch spacecraft pursuing telecommunications satellites operated by Intelsat and Eutelsat.
This time, Kosmos-2612 came exceptionally close to its target: hundreds or even tens of meters away, rather than tens of kilometers as before. Observational astronomer Marco Langbroek estimates that at their closest approach, at 1:35 a.m. GMT on October 18, the spacecraft were between 26 and 470 meters apart. Measurement errors make a more precise estimate impossible. Bart Hendrickx, an independent researcher of Russia’s space program, told Meduza that he knew of no previous encounter at such close range in low Earth orbit. In earlier encounters, he said, satellites had remained at least several dozen kilometers apart.
He said the complexity and methodical persistence of the maneuvers by Kosmos-2612 and its fellow satellites, numbered 2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614, were also surprising. All these spacecraft, along with satellite 2609, were launched aboard a single rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on April 16.
“The satellites used a considerable amount of fuel on these maneuvers. By May, it was already clear that these weren’t ordinary Earth-observation and communications satellites, which generally conserve their fuel. Perhaps [through this latest escalation] Russia is demonstrating its ability to change orbits quickly and unpredictably to threaten enemy satellites,” Hendrickx said.
Moscow calls these maneuvers “a tool of strategic deterrence” and a warning to commercial companies
The Russian military previously acknowledged launching inspector satellites but said their sole purpose was “monitoring the condition of Russian satellites” — and said they had carried out such monitoring. Now, following Kosmos-2612’s dangerous maneuvers, the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta has published an article by Yuri Knutov, a military expert, retired colonel, and director of the Air Defense Forces Museum in Balashikha, outside Moscow. The article says Russia’s actions “do not violate international law” and that the inspector satellites themselves are “a tool of strategic deterrence.”
“Russia is demonstrating its ability to ‘blind’ or at least identify sources of threats. The approach to ICEYE-X36 sends a clear signal: Any commercial company making its capabilities available for intelligence gathering against Russia must recognize that its spacecraft may be subjected to forced inspection in orbit,” Knutov wrote. He said both ICEYE satellites and the Starlink constellation, which is critical to Ukrainian military command and communications, had effectively become part of NATO’s intelligence apparatus.
Like analyst Georgy Trishkin, whose views we quoted here, Knutov believes the Kosmos maneuvers were intended to force the ICEYE satellite to take evasive action to avoid a collision and quickly use up its fuel, turning it into “a useless piece of metal that will eventually burn up in the upper atmosphere.”
Knutov said the Russian satellites were less vulnerable to such a tactic because modern inspector spacecraft have much larger fuel reserves than their predecessors. Earlier models could perform only two or three orbital maneuvers before running out of fuel, he said, whereas newer satellites can remain in orbit for extended periods, carry out complex close approaches, and track other spacecraft over long stretches.
This latest episode in the space cold war was clearly visible from Earth. On Monday, Spaceweather.com asked whether the close encounter between Kosmos and ICEYE would be visible through binoculars or a backyard telescope. By Tuesday, it had its answer: yes.
This image, taken by the Swiss company s2a systems, shows the encounter. The bright object in front is the ICEYE-X36 radar satellite. Its apparent magnitude is about 7, making it invisible to the naked eye but easy to see through binoculars or an amateur telescope. The fainter object behind it is Kosmos-2612.
Russia isn’t the only country with space programs like these
Other countries, particularly the United States and China, have their own programs to develop inspector satellites. These spacecraft are designed to approach other objects in space that aren’t built for such encounters — those without docking ports, for example. These approaches can have various purposes: intercepting radio transmissions, inspecting another spacecraft, diagnosing problems, or even destroying it.
Militaries initiated and funded nearly all of these programs, so the public first learned they existed from amateur astronomers tracking the strange behavior of uncataloged satellites. Since 2011, when these observers identified an American satellite nicknamed Prowler this way, dozens more inspector satellites and many cases of pursuit have been detected, most involving Russian spacecraft.
Russian satellite maneuvers are easier to track because of censorship in the Pentagon’s main space catalog
Unequal access to information partly explains this pattern of observations. The U.S. military maintains Space-Track, the main publicly accessible catalog of artificial objects in space. It withholds the full orbital parameters of some U.S. military and intelligence satellites or publishes them with a delay. Until 2018, the Pentagon even classified data on civilian spacecraft launched as secondary payloads alongside military ones.
The U.S. military does not conceal Russian satellites’ orbital data, so anyone with the relevant skills can use the available data to plot their movements rather than track them through a telescope.
In 2018, the State Department protested the “very abnormal behavior” of Russian satellites. The U.S. military has protested their “threatening” maneuvers and anti-satellite weapons tests (we wrote about these nesting-doll satellites). Then, in 2024, Washington accused Moscow of preparing to deploy nuclear weapons in space.
Yet the United States has operated GSSAP satellites since 2014. These are essentially the same kind of inspector satellites, used to monitor satellites in geostationary orbit. And in June 2026, the U.S. military launched Jackal, built by True Anomaly, and Puma, made by Rocket Lab, as part of the Victus Haze exercise to practice space “hunting” scenarios.
In September of this year, the Pentagon acknowledged for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space — both kinetic and nonkinetic. The next few years in Earth orbit will clearly be tense.
Inspector satellites are also being developed for entirely civilian purposes. One example is LINK, a spacecraft meant to attempt a rescue of the Swift space telescope, but its mission ended in failure.
It’s hard to predict what the Kosmos satellites will do next
What happens next depends largely on how much fuel the Russian satellites have left. They may continue maneuvering around ICEYE spacecraft. According to Langbroek, as of midday on October 21, Kosmos-2612 had stopped moving away from its target and was holding at a distance of 480 kilometers. Hendrickx cautioned that the pursuit might not be over: Kosmos-2612 could return if it had enough fuel. He also pointed to four other Russian satellites launched alongside it — Kosmos-2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614 — that operate in similar orbits and probably have the same mission. Both ICEYE-X36 and ICEYE-X37 could be targets, he said.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trilateral peace talks with Russia to restart, says Zelenskyy
articles.body:
- A trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow will take place in November aiming to restart stalled Russia-Ukraine peace talks, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. “We are ready to talk. If it’s a territorial issue, it must be addressed at a leadership level. Other issues fall within the remit of the technical groups. All this can therefore be discussed in November,” the Ukrainian president said on Sunday in an interview. Zelenskyy also renewed his push for a meeting between him and Vladimir Putin, believing that Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war.
- Zelenskyy says that at the trilateral talks, Ukraine will not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced postwar neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into Nato despite the reticence of some members.
- Meanwhile, US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, have been fully restored, according to Zelenskyy. He told Ukraine’s TSN television channel that SpaceX’s Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420km/h since early on Saturday, after a meeting with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo. Starshield was throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.
- The US has been trying to pressure Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it says push energy prices higher. However, Zelenskyy has repeatedly said Kyiv will only stop the strikes if Moscow stops hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or if the US allows Ukraine to use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or if it supplies Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
- Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post.
- Russia’s defence ministry said on Sunday its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian forces also hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. Reuters could not confirm the reports.
- A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person. The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, regional governor Alexander Shuvayev said.
- The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova. Iotova opposes military aid to Ukraine and favours dialogue with Russia, while Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Kyiv. The vote was held amid security concerns after a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Ukraine raises its stalled Patriot request with Washington again after almost a month without Hegseth’s signature
articles.body:
Ukraine has waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 October. He ordered his team to raise it with Washington again. Two other US holds on Ukraine, on Starlink speeds and intelligence sharing, have been lifted, leaving the interceptors as the last one.
Russia keeps firing ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities and the power grid before winter, and Patriots are the only systems in Ukraine that reliably stop Iskander-M, Kinzhal, and Zircon missiles. Zelenskyy has told EU leaders Ukraine needs 300 interceptors to get through winter, diplomatic sources told Radio Svoboda. The holds came as Washington pressed Kyiv to stop striking Russian refineries, which Trump blames for high US fuel prices before the midterms.
Zelenskyy: almost a month waiting for Hegseth’s signature
Zelenskyy held a meeting on weapons supplies with Ukraine’s defense minister, foreign minister, and commander-in-chief. They reported on interceptors for air defense, above all for Patriot systems. Afterward, Zelenskyy wrote:
“We are working in several directions: with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. In particular, for almost a month we have been waiting for Mr. Hegseth’s signature on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I have instructed the team to discuss this with the American side once again.”
Talks with other countries continue, he added. The meeting also covered preparations for November’s Ramstein meeting of Ukraine’s allies, where Zelenskyy wants decisions already on the table carried out faster.
Allies’ missiles need US approval
Some of the transfers come from friendly countries and need Hegseth’s approval, because the US must sign off on any re-transfer of its missiles, a US official and three people familiar with the matter said on 19 October. Hegseth has neither refused nor approved them.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays
A Ukrainian official said in mid-October that only “a couple” of interceptors were left. Hegseth has said the US wants “our guys” to have “the most possible” interceptors, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted nothing was “being deliberately denied to Ukraine.”
Two of three US holds lifted

Full Starlink speeds returned on 24 October, and missile warnings resumed after his 20 October call with Rubio. articles.title: ‘Enough for Years’: Ihnat Says Patriot Missiles Used in Middle East Could Have Protected Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukraine could have had enough Patriot air defense missiles to sustain its systems for several years if a significant portion of the interceptors had not been expended in the Middle East, Yuriy Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said.
Speaking on the RBC-Ukraine podcast Tse Baza (“This Is the Basics”), Ihnat said Ukrainian forces had adapted their tactics for using the US-made Patriot systems throughout Russia’s full-scale war, learning to employ them in different combat scenarios while conserving expensive interceptor missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s approach differs significantly from that of other countries, Ihnat said. Ukrainian crews can deploy Patriot systems for ambushes rather than keeping them at fixed positions, such as airfields or military bases, and then relocate after engaging targets.
“For instance, rather than using the Patriot as a stationary asset – the way the Americans typically deploy it at airfields or bases – it can be used, in a sense, as a ‘roving’ system: set up an ambush, shoot down five aircraft, and then withdraw safely,” he said.
Ihnat also pointed to an incident in Russia’s Bryansk region as an example of the capabilities Ukrainian forces have demonstrated with the system.
Another key difference, he said, is ammunition use. Ukrainian crews have learned to use a single interceptor against a single target, while air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at one target.
‘Interceptors Still Not Coming’ – Zelensky Says US Has Yet to Authorize Patriot Deliveries
The Patriot system has three operating modes: automatic, semi-automatic and manual. Ihnat said that in automatic mode, the system can launch multiple interceptors at once.
Without sufficient combat experience, crews could end up firing an entire salvo from one launcher at a single target, including a relatively inexpensive Shahed drone.
“Because of this lack of experience, they might have fired an entire salvo of interceptors from a launcher at a single Shahed drone or a single ballistic missile,” Ihnat said.
He estimated that the number of interceptors expended in the Middle East could have kept Ukraine’s Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years.
“That is why we now find ourselves in the current crisis; the ammunition expended in the Middle East would have been enough to keep our Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years,” Ihnat said.
Notably, in March, a senior Ukrainian Air Force officer speaking to The Times criticized Gulf forces for using excessive numbers of expensive interceptor missiles against relatively cheap Iranian Shahed drones, saying Ukrainian crews typically use one or two missiles even against more complex targets.
Ukrainian officers said their battlefield experience has not been fully incorporated despite sharing operational data with allies.
They also described the March 1 incident in which Kuwaiti air defenses shot down three US F-15E fighter jets as “clear negligence,” arguing that better coordination could have prevented the friendly-fire incident.
During the first four days of the Iran war, the US and its allies reportedly fired more than 800 Patriot missiles – more than Ukraine received over three years of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has received just 24 Patriot air defense missiles from the US over the past 90 days, despite needing around 350 interceptors per month to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with ABC News.
Zelensky contrasted the limited deliveries to Ukraine with the roughly 2,000 partner-supplied interceptors fired during the first 84 hours of fighting in the Middle East.
Ukrainian officials have warned that the allocation of US-made Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles to the region is affecting supplies available to defend Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
On Oct. 16, Zelensky asked European leaders to provide 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter, warning that deliveries of just two to four missiles every few months were insufficient to counter Russian attacks.
He proposed that European countries with existing Patriot stocks help bridge the gap until new procurement arrangements and defense projects become operational.
However, efforts to secure missiles from European stockpiles have faced resistance. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Athens would not transfer PAC-2 missiles if doing so compromised Greece’s own defense capabilities in the Eastern Mediterranean.

articles.title: Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal
articles.body:
SpaceX founder Elon Musk says that if Ukraine fires through Starlink, Russia would be entitled to shoot the network down. That is why Starlink must remain a civilian operation and cannot be used for outright offensive strikes that would put its very existence at risk.
The warning lands in the middle of a fight over Musk’s own hand on that network. Weeks ago, his company unexpectedly throttled the service Ukraine’s drones depend on amid US President Donald Trump diesel deal with Russia, which led to the disruption of a few operations on the front.
The US Treasury authorized the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel, effectively suspending sanctions on that trade until 7 April 2027, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said on its website on 9 October.
The diesel deal combining intelligence halt and military Starlink, with pressure on Ukraine to make a quick peace deal, has angered both Democrats and Republicans ahead of the US elections on 3 November, where Democrats could win.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian official interprets Musk's talk of strikes as an attempt to build an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision.
A civilian network, or a target
Musk was responding to a post warning that if Starlink shifted from a civilian network into a military system, Russia could treat it as a target for retaliation, and that destroying satellites in orbit could scatter enough debris to make space unusable for years or centuries.
“An adversary blowing up Starlink satellites would create a domino effect of destruction that would generate a vast field of debris, making space unusable," he writes.
When the shield and the warnings failed together
Overnight into 14 October, SpaceX quietly capped the speed of Starshield, the military version Ukraine’s drones run on, without telling Kyiv. Ukrainian units said the limit broke a series of missions, with connections dropping mid-flight and leaving drones hard to control.
At the same time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine relies on the network for air defense, not attack, to intercept the Russian drones Moscow sends to its cities, and that once the speed was cut, his forces could no longer stop some of them as effectively as before.
Simultaneously, Ukraine's other American lifeline also went dark: for about three days, the US stopped passing the intelligence that warns of Russian ballistic launches. On 12 October, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before the air-raid alert reached people, with no advance data from partners. In a strike during that window, three people were killed in the capital, the sirens sounding only after the blasts.
A Ukrainian official sees alibi-building
Meanwhile, Andrii Kovalenko, the ex-head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, read Musk’s statement as self-protection rather than physics
“Musk, having taken responsibility for the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield for Ukraine, is now trying to build himself an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision,” he wrote.
He said that regardless of who was behind the idea of restricting Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine, it represents a strategic setback for the US in the long run, as it risks portraying the country as an unreliable partner that may fail to honor its commitments.
"Europe purchases around 60% of its imported weapons from the US. Trust in the US as a security guarantor directly supports sales for American defense companies. Moves like this only undermine that trust and encourage European countries to develop their own systems," he said.
The US has sent a message that its guarantees may not be reliable and that even paid-for services can be subject to political decisions, Kovalenko stressed.

articles.title: Plane parts for Russia’s air force, rubber for its industry—Voronezh’s factories came under drone attack
articles.body:
Drones attacked the VASO aircraft plant in Russia's Voronezh overnight on 26 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+ reported. The plant builds Il-96 airliners and parts for Russia's military transport planes. A synthetic-rubber plant was also reportedly hit and fires broke out across Voronezh, while another rubber plant in Tolyatti, farther east, reportedly came under attack again.
Ukraine keeps hitting the plants behind Russia's weapons, from Voronezh's missile chips to Urals titanium for warplanes. Each supplier knocked out of rhythm slows how fast Russia replaces the hardware it loses and keeps using against Ukraine.
What the Voronezh plant builds
Supernova+ described VASO as part of Ilyushin, which belongs to Russia's state-owned United Aircraft Corporation (UAC). The channel published a photo of fire and smoke at the site. The plant lies about 190 km from the Ukrainian border.
VASO makes pylons, engine nacelles, and flap rails for the Il-76MD-90A, a modernized military transport plane, and sends them to Ulyanovsk, UAC's press service said in 2024. "We have reached the production pace of Il-76MD-90A aircraft kits that our Ulyanovsk colleagues need," Igor Butyrin, who runs the plant's Il-76 program, stated at the time. In 2016, the plant built an Il-96-300 that UAC handed over to the Rossiya special flight detachment of Russia's presidential property office.
A rubber plant and a bridge on the list too
Supernova+ also named Voronezhsintezkauchuk, a plant of Russian petrochemical group Sibur that makes synthetic rubbers. The channel later reported a hit on the plant's industrial zone and claimed an attack on the city's Northern Bridge. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published footage of a drone arriving, reportedly at the rubber plant.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev declared a missile alert at 04:47 Kyiv time, but no source has named a missile type. Kyiv has not commented. Ukraine's Air Force, which launches Storm Shadow cruise missiles, and its Navy, which fires Neptunes, have posted nothing on Voronezh.
Earlier this month, Ukraine's Navy said it hit six Su-34 bombers in Voronezh Oblast with Neptunes. Storm Shadows reportedly struck an electronics plant in Oryol on 23 October and a battery plant in Yelets two days later.
Fires across the city
Gusev claimed air defenses downed 113 drones over the region, more than 70 of them over the city. He listed fires at several industrial enterprises, which he said caused no serious consequences, plus a business center, an apartment block, and a school stadium. Russian Telegram channel Astra published video of a drone hitting the Galereya Chizhova business center. Exilenova+ footage showed cars burning below apartment blocks.
Damage in residential districts may have come from downed drones or from Russian air-defense missiles falling back on the city. During a 23 October attack on Gorodets, in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Exilenova+ claimed a Pantsir air-defense missile hit a house.
Russia still parks its best bombers in the open. Ukraine has spent a year knocking out the air defenses that were supposed to protect them
Gusev also claimed two men were killed and 17 people injured, many of them on a train struck by drone debris. Russian Railways said five passengers were hurt at Somovo station and traffic on the line stopped. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses downed 290 drones over 15 regions and the Moscow area.
Tolyatti's rubber plant reportedly attacked again
Locals reported an attack on the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, Exilenova+ said. The city lies about 890 km from the front line. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the same plant on 24 October. Its synthetic rubbers go into solid fuel for Russia's tactical and ballistic missiles, among other uses.
Until Kyiv comments or satellite imagery shows the site, the damage at VASO stays unconfirmed, and so does any delay to Russia's Il-76 parts line.

articles.title: Iran to meet with Saudi, Pakistan, Turkey for security talks
articles.body:
Iran began talks on Monday with the three countries of the Mecca security pact, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, to discuss regional issues as the months-long Middle East war remains locked in a stalemate, state television reported.
The meeting, requested by Pakistan, opened in capital Tehran and focused on "regional cooperation, the US-Israeli aggression against Iran and its consequences", Iran's state broadcaster said.
"As agreed, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Bagheri Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei. He was also to be present at all the meetings.
The representatives of the pact met with Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, according to the photos shared by the presidential website.
A man cycles past an anti-Israeli billboard in Enghelab Square in Tehran. [Getty]
UN chief calls for 'maximum restraint' by Iran and US
United Nations chief Antonio Guterres demanded that the United States and Iran refrain from relaunching the war as both sides intensified threats.
"I want to send a loud and clear message: we need maximum restraint and diplomatic solutions," Guterres wrote in a post on X during a visit to Cairo.
"If the sabre-rattling we are witnessing now translates itself into a major mutual escalation, the situation in the region can get out of control," he warned. "And navigational rights and freedoms, in accordance with international law, must be fully restored in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab."
Egypt parliament authorises defensive support to Saudi
Egypt's parliament authorised on Monday sending military support to Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi attacks, following a request from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
The House of Representatives "approved authorising President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia", state newspaper Al-Ahram reported.
Tehran talks aim to stop regional escalation: Saudi Arabia
Discussions in Iran’s Tehran among the Mecca Pact states, Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish officials, and Iran aims to prevent further fighting in the region, Riyadh’s Foreign Ministry says.
"The kingdom emphasises the importance of opening channels for negotiation to prevent a resurgence of military escalation in the region, and to pave the way for an agreement that ends the crisis and secures peace and stability," it said in a statement.
Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
Earlier Iranian state media has announced that the meeting has begun.

Thousands of trucks remain stranded on both sides of the Iran-Pakistan border despite the resumption of limited overland trade between the two countries, southwest Pakistan business representatives told AFP on Monday.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the chamber of commerce for Gwadar city on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast, said the frontier with Iran was "only partially open" to trade, with a vast backlog of vehicles at the border.
There were "three to four thousand trucks on the Iranian side and two to three thousand trucks on the Pakistani side", Kalmati said.
Only certain vehicles were being allowed across the border to clear the backlog after a week-long closure, he said.
Iran's ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said on X on Sunday there were no restrictions on the Iranian side, including for the export of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).
He blamed the closures on "changes in the implementation of Pakistan's E-Form procedure for imports from Iran", which he said "have created a situation in which traders are effectively and literally unable to dispatch cargo from Iran to Pakistan".
UN probe accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
Jordan's Director of General Security announced that the suspects in the Karak church attack "are from one family—two brothers and their brother-in-law," adding that "they live near Hammoud village."
Five Palestinians, including a young girl, were killed Monday in Israeli airstrikes across the Gaza Strip, medical sources and first responders said.
Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said a total of 13 people had been killed and about 60 wounded by Israeli fire and airstrikes in Gaza in the past 24 hours.
"We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli airstrike targeting a camp for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Yunis," Bassal told AFP.
Israel's military told AFP it was "not aware" of any military activity in that area on Monday.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Yunis confirmed the three deaths.
"Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile," the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.

Gaza's civil defence said a fourth person was killed in an airstrike on a tent housing displaced Palestinians near Khan Yunis.
In Gaza City's Rimal neighbourhood, a third airstrike killed one and injured three, according to the city's Al-Shifa hospital.

Pakistan's powerful army chief Asim Munir travelled to Iran on Monday, the Pakistani military said, after Tehran announced talks in the Islamic republic on regional security.
"Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir ... is visiting Tehran, Iran for an official visit," the Pakistani military's media wing said in a statement without elaborating on the purpose of the trip, one of several made by the army chief to Iran since Pakistan became a mediator in attempts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said an operation in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage facility.
Spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X that the operation also aimed at cutting off the Houthis' supply lines between areas under their control and targeted rebel fortifications and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen.
Al-Malki said the coalition would continue to use "deterrent operational measures" to protect against the Houthis' "brutal attacks" inside the kingdom and in Yemen.
Oil spill off UAE widens, prompting more beach closures
An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

"We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli airstrike targeting a camp for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Yunis," Bassal told AFP.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Yunis confirmed the three deaths.
"Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile," the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.
The hospital identified the deceased as Hossam al-Zamli, Tamer Abu Sneima, and Jouri al-Soufi, a young girl. The Gaza education ministry gave her age as seven.
A security source in Gaza told AFP that "several tanks and military vehicles, accompanied by a military bulldozer, advanced on Monday morning into the area west of the Yellow Line in the eastern part of Deir al-Balah", in central Gaza.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said Monday that reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders over fresh action in the war with Iran were "entirely baseless".
Israel's Channel 12 reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive.
The premier dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterised it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu bloc's judgement on the eve of close elections.
"The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X, insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two.
In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received.
The outlet did not offer details of the directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain.
Katz stated "unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel's part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections".
Iran says outcome of Israeli elections 'makes no difference'
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference".
"It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls.
US says helped Gulf nations export 1.5 bn barrels of oil
US Central Command on Sunday said it helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the Strait of Hormuz since summer, bypassing an Iranian blockade.
"U.S. forces reach the milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer," CENTCOM said in a statement posted on X.
"More than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months," it added, stating that "over 95% of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz have sailed through safely".
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," said CENTCOM chief admiral Brad Cooper, who was visiting US troops in Hormuz.
Israel presses ahead with West Bank attack as election nears
The Israeli military pressed ahead Sunday with a massive military attack on the occupied West Bank that has displaced thousands of Palestinians and placed major restrictions on movement.
The attack, focused on the city of Hebron, came as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
In new measures, the army said that most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Israel’s elections on Tuesday.
The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said.
The meeting follows eight months of war in the Middle East and recent US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran.
"As agreed, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defence minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday.
"The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X.

Spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X that the operation also aimed at cutting off the Houthis' supply lines between areas under their control and targeted rebel fortifications and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen.
Al-Malki said the coalition would continue to use "deterrent operational measures" to protect against the Houthis' "brutal attacks" inside the kingdom and in Yemen.
Oil spill off UAE widens, prompting more beach closures
An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts to stop oil leaking from a tanker underway. [Getty]
Israeli strike in Gaza kills three including child
Three Palestinians, including a young girl, were killed Monday in an Israeli airstrike on a camp for displaced people in the southern Gaza Strip, medical sources and first responders said.
Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said a total of 11 people had been killed and 50 wounded by Israeli fire and airstrikes in Gaza over the past 24 hours.
"We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli airstrike targeting a camp for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Yunis," Bassal told AFP.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Yunis confirmed the three deaths.
"Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile," the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.
The hospital identified the deceased as Hossam al-Zamli, Tamer Abu Sneima, and Jouri al-Soufi, a young girl. The Gaza education ministry gave her age as seven.
A security source in Gaza told AFP that "several tanks and military vehicles, accompanied by a military bulldozer, advanced on Monday morning into the area west of the Yellow Line in the eastern part of Deir al-Balah", in central Gaza.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said Monday that reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders over fresh action in the war with Iran were "entirely baseless".
Israel's Channel 12 reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive.
The premier dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterised it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu bloc's judgement on the eve of close elections.
"The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X, insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two.
In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received.
The outlet did not offer details of the directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain.
Katz stated "unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel's part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections".
Iran says outcome of Israeli elections 'makes no difference'
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference".
"It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls.
US says helped Gulf nations export 1.5 bn barrels of oil
US Central Command on Sunday said it helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the Strait of Hormuz since summer, bypassing an Iranian blockade.
"U.S. forces reach the milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer," CENTCOM said in a statement posted on X.
"More than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months," it added, stating that "over 95% of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz have sailed through safely".
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," said CENTCOM chief admiral Brad Cooper, who was visiting US troops in Hormuz.
Israel presses ahead with West Bank attack as election nears
The Israeli military pressed ahead Sunday with a massive military attack on the occupied West Bank that has displaced thousands of Palestinians and placed major restrictions on movement.
The attack, focused on the city of Hebron, came as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
In new measures, the army said that most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Israel’s elections on Tuesday.
The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said.
The meeting follows eight months of war in the Middle East and recent US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran.
"As agreed, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defence minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday.
"The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X.

articles.title: US holding up air defense missiles for Ukraine for nearly a month, Zelensky says
articles.body:
US holding up air defense missiles for Ukraine for nearly a month, Zelensky says
Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 26.
The delay, first reported by the Kyiv Independent, affects missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for. Ukraine relies on Patriot systems to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to stop, making timely deliveries critical to the country's air defenses.
"I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again," Zelensky said.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States, a senior Ukrainian military official said.
Zelensky has said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that the batch awaiting Hegseth's approval was "significant."
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Kyiv has also had problems with military-grade Starlink service, Starshield, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the use of interceptor drones to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as another example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.

articles.title: Russia’s Energia Plant Struck by Storm Shadow Missiles, Fire Breaks Out
articles.body:
The Energia plant, which manufactures power sources for cruise and ballistic missiles, including those used in Russia’s Iskander missile systems, has been struck by Storm Shadow cruise missiles.
The Exilenova+ community published a video of the strike.
Eyewitness videos show at least three impacts on the facility’s grounds. A fire broke out at the site. According to Militarnyi’s analysis, Workshop No. 4 was hit.
This is the second attack using Storm Shadow cruise missiles against a Russian facility involved in ballistic missile production. On October 23, the Proton defense plant in the city of Oryol was hit.
Shortly before the strike, it was reported that the United Kingdom would provide Ukraine with an additional batch of Storm Shadow cruise missiles. They are intended to help Ukraine’s Defense Forces disrupt Russian military operations targeting Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
The Energia plant in Yelets, Lipetsk region, is one of Russia’s largest manufacturers of autonomous power sources for aircraft, naval and river vessels, missile and artillery systems, radio equipment, and emergency communication systems.
The facility specializes in developing and manufacturing electrochemical power sources, including primary cells, rechargeable batteries, and specialized power sources for military equipment. Since 2013, it has been mass-producing lithium-ion batteries in various sizes and electrochemical configurations. The plant also manufactures electrochemical capacitors and nickel-cadmium batteries.
In particular, Energia manufactures power sources for universal glide and correction modules (UMPK) installed on Russian aerial bombs. These modules convert unguided aerial munitions into guided glide bombs, which Russian forces use extensively to strike Ukraine.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the plant also participates in the production chain for UMPB D-30SN universal inter-service glide munitions. As part of this cooperation, it supplies 9B-287 batteries to JSC PEMZ Molot.
In addition to aerial munitions, the plant supplies power sources for Russian cruise and ballistic missiles. It manufactures 9B280-1 power cells for 9M727 cruise missiles used by the Iskander-K system and 9B283 thermal batteries for 9M723 ballistic missiles used by the Iskander-M system. It also supplies KhIT 59I6 power sources for RM-48U ballistic missiles launched by the S-400 system.
The plant also participates in the production chain for 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles, manufacturing T-657 chemical power sources. For Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, the facility supplies 9-ZV-7760.00.01.00 onboard batteries.
The facility also produces power sources for surface-to-air weapons. According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the plant manufactures 9B281 batteries for 95Ya6 guided missiles used by the Pantsir system.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces have attacked the Energia plant several times. The first strike took place on May 23, 2025, when Ukrainian drones destroyed one of its production workshops. The facility was attacked again by strike drones on the nights of May 24 and July 3 and 15. On January 4, 2026, the plant was attacked again, sparking a fire on its grounds.
Later, satellite imagery confirmed damage to a production workshop that, according to OSINT researchers, had been hit by a Ukrainian missile.
