articles.title: With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
articles.body:
With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
Anton, a soldier with Ukraine's 112th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, stands beside an Oktava electronic warfare system outside Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Jakub Laichter / The Kyiv Independent)
In a cornfield north of Kyiv, pieces of blackened metal are scattered among rows of dried stalks. They are all that remains of a Russian Geran attack drone, shot down by Ukrainian fighter jets as it flew toward the capital during one of Russia's mass aerial assaults.
"Last year we had so many of them," says Halyna Prykhodko, deputy director of the Branytsia division of the agricultural company Zemlya i Volya. "We found three, four, even five in the fields."
Above Prykhodko's land is one of the routes Russian drones take to approach Kyiv. Ukrainian forces try to intercept them over the countryside before they reach the capital and crash into homes and critical infrastructure.
Since late summer, Russia has been terrorizing Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.
Defending Kyiv requires a layered system of air defenses, from sophisticated missile systems and fighter jets, to mobile machine-gun and interceptor-drone units.
Over two days, the Kyiv Independent accompanied soldiers of the 112th Territorial Defense Brigade at several positions outside the capital, observing how their units hunt incoming Russian drones and adapt to Russia's evolving weapons and tactics.
read also
A Coordinated Effort
Radar stations and other detection systems are the first link in a wider system coordinating Kyiv's air defenses. They track approaching Russian drones, relaying information through command posts that direct the response of individual units.
"Every unit is subordinate to its own combat command post," says Senior Sgt. Serhii, who leads a mobile fire group. His surname is withheld for security reasons. "It gathers all the information from higher commanders and other groups, and issues orders to each group."
His three-man mobile fire group is armed with a truck-mounted Browning M2HB heavy machine gun, a SkyLock targeting system, and thermal-imaging equipment.
One soldier mans the machine gun, another commands the group and operates observation equipment, and a third covers them with an assault rifle.
When a drone approaches their sector, the soldiers receive information about its direction, altitude, and distance. They must then locate it using their observation equipment, adjusting for discrepancies between the target's reported and actual positions.
The crews operate within designated firing sectors, limiting where they can engage targets to avoid endangering civilians or friendly aircraft.
The gunner must account for the target's speed, distance, and direction of travel, calculating how far ahead to fire so that the bullets and aircraft arrive at the same time at the same point.
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is."
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is," explains Volodymyr, a soldier in the mobile fire group.
Repeated practice and experience are essential, he says, until judging a target's movement and calculating the necessary lead become almost instinctive.
Weather conditions, altitude, and speed further determine whether a target can be engaged. Thermal-imaging equipment helps soldiers detect drones at night, but cloud cover can obscure them, and faster, higher-flying jet-powered drones present greater difficulties.
"Within five seconds I have to engage it as much as I possibly can," says Volodymyr.
It's his birthday when the Kyiv Independent visits the mobile fire group. He spends it at the group's position, surrounded by fields.
"Grand celebrations," he jokes when asked how he plans to mark the occasion. "I've got these wide fields. I can walk over there, walk over here. Not many options."
Other crews use shoulder-fired missiles to engage targets beyond the reach of machine guns.
"Bodya," another soldier, operates a Soviet-designed 9K38 Igla man-portable air-defense system, which uses a heat-seeking missile to pursue aerial targets. Even with a guided missile, soldiers have very little time to engage a fast-moving target.
With conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones, Bodya explains, the sound of the approaching engine can provide some warning. Jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, however, travel much faster, and by the time crews hear one, it can be almost on top of them. Some targets pass through his unit's engagement area in as little as 20 seconds, he says.
Ukraine primarily uses systems such as NASAMS and IRIS-T against Russian cruise missiles, aircraft, and other aerial threats, but to intercept ballistic missiles, Ukraine has to rely on its scarce arsenal of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Interceptor drones have become another means of bringing down Russian targets, particularly conventional Shahed-type drones, without expending costly surface-to-air missiles.
A soldier with the call sign Gendalf shows the Kyiv Independent the Sting interceptor drones operated by his unit. Equipped with cameras, the interceptor drones transmit live video to operators who guide them toward incoming Russian drones.
But Russia's increasing use of jet-powered drones, some capable of flying at about 600 kilometers per hour, has created a problem for operators like Gendalf.
read also
Reaching about 320 kilometers per hour at full throttle, the conventional rotary-wing interceptors available to his unit struggle to match the jet-powered drones' speed, he says.
Beyond these different means of kinetic interception, electronic warfare provides another layer of defense by targeting the signals Russian drones rely on.
At an electronic warfare unit, Maj. "Secret," the brigade's head of electronic warfare and electronic intelligence, demonstrates a sensitive spectrum analyzer developed within the brigade. The device allows soldiers to detect and analyze radio-frequency signals, including those transmitted by Russian drones.
"Here we see all the signals that are nearby," he says, pointing to a series of transmissions appearing on the screen.
"First, we have to detect the signals and understand what we need to jam," Secret explains. "What matters is that there's data exchange," he says. "I can see the flow of data in real time."
Electronic warfare can disrupt an incoming drone in two main ways. First, jamming interferes with the signals it relies on, potentially severing its connection to an operator. Second, spoofing feeds the aircraft false information, potentially misleading its navigation or diverting it from its intended course.
But disrupting a communication link does not necessarily stop an attack. Some drones can continue toward preprogrammed coordinates without further instructions, meaning electronic warfare can only complement kinetic interception.
The Race to Adapt
One of the most significant developments since late summer has been Russia's growing use of jet-powered Geran drones. Some variants fly at altitudes of 5 to 6 kilometers, beyond the effective range of mobile machine-gun crews.
Soldiers defending Kyiv also describe Russian drones changing their routes and maneuvering when Ukrainian interceptors approach. Some newer Geran variants carry cameras and mesh radios that allow operators to receive a live video feed and redirect the aircraft during flight.
Ukraine is adapting its interceptors in response.
On Oct. 18, Andrii Hrytseniuk, then head of Brave1, Ukraine's government-backed defense innovation initiative, said seven types of Ukrainian interceptors had already successfully intercepted jet-powered Russian drones. Twenty-two teams joined the effort to develop high-speed systems, including models powered by miniature jet engines.
The government had ordered more than 1,000 of these new interceptors, but production is still being expanded, he said.
A similar race is playing out in electronic warfare.
read also
The electronic warfare unit studies the wreckage of drones brought down by Ukrainian forces and examines their electronics to understand how Russia is adapting its weapons.
"We dig around in these burned-out remains, looking at how everything is configured, what electronic components they use, which antennas, which parts," Secret says.
Russian forces continually modify the communications systems carried by their drones, forcing Ukrainian units to adapt the equipment used to detect and disrupt their signals, Secret says.
"They change the signal's form, and we adapt to that form," he says.
Equipment purchased just a year earlier may no longer be as effective against modified drones. But older systems cannot simply be discarded, since Russian forces can still use the technologies those systems were designed to counter.
Secret compares the process to constantly renovating an apartment without ever being able to remove the old wallpaper.
"Every six months, every three months, the fashion changes," he says. "And without stripping off the old wallpaper, you have to glue new wallpaper over it."
"And the wallpaper is, first of all, extremely expensive and very difficult to obtain," he adds.
Russia is also changing its tactics to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
"They're coming in from all directions," one air defense officer says, describing a hypothetical attack involving 15 drones.
Most might be shot down, but a handful could get through. He believes Russian forces study the results to identify routes for subsequent strikes.
"They're probing, feeling things out," he says. "Then, yes, everything's clear, a mass attack."
Meanwhile, the pace of attacks is placing a growing strain on the soldiers defending Kyiv.
"The tactic is constant exhaustion, non-stop," says Serhii.
During particularly intense periods, he says, his men have worked 20-hour shifts, leaving just four hours for sleep. And during the hours spent on alert, some targets remain beyond their reach.
One machine gunner recalls a jet-powered Russian drone passing so high overhead that he could barely make it out.
"I couldn't even see it with my eyes," he says.
But he knows how to calculate the lead needed to hit a moving drone.
"I'd tear it apart if it were lower," he says.

articles.title: Guided bombs on Izium, strikes on Zaporizhzhia: Russian overnight attacks wound six, later strikes kill three
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 140 drones, including Shahed and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoys, and four missiles overnight on 26 October, the Ukrainian Air Force reported. The missiles were one Kh-31P anti-radiation missile and three Kh-59/69 air-launched guided missiles, launched from occupied parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts.
Jet-powered Shaheds are becoming a larger part of Russia’s aerial campaign, challenging Ukraine’s air defenses and prompting efforts to develop faster interceptors. Alongside guided bomb attacks and strikes on energy infrastructure, these attacks add to the pressure on Ukraine’s defenses as winter approaches, and Ukraine says Russia has a plan for it.
Air defenses downed or suppressed 112 drones, including 56 of the 70 jet-powered Shaheds, and three Kh-59/69 missiles, according to preliminary Air Force figures. Hits were recorded at 15 locations, and debris fell at four more.
Four wounded in Zaporizhzhia
Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia overnight wounded two women aged 22 and 30, and two men aged 40 and 61, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. The strikes damaged the windows of a hotel and two buses, a private house, and four outbuildings, and three cars caught fire. The oblast administration had first reported one wounded.
Later in the morning, Russian forces hit a shopping center building that had already closed, the administration said. The building caught fire. According to preliminary information, no one was hurt.
Guided bombs hit two districts of Izium
At about 02:40 on 26 October, Russian forces struck two districts of Izium in Kharkiv Oblast with guided aerial bombs, and three people needed medical help, the city military administration said, as Suspilne Kharkiv reported. More than 10 private houses and a youth sports school were damaged, and several streets lost power and internet.
Russia struck a burning Odesa Oblast plant twice more as firefighters worked
Overnight, a Russian attack destroyed an industrial enterprise in Odesa Oblast and set it on fire, the DSNS reported. As firefighters put out the blaze, Russian forces struck the site twice more. The rescuers were in shelter and were not hurt, but fire equipment was damaged. At another address, four garages were damaged and a car was destroyed. The oblast administration said there were no casualties.
Energy facility hit in Khmelnytskyi Oblast
On the evening of 25 October, a Russian attack damaged an energy facility in Kamianets-Podilskyi district of Khmelnytskyi Oblast, causing emergency power outages, the oblast administration said. Windows were also damaged in two residential buildings. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, Russian drones attacked the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast more than 10 times overnight, damaging a high-rise and an administrative building, the oblast administration reported. No one was hurt. Mykolaiv Oblast also came under Shahed attack overnight, with no casualties, according to its administration.
The attack continued into the day. On the morning of 26 October, a Russian strike hit a civilian infrastructure site in Vinnytsia, the oblast administration said. Preliminary reports showed no casualties.
Strikes on 26 October kill three in Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts
On 26 October, Russian aircraft dropped four guided bombs on homes and shops in the center of Yasnohirka near Kramatorsk, killing one person and wounding 10, the DSNS said. Among the wounded is a 13-year-old girl, Donetsk oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. In Sloviansk, a Russian airstrike destroyed a private house, and rescuers recovered the body of its owner, the DSNS said.
A Russian drone strike on Pavlohrad in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed one person and injured seven, including two children, the DSNS said. The injured include two 10-year-old girls, the oblast administration said.
Six hurt in Kharkiv Oblast over the past day
Over the past 24 hours, Russian attacks hurt six people in Kharkiv Oblast, oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. In Kharkiv, a 60-year-old man and a 14-year-old boy suffered acute stress reactions. Two women aged 51 and 71 were wounded in Krasnopavlivka. His count lists two wounded men in Izium, aged 72 and 52, while the city administration says three people there needed medical help. Russian attacks also set fire to a house in Kotliary, a production building in Vilshany, a building in Derhachi, a house in Mykolaivka, and a site in Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district, the DSNS reported.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day injured five people, the National Police said, including two women aged 76 and 56 hit by a drone in Sumy community.
On 25 October: two killed in Kherson and Donetsk oblasts
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian attacks on 25 October injured a man at a hangar in Pryluky district and a woman at a grain store in the Novhorod-Siverskyi area, the oblast administration said. Drones also damaged a school in a village of Koriukivka community, and a strike destroyed 700 metric tons of potatoes at an enterprise in Mena community, the administration said. A large warehouse fire broke out in Koriukivka district, the DSNS said.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and wounded eight in the 24 hours to 06:00 on 26 October, the oblast administration reported. On 25 October, a Russian drone strike on a minibus in Kherson’s Central district killed one person and wounded six, the administration said after one more man sought medical help. Police said the minibus was hit by an FPV drone.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces killed one person in Kramatorsk and wounded 10 across the oblast on 25 October, Filashkin said. Russia hit Kramatorsk with drones and six KAB-250 guided bombs, and 18 hits on Sloviansk wounded four, police said.
On 25 October, a Russian attack on Synelnykove district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast sent a 30-year-old man to hospital, the oblast administration said. In Vinnytsia, the number of people injured in the Russian attack on the morning of 25 October rose to seven, two of them hospitalized, the DSNS said. In Uman, an 86-year-old woman burned in the Russian attack on 21 October died in hospital, the Cherkasy oblast administration said.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian plant supplying batteries for ballistic missiles and glide bombs with Storm Shadow missiles, OSINT reports – another hit on Russia’s weapons supply chain
articles.body:
Ukraine reportedly struck the Energiya plant in Yelets, Russia’s Lipetsk Oblast, with UK-supplied Storm Shadow cruise missiles on 25 October, according to the OSINT channel Exilenova+.
The plant manufactures batteries and power sources used in Russian weapons systems, including Iskander and Kinzhal missiles, air defense systems, and guided aerial bombs, according to Exilenova+. The reported strike targeted a facility that supplies components for Russia’s military-industrial complex as Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
According to Exilenova+, Energiya is Russia's only producer of batteries for glide bomb planning and correction modules, as well as a key supplier of specialized power sources for several missile systems.
Storm Shadow missiles reportedly hit plant buildings
Exilenova+ reported multiple missile impacts at the Energiya plant, sharing footage and photos showing explosions, thick smoke, and fires at the facility. The channel later reported that the plant was still burning and that the surrounding area had been cordoned off, with numerous ambulances heading to the site.
Dnipro OSINT reported that at least two missiles struck two buildings at the plant.
The Energiya plant is located in Yelets, approximately 250 km (150 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Plant produces components for Russian weapons
According to Dnipro OSINT, Energiya specializes in developing and manufacturing chemical power sources. Its products are used in several Russian weapons systems, including Iskander-K and Iskander-M missiles, Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, Zircon missiles, and Pantsir air defense systems. The plant also supplies power sources for UMPB D-30SN guided aerial bombs.
Many of these weapons are used in Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, killing civilians and destroying residential buildings and civilian infrastructure.
UN food aid warehouse in Dnipro struck by Russian Iskander missile, impacting supplies for 130,000 people
Dnipro OSINT said the plant had been attacked at least four times before the 25 October strike.
The strike comes two days after a reported Ukrainian Storm Shadow missile attack on the Proton electronics plant in Russia’s Oryol on 23 October, which produces electronic components used in Russian weapons systems, including Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.

articles.title: Ex-Mossad chief Barnea intended for Iran to see Israel's operations to overwhelm IRGC
articles.body:
When the Mossad took the stunning move of publishing multiple videos in real time of its agents acting against the regime within Iran in June 2025, one of the main reasons was to overwhelm and confuse the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), former Mossad chief David Barnea has revealed.
Leaked on Sunday from comments he made to a closed audience at the Priority Summit this past Thursday.
On June 13, 2025, the Mossad released sensational and rare video footage of its co-lead role with the air force in Israel’s preemptive strike on Iran’s ballistic missiles and air defenses.
Three videos showed the Mossad targeting ballistic missile targets, air defense targets, and general preparations for the attacks (with the agents’ faces covered up).
From the perspective of the videos, it appeared that the Mossad used drones from inside Iran to attack various targets.
Iran had previously accused the Mossad of using drones to attack the Karaj facility in June 2021 as well as other operations.
Mossad's warehouse of drones used to sabotage Iran
It was later confirmed that the Mossad used an entire warehouse of drones to attack and sabotage Iran, along with helping with a large number of remote-controlled vehicles attacking regime targets, and a significant number of human agents on the ground also assisting in assassinations.
Although far more information was quickly publicized about the IDF’s actions, these videos gave readers a rare front-row and real-time seat into what normally were entirely clandestine operations which the Mossad would not even admit to.
Barnea said at the Priority Summit that the video was deliberately published to trigger mass arrests and make it more difficult for the IRGC to identify actual Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said in a video which Yediot Ahronot shared, and regarding which the Jerusalem Post confirmed the authenticity. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” adding that Iran did release all of the detainees.
IRGC arrested over 20,000 people on second day of war
The former Mossad chief said that the IRGC arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said, emphasizing that the IRGC would have no way of knowing who was a real agent with such a vast number of detainees,
Barnea added that many of those arrested or executed by the IRGC as “Mossad agents” had nothing to do with the agency.
In addition, he said that nearly all of the Mossad agents were never caught, and at the end of the June 2025 operation, he even publicly taunted the IRGC, issuing a statement, “We will [continue to] be there, like we have been there.”
His explanation may close the book on the unexplained mystery of why the Mossad would have risked broadcasting some of its agents’ actions in real time during the June 2025 operation.
In September 2025, the Post reported exclusively that dozens of Mossad women penetrated Iran and were on the ground performing a variety of kinds of operations during Israel’s attacks on Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs in June 2025.
While the Mossad does not want to bring too much attention to any one sub-group of potential spies, the Post’s impression was that the Mossad women of 2025 were doing more of every kind of spy role as compared to their sisters of yesterday.
In that same September report, the Post noted that Barnea sent hundreds of Mossad agents, or individuals being run by agents, into operations in Iran simultaneously. All of the varying groups of staff were highly coordinated.
The spy chief directed a project leading to a diverse spectrum of all of the different kinds of agents and backgrounds of those agents one could imagine.
On top of actual Israeli Mossad agents, the spy service has reached new levels in recruiting and training local dissident Iranian agents to act against the ayatollahs’ regime, the Post reported at the time.
While the early 2026 war with Iran is viewed by many as a mixed bag, the June 2025 war was viewed as the most successful Israeli operation of the last three years, along with the exploding beepers used against Hezbollah.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
Russian forces have launched an overnight attack targeting the Ukrainian military logistics network in the northeastern Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said. The list of targets included three hubs used to store and redistribute supplies for the armed forces and dual-use goods, the ministry said in a statement published on Sunday.
Separately, Russia also struck a bulk freighter in the Black Sea that was carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port city of Chernomorsk, the ministry added. The attacks were part of a broader operation that involved strikes on Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used to support the military, as well as drone storages and launch sites in a total of 159 locations over the past 24 hours.
Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on the city of Kharkov, adding that an “industrial facility” was among the targets.
Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistics facilities in response to Kiev’s continued attacks on the Russian civilian and energy infrastructure. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the Ukrainian attacks as “terrorist acts” aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the nation’s air defense systems intercepted a total of 532 Ukrainian drones during Sunday night alone. The drones were used in attempted attacks on more than two dozen Russian regions, the ministry stated.
Ukraine’s tactics have led to tension between Kiev and Washington. US President Donald Trump stated recently it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” and find a new person to negotiate peace instead of Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago. The American president also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a deal with Moscow and criticized him for continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s repeated requests to stop.
Zelensky has said that Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches twice in one week in October. He maintained however, that cooperation between Kiev and Washington had not been suspended, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
In the meantime, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Kiev of abusing his company’s Starlink civilian satellite internet network to launch offensive drone strikes. According to the US-based businessman, a “loophole” allowing the Ukrainian forces to do so was closed.

articles.title: From China to Germany: HUR identified foreign equipment at Russian ballistic missile production facilities
articles.body:
From China to Germany: HUR identified foreign equipment at Russian ballistic missile production facilities
Kyiv • UNN
HUR released data on 30 units of foreign equipment in the Russian military-industrial complex. They are used to produce Iskanders, Kinz hals, and Zircons.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine published information on 30 units of foreign-made technological equipment used by Russian enterprises to manufacture ballistic missiles and their components. This was reported by UNN with reference to data from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Despite sanctions restrictions, Russia’s military-industrial complex continues to depend on foreign technologies.
Details
On the War&Sanctions portal, Ukrainian intelligence published data on equipment manufactured in China, Germany, Taiwan, the United States, Turkey, Switzerland, and Italy, which is used by Russian enterprises to manufacture missiles, altimeters, aerodynamic control surfaces, gyroscopes, and other weapons components. The Main Directorate of Intelligence notes that Russia is still unable to fully replace the industrial equipment of the world’s leading manufacturers with domestic analogues.
At the same time, the number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones, is increasing at Russian defense enterprises. Chinese equipment also depends on foreign components, including European, Japanese, and Taiwanese numerical control systems, servomotors, high-precision spindles, bearings, and measurement systems.
Among the equipment identified by intelligence:
-  the GX-650 five-axis universal machining center manufactured by the Chinese company Hyper Machine Tool, which is used by the Votkinsk Plant. The enterprise manufactures 9M723 "Iskander-M" ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 "Kinzhal" air-launched ballistic missile; 
-  turning and milling machining centers manufactured by the Chinese company Shtral, which are used by the "PEMZ \"Molot\"" enterprise to produce electronic equipment units for "Iskander-M" missiles; 
-  measurement equipment manufactured by the German company Rohde & Schwarz, installed at the "UPKB \"Detal\"" enterprise, which manufactures altimeters for "Zircon" missiles. 
The Main Directorate of Intelligence emphasizes that, in order to limit Russia’s ability to continue producing weapons, it is necessary to strengthen international control over the supply of industrial equipment and components. In particular, intelligence calls for checking the end users of products and the actual locations where they are used, controlling the supply of spare parts, software, and consumables, and regularly auditing distributors and intermediaries.
They propose paying particular attention to investigating cases in which foreign products reach Russia’s military-industrial complex and identifying their supply chains.
In addition, Ukrainian intelligence calls for restricting the supply of numerical control systems, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers whose equipment is delivered to Russian defense industry enterprises.
We remind you
On October 24, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy imposed sanctions against those involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: 'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
articles.body:
'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

articles.title: High-level delegation in Iran in push to avert flare-up of conflict with US
articles.body:
High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent renewed fighting between Iran and the US and Israel as rhetoric sharpens on both sides.
Security officials and diplomats at Monday’s meeting were expected to discuss how Iran could persuade the Houthis in Yemen to end their crippling missile and drone attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. With fighting raging across Yemen, the Houthis claimed to have closed Riyadh airport and inflicted heavy damage on the Saudi economy.
The officials were also understood to be discussing Iran’s possible inclusion in a new security pact involving Islamic countries.
The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, Ibrahim Kalın, were to meet Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.
The three countries signed a defence agreement in Mecca in August. Some in Iran feared the deal was constructed to challenge Tehran, but the signatory countries have insisted it is simply a mutual defence pact.
The balance between exploring a new long-term security architecture and demanding Iran start to compromise in the conflicts in which it is engaged will be critical. It is possible the two sides came to the meeting with different priorities.
The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role, and the US-Iran conflict has potentially reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.
No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attack on Iran either last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the meeting could pave the way for broader regional cooperation on security based on shared interest.
“The events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, have shown that sustainable and reliable security in our region will only be possible by building trust and cooperation among the countries of the region,” he said.
Javad Zarif, a former foreign minister and long-term advocate of a regional security alliance called for “a comprehensive regional network based on non-aggression, mutual trust building, and shared prosperity”.
“Regional security is not imported, it must be created by the people of this very region together,” he said.
He published his message alongside an image of verses 103 and 159 from Surah Ali ‘Imran, the third chapter of the Qur’an. The verses emphasise being saved from a fiery pit by avoiding division, fostering unity, seeking forgiveness and consulting others.
The meeting takes place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators, it was confirmed, spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that modern-day US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity in the region.
The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners also increasingly argue Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb, ending the fatwa on the possession of a weapon of mass destruction.
A pact likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

articles.title: France works with 10 European nations to increase strength as nuclear deterrent - report
articles.body:
France is working with 10 other European nations to expand its capacity as a nuclear weapons power on the continent and a deterrent to Russian aggression as Europe's faith in the US's commitment to its security wanes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday morning.
The 'forward deterrence' plan involves the creation of new infrastructure, communications, early-warning and intelligence-sharing links with France's allies as well as deployments of French nuclear-enabled Rafale jet fighters across Europe.
The UK, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have all joined the project with varying degrees of involvement since French President Emmanuel Macron announced it in March.
“We don’t have any plans to put nuclear weapons on Finnish soil in peacetime. But we do have plans for creating a strategic dilemma for Russia,” said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
“We felt it would be useful for our security to get information, to be involved in it. We don’t know where this is going to end, it’s probably a 10- to 15-years process.”
Instead of the countries all gathering together to work on the plan, France has been holding individual talks, leading European partner nations to constantly communicate with each other to compare what the French have told them, WSJ cited senior defense officials as saying.
European countries doubt US reliability
The plan comes as faith in the US's willingness to defend Europe wanes. Doubts over if the US would risk nuclear war over the defense of a European ally have increased as US President Donald Trump strikes energy deals with Russian President Vladimir Putin and puts increasing pressure on Ukraine, WSJ wrote.
France claims that the French program is more credible as the safety of European countries is of far more direct importance.
“There is one difference between France and the US–we share the same geography, we are part and parcel of the same continent, we have economic and sociological continuity with our neighbors writ large,” Chatel, Macron’s adviser, said at the Warsaw Security Conference.
In his speech announcing the initiative in March, Macron emphasized that France's vital interests were directly affected by its allies.
“Could we consider that the survival of our closest partners may be put at risk without it affecting our vital interests?” Macron said.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said that the plan was not intended to "replace anything. It supplements the nuclear guarantees that were already there" from the US.
Program under French control
Macron also announced that France would resume making nuclear devices for the first time in decades and that the size of its stockpile would become confidential. Despite the involvement of other countries, the nuclear force will be entirely under French control, WSJ wrote.
“The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” one government minister of another European nation said.
According to the WSJ report, the decision was made to make the forward deterrence strategy acceptable across the political spectrum, including to the far-right party of Marine LePen who is polling ahead in the race for the presidency in next spring's elections.

articles.title: Why is the Middle East waiting out the Trump presidency?
articles.body:
There appears to be little prospect of lasting peace between Iran and the United States while Donald Trump remains in the White House. This is a view that an increasing number of serious actors across the region now seem to share. Eight months into Iran war, Washington has neither broken Tehran’s resolve nor found a clear path out. The president’s own remarks point to a narrowing set of options. Trump told TIME he does not believe peace with Iran is ever possible, a striking admission from the leader still expected to negotiate one.
Tehran, for its part, has set conditions it knows this administration cannot meet, insisting that sanctions and threats be lifted before talks resume and that not a single gram of enriched uranium leaves the country. Neither side is bargaining towards a settlement. Each is waiting for the political ground beneath the other to shift.
Trump’s problem is that the ground is shifting under him first, as the 3rd November midterms approach with his approval rating near 39 per cent and crude trading above 110 dollars a barrel. The House has voted three times to restrict his war powers in Iran, with Republican candidates in competitive seats now campaigning openly on ending the war to lower petrol prices. Facing a likely defeat, the president has promised no strikes before polling day while Central Command has reportedly been told to prepare for resuming major combat operations. Therefore, it is quite likely that Trump may order striking Iran even before the mid-term day.
Analysts have noted that a Republican defeat could strengthen this incentive, as a president with little left to lose at the ballot box faces fewer costs for escalation. Yet such strikes would do little damage control, since a Politico survey found 46 per cent of voters said ending the war before the election would not change their vote at all. Iran has meanwhile fortified its nuclear sites and warned that regional energy infrastructure would be targeted, so any parting blow risks sending oil prices even higher.
The president’s own inner circle appears to have read the same numbers and is quietly positioning itself for the aftermath. Vice President JD Vance, reportedly sceptical from the outset, has kept his distance and this week declined to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, his chief rival for 2028, spent the same week in India on a trip devoted largely to trade rather than Iran.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, by contrast, made an unannounced visit to Israel a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu, keeping himself firmly in the frame. Commentators suggested as early as April that Hegseth was being set up as the fall guy should the war end badly. His visibility since has only reinforced that impression.
The Gulf states have reached the same conclusion. They are hedging accordingly against an American policy they no longer trust to last. The UAE joined the campaign against Iran in February, yet they opened a backchannel with Iranians lately after the realization that it is better to deal directly instead of relying on the US. Moreover, the UAE, by the virtue of being in support of the Saudis vis-à-vis Yemen, is trying to find a diplomatic way to lower tensions. It signals a striking reversal in barely eight months. Having absorbed thousands of Iranian missiles and drones, Abu Dhabi appears to be securing its own understandings before Washington’s next round begins.
Yemen shows how the burden is being shifted, since the United States has twice rebuffed Saudi requests for airstrikes against the Houthis and says it will not take kinetic action for now. Instead, the UAE has reportedly agreed to resume funding anti-Houthi forces in southern Yemen. This is an arrangement that lets Washington stay out while a partner carries the fight on its behalf.
Iran’s strategy rests on patience and its leaders appear confident they can absorb another year or so of American pressure before the political weather in Washington changes. Its posture towards Saudi Arabia fits this reading more closely than the images of burning airports suggest. Houthi strikes have killed at least 19 people at Saudi airports, and the Wall Street Journal has reported Revolutionary Guard officers helping to direct them. Yet within days of the deadliest attack, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Riyadh to offer mediation with the Houthis and insist the crisis had no military solution.
The aim is not to destroy Saudi infrastructure but to convince the kingdom that American protection is unreliable and that any opening to Israel will carry a heavy price. Riyadh has begun to absorb that lesson, but the pressure is unlikely to ease while Trump remains in office and Tehran sees no reason to settle.
The real question is how Israel reacts to all this, both during the remainder of Netanyahu’s tenure and after it. Trump has endorsed Netanyahu so he can help “finish the job” against Iran, and Israel has reportedly asked that any renewed strikes wait until after its 27 October vote. Polls give Netanyahu’s coalition fewer than 50 of the 61 seats needed to govern, raising the prospect of a weakened caretaker with every reason to keep the Iran file burning.
A successor led by Gadi Eisenkot would hardly soften Israel’s line on the Iranian nuclear programme, but it might be less willing to tie national strategy to American president’s fortunes. Should Israel strike alone after an American exit, Gulf hedging would only accelerate and normalisation with Riyadh would recede further from view.
Tehran and the Gulf have made their calculations. Both now wait for a different figure in the Oval Office.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine Offered US 3 Ways to Stop Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries
articles.body:
Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries at the request of US President Donald Trump’s team, but only if one of three conditions was met, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with journalist Alla Mazur.
Speaking on the TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week) program, Zelensky said that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries could not have a significant impact on global prices, noting that Russia accounts for only 2% of global diesel exports, while the remaining 98% comes from other exporters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“How can one reach an ‘energy truce’ with the Russians? You might be hated, but you should at least be respected as an adversary. They must respect Ukraine – and our strength. He [Putin] inflicts great pain upon us, and we respond. It is a matter of justice,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine had proposed three possible ways to resolve the dispute to the American side. However, none of the proposals had been implemented, which is why Ukraine continues to strike Russian oil refineries, he said.
“I said: if you want us to stop hitting diesel facilities and refineries, then they [the Russians] must stop striking our power infrastructure. That is fair – an ‘energy truce.’ A second option: you enable Starlink coverage over Russia, and we show you the locations of their ballistic missile launchers. We want to destroy them.
Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine
“The third option is this: if you won’t enable Starlink for us – which is entirely up to you – and you’ve said that Musk doesn’t want to, then give us something that doesn’t depend on Musk or Putin: missiles for the Patriot systems,” Zelensky said.
He added that Ukraine had received none of the three proposed forms of support.
“That is why the reaction is what it is – we are fighting for our lives,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky warns against lifting sanctions before negotiations
Zelensky also said that lifting sanctions against Russia should be considered only as part of the process of ending the war, rather than as a precondition for negotiations.
“I would not want us to approach the meeting of the three leaders – Ukraine, the United States, and Russia – having already lifted all sanctions against the Russian Federation. This is a crucial point. Sanctions were imposed in response to aggression, not as a price for the mere opportunity to talk.”
He said he had conveyed this position to the American delegation, cautioning that Russia could benefit from sanctions relief before any agreement on ending the war had been reached.
He warned that once sanctions were lifted, restoring them could prove difficult, requiring Ukraine and its partners to rebuild international support for a new round of restrictions.
“Without sanctions, we could reach a point in the trilateral dialogue where the future remains uncertain, yet the sanctions have already been removed,” Zelensky added.
He said that the international community had adopted more than 20 separate sanctions packages against Russia and questioned whether the same political resolve could be mobilized again if Moscow failed to follow through on its commitments.
“I do not want us to find ourselves without any leverage – lacking sanctions, funds, or frozen assets – when we sit down with Putin. Because then, as Mr. Trump put it, we would truly have very few cards left in our deck,” Zelensky added.
Ukraine, US, EU and NATO plan security talks in Brussels
Zelensky also said Ukraine, the United States, the European Union and NATO planned to hold a broad meeting in Brussels this week to discuss security issues, guarantees and European integration.
According to the president, the format of the discussions had expanded following a visit by the American delegation to St. Petersburg and a preliminary briefing to Ukraine.
The talks had initially been limited in scope, but the Americans were now seeking a broader discussion, Zelensky said.
“The Americans [after Oslo] went to St. Petersburg; we received a ‘brief’ from them, but now they want more than just a ‘brief’ – they want a broad discussion regarding security, guarantees, the EU, and involvement,” he added.
The meeting was expected to take place this week, tentatively on Tuesday or Wednesday. Zelensky said the participants would include representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU at the presidential level, as well as NATO, represented by the alliance’s secretary-general.

articles.title: German firm develops low-cost interceptor to stop mass drone attacks
articles.body:
- Helsing unveiled Contra, an AI-controlled air defense system, with two new interceptors: the jet-powered AD-1 Inferno and the Mach 2.5 AD-2 Ambush.
- The company said it will mass-produce the interceptors at prices well below existing missiles but did not disclose customers, costs or timelines.
German defense AI company Helsing on Oct. 26 unveiled Contra, an autonomous, AI-controlled air defense system designed to protect countries against large-scale drone and missile attacks, along with two new interceptor missiles, the jet-powered AD-1 Inferno and the rocket-powered AD-2 Ambush, the company announced.
Helsing said Contra fuses data from sensors and weapons into a single air picture so it can detect and engage hundreds or even thousands of incoming drones and missiles at the same time, while operators keep control over decisions and target priorities through the company’s Altra command-and-control software. The company did not name any customers, say when the system could enter service, or disclose whether the interceptors have been flight-tested.
The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor that can loiter in the air, operate in swarms and re-engage targets if it misses on the first pass, which Helsing said makes it suited to fast jet-powered drones. The AD-2 Ambush uses a solid rocket motor for quick intercepts, reaching Mach 2.5 with a range of more than 20 km (12 miles), and is intended for higher-flying threats.
Both missiles are launched from containers, receive course updates in flight from Contra’s ground radar stations, and carry their own radar seeker to find the target in the final phase of flight, which allows them to work at night and in bad weather. Helsing said the system can also take in third-party weapons such as other interceptors, counter-drone lasers, guns and net-based systems within days, and that it is already demonstrating several such integrations to military customers.
The company said it will mass-produce the interceptors at its Resilience Factories at prices significantly lower than existing interceptor missiles, though it did not give a unit cost.
“Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high – affordable and at industrial scale,” said Niklas Köhler, Helsing’s co-founder and president.
Helsing tied the launch to Russia’s growing production of jet-powered attack drones and cruise missiles, citing recent intelligence reports that output of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones alone has reached 4,000 units a month and that Russia is building additional launch sites that put parts of the European Union within range.
Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Munich, Helsing began as a software company and has since moved into hardware, including the HX-2 strike drone and the CA-1 Europa uncrewed combat aircraft. In July, it raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation and selected West Virginia for its first U.S. Resilience Factory, and on Oct. 20 it announced a commercial partnership with Swiss-Dutch drone and missile maker Destinus.

articles.body:
Zelensky says US warnings on ballistic strikes have fully resumed
- US warnings of imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes have fully resumed, Zelensky said, helping Ukraine’s air defences after recent problems.
- He said Starshield internet speeds returned to up to 420kmh after earlier throttling, following talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.

articles.title: ‘Within 96 hours’: US ready for major Iran strikes if Trump gives order
articles.body:
American forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch a major new military offensive against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump, two U.S. officials told CNN in a report published Monday. The necessary forces are already deployed in the region, but Trump has not made a final decision on whether to authorize the operation. 
The potential campaign would be considerably broader than the limited strikes carried out against Iranian military assets in recent months. U.S. Central Command and the Pentagon have developed an extensive list of possible targets, including nuclear facilities, military installations and energy infrastructure.
Unlike earlier operations focused on missile launchers, radar installations and other equipment that Iran could replace relatively quickly, the new plans envision a more substantial campaign against the Iranian regime's military capabilities and infrastructure.
"It will be a big effort," one American official said.
Current and former U.S. officials familiar with the planning believe Trump could order renewed large-scale operations before the end of the year, with several considering an attack after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections the more likely scenario.
However, the president has not committed to military action. Officials cautioned that Trump has previously appeared close to approving major operations before reversing course.
The White House declined to comment on the report. A senior Pentagon official emphasized that developing military options is part of the department's responsibility and does not, by itself, indicate that the president has ordered an attack.
Trump rejected Netanyahu's push for strikes before Israeli election
The American military preparations are unfolding against the backdrop of a disagreement between Washington and Jerusalem over the timing of renewed attacks on Iran.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pressing for additional military action against Tehran, but senior American officials, including Trump, have urged Israel to postpone its plans until the two countries are prepared to conduct coordinated operations, according to two U.S. officials and an Israeli security source.
An Israeli security source said Netanyahu had sought Trump's approval for a joint attack before Israel's October 27 election, but the president refused.
According to that source, one factor behind Trump's decision was a warning from IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir to Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Zamir reportedly warned that an attack at such a sensitive moment could provoke Iranian retaliation, disrupt the Israeli election and potentially force its postponement.
Israel had been preparing for possible additional strikes over the past week and sought American assistance to support those operations. But officials in Washington reportedly instructed Israel to hold off, indicating that a joint offensive could follow after the U.S. midterms.
Israel appears to have accepted the delay for now, partly because of its dependence on American missile defense assistance. Israeli interceptor supplies have come under considerable strain during the conflict, and any renewed confrontation with Iran would likely trigger another wave of missile attacks.
The reported disagreement also comes amid growing scrutiny of Netanyahu's intentions regarding Iran. Recent U.S. intelligence assessments suggest that the prime minister and his allies have not established a clearly defined strategic objective beyond continuing to weaken the Iranian regime and demonstrating military progress, according to a source familiar with those assessments.
Netanyahu, however, has publicly articulated a more ambitious goal. Speaking at an IDF officers' graduation ceremony last week, he said he had instructed the military, Mossad and other security agencies to work toward overthrowing the Iranian regime.
Intelligence warns of immediate Iranian retaliation
American intelligence assessments indicate that both Iran and the Houthis in Yemen are taking the possibility of renewed U.S. and Israeli attacks seriously.
According to sources familiar with the assessments, Tehran and the Houthis would likely respond quickly to a new offensive by attacking American military personnel and facilities across the Middle East, potentially extending their operations beyond the region.
Intelligence officials do not currently believe Iran or the Houthis are likely to launch a major preemptive attack against American forces or Israel. However, they assess that both would be prepared to retaliate if Iran came under attack first.
An unclassified October 23 memorandum from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Iran had intensified efforts to target American personnel. The intelligence assessment indicated that some Iranian plots had reached advanced stages, including in countries outside the Middle East.
The growing threat is already affecting the American diplomatic and military presence in the region.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been placed under an ordered departure for certain personnel, and officials expect additional diplomatic missions to face similar restrictions or reductions in staffing.
Meanwhile, nonessential American military personnel who were expected to deploy to the Middle East as part of upcoming troop rotations have reportedly been told their assignments have been canceled.
The measures reflect concern that any new confrontation could quickly extend beyond Iranian territory and place American personnel across the region at risk.
The Strait of Hormuz adds pressure for military action
Another factor influencing Washington's calculations is the increasingly difficult situation in the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with international shipping routes.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, visited the strait Sunday as American forces continued enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and assisting commercial shipping through the area.
Cooper flew over the waterway by helicopter to assess conditions and met service members involved in clearing Iranian naval mines.
Although more oil tankers have begun passing through the strait, energy prices remain elevated, partly because of continuing concerns about Iranian attacks on shipping.
One American official described the existing situation around the strait as unsustainable over the long term. Without a diplomatic breakthrough, restoring more predictable maritime traffic could become another reason for Trump to authorize renewed military operations.
Yet significant uncertainty remains about what a new offensive would accomplish. Iranian forces have gained experience with American tactics, potentially complicating efforts to destroy intended targets. U.S. officials also acknowledge unresolved questions about Washington's broader strategy for ending the conflict.
For now, the military preparations continue while the political decision remains outstanding. Israel has reportedly delayed its immediate plans, Iran is preparing for possible renewed attacks, and American forces are positioned to act within days if Trump gives the order.
The timetable is therefore not a countdown to war. It represents the military's readiness to carry out a presidential decision that has yet to be made.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
articles.body:

Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
Europe’s answer to Russia’s growing jet-drone arsenal is taking shape around a simple idea: use AI to coordinate mass interceptions, then kill fast threats with cheaper missiles instead of burning through million-euro air-defense rounds.
European defense technology company Helsing has unveiled Contra, a new AI-controlled air-defense system built to counter large-scale drone and missile attacks, alongside two new interceptors designed to chase down fast jet-powered UAVs and cruise missiles, according to a press releaseHelsing shared with UNITED24 Media on October 26.
The system is particularly relevant to Ukraine, which is already facing a growing Russian arsenal of jet-powered Geran drones.
Helsing says recent intelligence assessments indicate Russia has sharply increased production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 systems, with output reportedly reaching as many as 4,000 units per month while Moscow expands the number of launch sites.
Built for the jet-Shahed problem
Contra is designed for exactly that kind of saturation threat.
According to Helsing, the system can detect and coordinate engagements against hundreds or even thousands of incoming drones and missiles at the same time by combining multiple sensors and weapons into a single air picture. Its sensor architecture can include radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic systems, while the Altra command-and-control platform keeps human operators in control of targeting priorities and decisions.
The architecture is also intended to remain functional under battlefield disruption, including jamming, broken communications links, and the loss of individual nodes.
For Ukraine, that matters because Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran variants are substantially faster than conventional Shahed-type drones, increasing the pressure on both interceptor drones and traditional surface-to-air missile systems.
Two new interceptors for two different threats
At the center of Contra are two Helsing-developed interceptors.
The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor intended to fill the gap between slower electric or propeller-driven drone interceptors and traditional missiles that are too expensive to fire in large numbers. Helsing says AD-1 can loiter after launch, operate in swarms, and re-engage targets in flight while receiving midcourse updates from Contra ground radars.
Company specifications list a maximum speed above 700 km/h and an operating altitude exceeding 9,000 meters.
The AD-2 Ambush, meanwhile, uses a solid rocket motor and is intended for faster and higher-flying threats. Helsing says it is designed to defeat high-speed one-way drones and subsonic cruise missiles beyond AD-1’s reach.
In its announcement, Helsing said AD-2 can reach roughly Mach 2.5 and engage targets beyond 20 kilometers.
Both interceptors use onboard radar seekers for terminal guidance, allowing them to operate in darkness, cloud, and fog—conditions where cheaper optical or infrared seekers can struggle. Helsing’s technical brief specifically emphasizes that the radar seekers are intended to maintain performance when visibility is poor.
Built for mass attacks, not one-off shots
Helsing is positioning Contra as more than a closed missile system.
The architecture is designed to integrate third-party weapons—including other interceptors, anti-drone lasers, guns, and even net-based systems—within days.
That would allow operators to choose different weapons for different targets rather than firing an expensive missile at every incoming drone.
The same command architecture is intended to protect population centers, borders, military bases, and maneuvering forces, with the sensor and weapon mix changing depending on the mission.
Helsing says both AD-1 and AD-2 are intended for mass production through separate European supply chains, reducing dependence on a single production line.
Niklas Köhler, Helsing co-founder and president, framed the system around the cost problem now confronting Ukraine and Europe.
“Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high—affordable and at industrial scale,” he said.
Ukraine already fighting the threat Contra was built for
For Ukraine, that dilemma is no longer theoretical.
Russia is moving beyond slower propeller-driven Shahed-type drones toward faster jet-powered systems such as the Geran-4 and Geran-5, forcing Ukraine to field increasingly fast interceptor drones, fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missiles, and other layers of defense.
The challenge is not simply destroying one fast drone, but doing so repeatedly during mass attacks without exhausting expensive interceptor stocks.
Contra is Helsing’s attempt to turn those different defensive layers into one coordinated network—using AI to manage the air picture while cheaper, mass-produced interceptors take on threats that would otherwise consume far more expensive missiles.
If Russia continues scaling jet-powered drone production at the rate Helsing describes, that cost equation could become one of the defining problems for both Ukrainian and European air defense.
Earlier, German defense company Helsing’s Ukraine-proven HX-2 drone performed successfully during tests with US soldiers in Lithuania.

articles.title: Ukrainian strike reportedly damages chemical plant in Russia's Voronezh
articles.body:
A chemical plant producing dual-use goods in the southwestern Russian city of Voronezh was likely hit in a Ukrainian drone attack, independent Russian media outlet Astra said on Oct. 26.
Astra cited videos taken by local residents showing black smoke rising over the territory of the plant, known as Voronezhsintezkauchuk, owned by Russia's largest petrochemical company, Sibur. The plant produces over 385,000 metric tons of synthetic rubbers and thermoplastic elastomers per year, including those used to manufacture tires for military aircraft and heavy wheeled vehicles, according to Astra.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev said fires broke out at several unspecified industrial facilities without serious consequences. According to the Russian governor, two people were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured in the attack on Voronezh. He added that the attack also sparked fires in other places, including a business center, an apartment building, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative in the city.
Gusev claimed that Russian air defenses had downed 113 Ukrainian drones over Voronezh and several districts of the region overnight and on the morning of Oct. 26, with over 70 of them heading toward the regional capital.
Videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel exilenova+ appear to show several drone strikes and burning buildings in what seems to be Voronezh. It is not clear whether the reported drones were affected by Russian air defense fire.
Neither Ukrainian nor Russian officials have confirmed the attack on Voronezhsintezkauchuk. Ukrainian defense company Fire Point claimed that its FP-1 deep-strike drones had been used in the attack on the chemical plant. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claim. Verifying reports of attacks inside Russia has become difficult due to Moscow's digital censorship.
The reported attack comes as Ukraine has intensified its long-range strikes inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories since the summer, hitting targets such as oil refineries, military-industrial plants, and airfields, aimed at degrading Russia's military-industrial capacity.
Ukraine previously reported hitting Voronezhsintezkauchuk in September. Ukraine's General Staff said at the time that the facility was involved in the production of solid rocket propellant, including for Iskander ballistic missiles.

articles.title: UK and France Hold One of Their Largest Airborne Exercises in 20 Years
articles.body:
The United Kingdom and France have conducted the large-scale Rhino Titan military exercise in Germany, involving more than 2,500 troops.
Sky News reported this, citing the UK Ministry of Defence.
The seven-week exercise took place at the Sennelager training area in Germany. Its purpose was to test British and French units’ readiness to deploy rapidly and defend NATO territory against a potential attack.
One of the key stages involved parachuting around 600 British and French troops from four Royal Air Force A400M Atlas transport aircraft.
According to the UK Ministry of Defence, this was one of the United Kingdom’s largest airborne operations in the past two decades.
During the exercise, troops practiced parachuting personnel and dropping specialized equipment from low altitudes on a scale not previously attempted in this way.
The main UK contingent was provided by the 16 Air Assault Brigade, which serves as the UK’s Global Response Force and maintains a high state of readiness.
Under the exercise scenario, troops faced a simulated adversary that made extensive use of drones and electronic warfare systems.
Three Royal Air Force Chinook transport helicopters also took part. Their crews practiced airlifting a casualty reception station.
Brig. Ed Cartwright, commander of the 16 Air Assault Brigade, said the exercise allowed troops to rehearse a realistic scenario involving the defense of NATO territory against an adversary using drones and electronic warfare.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting emphasized that modern threats require new approaches to warfare.
“Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend NATO territory,” Streeting said.
British troops announced preparations for Rhino Titan in spring 2026. The Royal Artillery publication reported plans for a large-scale airborne operation in Germany as part of the Year of Air Manoeuvre program.
The exercise follows training conducted by the two countries on October 20-21, simulating a nuclear airstrike involving Rafale and Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets.
Militarnyi previously reported on joint exercises involving British and French paratroopers during Exercise Orion 26, held in France from February 23 to March 3.

articles.body:
German defence company Helsing has presented the AD-1 Inferno jet-powered interceptor drone, designed to counter high-speed strike UAVs and cruise missiles.
Militarnyi reports this from a presentation by the company’s co-founder, Gundbert Scherf, in Berlin.
The AD-1 Inferno is powered by a jet engine and can patrol a designated area of airspace while waiting for targets, operate as part of a swarm, and make repeated interception attempts.
During the midcourse phase, the interceptor receives guidance commands from radar stations, then uses its own radar seeker to engage the target in the terminal phase.
According to the developers, this enables the interception of aerial targets regardless of weather conditions or time of day, including at night.
During the presentation, Helsing representatives emphasized that modern aerial threats require interception systems capable of operating at altitudes of up to 9–10 km.
AD-1 Inferno is container-launched. According to the manufacturer, a single container can hold around 20 interceptors.
Standard trucks or rail can transport these containers, which should simplify deployment of the air defense system.
The AD-1 Inferno is being developed as one of the components of Contra, a new autonomous air defense system that Helsing also unveiled on October 26.
The system uses artificial intelligence to fuse data from various sensors and coordinate effectors. According to the company, it is designed to track and intercept hundreds or even thousands of aerial targets simultaneously.
At the core of Contra is the Altra command-and-control platform, which automates system operations while allowing operators to retain control over decision-making and target prioritization.
Production is planned to be held at Helsing Resilience Factories. According to the developers, the interceptors are intended to be significantly cheaper than conventional SAMs.
Helsing is also the developer of the HX-2 AI strike drones. In February 2025, the company announced an order to produce 6,000 drones for Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign-made equipment used by Russian ballistic missile manufacturers
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign-made equipment used by Russian ballistic missile manufacturers
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 30 items of foreign-made technological equipment used by Russian firms involved in the production of ballistic missiles and their components.
Source: War&Sanctions portal
Quote from the DIU: "Today we are publishing [details of] 30 items of technological equipment manufactured in China, Germany, Taiwan, the US, Türkiye, Switzerland and Italy which are used by Russian factories producing ballistic missiles and their components, including altimeters, aerodynamic rudders, gyroscopes, and so on."
DIU noted an increase in the number of Chinese machine tools and machining centres, particularly five-axis ones.
Quote: "It is important to note that Chinese machine tools use European, Japanese and Taiwanese components – CNC systems, servo drives, high-precision spindles and bearings, measuring and rotary systems, linear guides, thermal stabilisation and machining process control devices, etc."
Details: The list includes the GX-650 five-axis universal machining centre made by the Chinese manufacturer Hyper Machine Tool, which is used by the Votkinsk Plant, a manufacturer of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and the missile body of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
The list also includes turning and milling machining centres by the Chinese manufacturer Shtral, which are used in the production processes at PEMZ Molot JSC. The company manufactures electronic equipment units for Iskander-M missiles.
In addition, measuring equipment from the German firm Rohde & Schwarz has been installed at UPKB Detal, a company that manufactures altimeters for Zircon missiles.
DIU stressed the need to tighten control over the end users of the equipment, in particular by conducting on-site inspections at the locations where it is installed. The intelligence agency also urged that the supply of spare parts, software, consumables and maintenance be monitored.
In particular, they propose checking distributors and intermediaries, investigating cases of equipment that ends up in the Russian defence industry, and restricting the supply of CNC systems and other components to Chinese manufacturers whose products are used by Russian defence firms.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that DIU had released data on 13 items of foreign technological equipment used to produce Kometa navigation modules for Russian missiles and drones.
- DIU has also revealed details of the components of the Russian Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile and the companies involved in its production.
