Drones Strike Russia’s Titanium Giant Supplying Su-34 Fighters and Iskander Missiles
Drones struck the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Russia’s Perm region overnight on October 25, targeting a major titanium production facility supplying materials used in Russian military aircraft and missile systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack took place in Berezniki, where AVISMA operates as part of VSMPO-AVISMA, Russia’s largest titanium producer. The facility manufactures titanium sponge, a key raw material used in aircraft engines, fighter jets, and missile components. Footage of the reported strike was published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Perm region Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed the drone attack on October 25, claiming Russian air defenses intercepted 11 drones. He acknowledged minor damage to an industrial facility and reported that five employees had been injured. According to Makhonin, the facility continued operating.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), VSMPO-AVISMA produced approximately 33,500 metric tons of titanium sponge in 2024, accounting for roughly 96% of Russia’s total production.
The corporation supplies titanium alloys to Russian aircraft manufacturers Sukhoi and Irkut, which produce Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35 fighter jets. Its products are also used in Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has identified VSMPO-AVISMA as a supplier involved in the production chains of Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35S fighter jets.
The company also supplies Russia’s missile industry, including the Votkinsk Machine Building Plant, which manufactures Iskander ballistic missiles and Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The reported strike follows Ukrainian attacks on two Russian defense-related facilities on October 24. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed strikes on the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Orel and the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in the Samara region, both linked to Russia’s cruise and ballistic missile production.

articles.title: Putin May Use Ukraine Peace Talks to Demand NATO Retreat to Its 1997 Footprint
articles.body:

Putin May Use Ukraine Peace Talks to Demand NATO Retreat to Its 1997 Footprint
Russia is expected to use a new round of Ukraine peace talks to press for concessions that could weaken NATO’s eastern defenses, including a possible demand that the alliance roll back its military footprint to 1997 levels, The Telegraph reported on October 26.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said European countries should join negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States because Europe would be central to any eventual agreement.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
But diplomatic sources told The Telegraph that Moscow also sees European participation as an opportunity to revive its longstanding demands over NATO expansion—something Russian leader Vladimir Putin has repeatedly described as a “root cause” of the war.
One likely Russian demand would be to reduce NATO’s military presence to where it stood before former Eastern Bloc states joined the alliance. In practice, that could mean pressure for NATO forces to withdraw from Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Finland—all countries that border Russia.
The Kremlin has previously suggested that Putin could show flexibility on other issues if Moscow’s core demands are accepted, including major restrictions on Ukraine’s sovereignty and NATO’s presence in Eastern Europe.
Russia agreed last week to take part in technical three-way talks in Abu Dhabi next month after a lengthy pause in US-mediated negotiations.
Ushakov played down expectations for an immediate breakthrough, calling the meeting a “trial run.”
Previous negotiations failed to produce a ceasefire, in part because Moscow continued demanding that Ukraine surrender territory in Donbas that Russian forces have not captured.
Moscow also appears to believe Washington could pressure Kyiv into accepting such terms.
“Before, it seemed after Anchorage, that the US administration might be able to dictate something and force Kyiv to comply. But so far, this hasn’t really worked out. That’s because it’s not enough to talk only to Kyiv; we need to talk to the whole of Europe, which fully supports Kyiv, ” Ushakov said.
Ukrainian and European officials have indicated they are willing to discuss the “wider context of post-war security arrangements in Europe” during the Abu Dhabi talks.
The proposal was reportedly delivered by US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff during a three-hour meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg last week.
Despite Moscow’s renewed interest in negotiations, European officials say their opposition to Russia’s NATO demands has not changed.
“Our position remains the same as in January 2022,” one European official said.
At the time, NATO agreed that Russia’s security concerns could be discussed but rejected Moscow’s demand that the alliance withdraw troops and nuclear capabilities from its eastern members.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the upcoming trilateral talks would not themselves end the war but could focus on more limited agreements, including ceasefires covering energy infrastructure and grain exports as well as prisoner exchanges.
Previously, Putin ordered an escalation of sabotage operations against NATO countries, potentially setting the stage for a new wave of hybrid attacks across Europe.

articles.title: Zelenskiy says US fully resumes warnings on ballistic strikes
articles.body:
KYIV, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues.
Speaking to Ukraine’s TSN television channel, he said SpaceX’s Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420 kilometres per hour since early on Saturday morning, after it had been throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.
Zelenskiy said he discussed both issues in a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, casting the changes as results of that meeting.
The US has pressed Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it argues added to high energy prices, a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran and US midterm elections next month.
Zelenskiy said that in order for Kyiv to halt the strikes, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or the US should allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
Speaking about the upcoming technical talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in November, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced post-war neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into NATO despite the reticence of some members.
Zelenskiy also renewed his push for a trilateral US-brokered meeting between him and Vladimir Putin.
The Ukrainian leader has long argued Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war or meaningfully discuss core issues, such as the fate of the nearly 20% of Ukraine that Russia occupies.
“The issue of territories is a red line that can be discussed exclusively at the level of leaders,” Zelenskiy said.
(Reporting by Max Hunder, Bogdan Kochubey and Jekaterīna Golubkova; Editing by Chris Reese)

articles.title: Turkey warns Washington against renewed strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Turkey warns Washington against renewed strikes on Iran
TEHRAN– Turkey has warned the United States against launching fresh military strikes on Iran, saying a new attack would widen the conflict across West Asia and that diplomacy remains the only viable path toward ending the war.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan delivered the message on October 23 after meeting with his counterparts from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in Istanbul. He said the eight countries shared the view that renewed military action against Iran would further destabilize the region.
“We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region,” Fidan said at a joint press conference.
“A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment,” he added, stressing that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to bring the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran to an end.
The meeting brought together foreign ministers from the so-called Regional Four (R4) and the European Union’s E3, alongside Italy, in the first collective gathering of the group in this format.
Discussions focused on the war involving Iran, the risk of further regional escalation, attacks on Saudi Arabia attributed to Yemen’s Ansarallah movement, and the conflict in Ukraine.
The meeting came amid growing reports that Washington was considering renewed military action against Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, raising concerns among regional and European governments about the prospect of a wider confrontation.
European powers call for de-escalation
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also underscored the need for a diplomatic solution, saying the conflict had continued for too long and imposed an excessive burden on the British public.
 
“The very clear message” is that “diplomacy, dialogue and de-escalation has to be the answer to this conflict,” Miliband told broadcaster ITN. “Frankly, this conflict has gone on too long, the British people have suffered too much from it and we cannot afford months more of it.”
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned that further escalation would leave all sides worse off and push oil prices higher, highlighting the potential consequences of a prolonged conflict for global energy markets.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France and Britain were prepared to engage in talks with Tehran to address concerns over Iran’s nuclear program.
The statements reflect mounting concern among European governments that renewed hostilities could deepen instability across West Asia, disrupt energy supplies and carry significant economic consequences beyond the region.
The diplomatic push came after The New York Times reported on October 21 that US and Israeli military officials had drawn up detailed plans for renewed strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections.
Citing US officials, the newspaper reported that potential targets could include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone capabilities.
The report intensified concerns over the possibility of another military campaign against Iran and the risk that attacks on critical infrastructure could trigger a broader cycle of retaliation.
Iranian media citing officials that a possible Iranian response to renewed US-Israeli attacks could extend beyond conventional military targets to include undersea cables, data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure in West Asia owned wholly or partly by US investors and commercial interests.
Such scenarios underscore the potential for a wider conflict to affect critical digital infrastructure and economic assets, alongside its more immediate military and energy consequences.
According to Reuters, Fidan said the Istanbul meeting had also addressed possible parameters for preventing the conflict from spreading further, although he did not disclose details of the discussions.

articles.title: GUR discloses data on foreign tech equipment used by Russian ballistic missile makers
articles.body:
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (GUR) published data on the War&Sanctions portal regarding three dozen units of foreign-made technological equipment used by cooperation enterprises producing Russian ballistic armaments, the GUR press service reported.
"The Russian military-industrial complex retains a significant dependence on foreign technologies. In particular, despite all efforts, Russia is still unable to replace industrial equipment from global manufacturers with localized analogs. Today we are publishing 30 units of technological equipment of Chinese, German, Taiwanese, American, Turkish, Swiss, and Italian manufacture used by Russian factories producing ballistic missiles and their components – altimeters, aerodynamic rudders, gyroscopes, etc. Characteristic is the growing number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones," the message on Telegram reads.
It is noted that Chinese machine tools utilize European, Japanese, and Taiwanese components – CNC systems, servo drives, high-precision spindles and bearings, measuring and rotary systems, linear guides, thermal stabilization tools, and machining process control systems, among others.
The publication notably includes a 5-axis universal machining center GX-650 manufactured by Hyper Machine Tool (PRC), used by Votkinsk Plant – a manufacturer of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile; Shtral (PRC) turning and milling machining centers involved in the production processes of JSC PEMZ Molot, which produces electronic equipment units for Iskander-M missiles; and measuring equipment from German manufacturer Rohde & Schwarz installed at UPKB Detal, which produces altimeters for Zircon missiles.
GUR reminded that in order to deprive the aggressor of the capability to continue the war, it is necessary, in particular: to strengthen end-user control and the actual location of product use, including introducing on-site inspections by authorized representatives at the declared equipment installation address; and to extend enhanced control procedures to spare parts, components, technical fluids, consumables, software, updates, and maintenance required for equipment operation.
GUR also noted that it is necessary to regularly conduct audits of distributors, dealers, and other intermediaries, especially those supplying to high-risk jurisdictions, as well as to identify signs of re-export or end-user changes, investigate cases where a manufacturer's products are detected in the Russian military-industrial complex, establish their supply chains, and take measures to halt further deliveries through relevant intermediaries.
In addition, it is necessary to restrict deliveries of CNCs, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers that supply their equipment to Russian military-industrial complex enterprises, the message states.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill four and injure 28, authorities say
articles.body:
Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russia has launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine over the past week.
Russian strikes on Ukraine's eastern Dnipro region on Saturday night left four people dead and 22 injured, authorities have announced, with a separate attack on Vinnytsia in west-central Ukraine injuring another six people.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said Russian forces had targeted the Dnipro area with drones and aerial bombs, striking three districts more than 20 times.
The attacks damaged infrastructure in Dnipro city and destroyed private homes, apartment buildings, stores and cars in the Synelnykivskyi district, he said. A private home was also damaged in the Nikopol district, he added.
In a post on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone had also hit a high-rise apartment building in Vinnytsia, while a hypermarket had been targeted in Kharkiv in the northeast of the country.
"In Kharkiv, the Russians first struck a home improvement hypermarket and then carried out a cynical double-tap strike on the emergency services that arrived at the scene," he wrote, adding that an unspecified number of emergency responders had been injured.
The Ukrainian leader also reported overnight strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, including a thermal power plant and substations.
According to Zelenskyy, Russia has launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine over the past week.
Ukrainian forces hit back on Saturday and overnight with their own strikes against Russian targets, including army radar stations, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
Ukraine's military also struck command posts as well as Russian "personnel concentrations," per the General Staff.
"Striking radars creates gaps in the enemy’s radar coverage and expands the Defence Forces of Ukraine’s ability to employ unmanned systems at all levels," it said.
Starlink access restored
It comes after Kyiv announced on Saturday that its forces had re-established a "stable" connection to Elon Musk's Starlink network amid a dispute with the US.
"The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient," Zelenskyy said. "This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered 'shaheds.'"
Starlink, and its military version Starshield, have proved crucial to the Ukrainian military's operations as it has continued to battle Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

articles.title: Trump rules out Iran strike Sunday as tensions mount across Middle East
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch an attack on Iran that day, even as tensions between Washington and Tehran continued to simmer, American military forces maintained a heightened presence in the Strait of Hormuz and the State Department ordered some embassy personnel to leave Saudi Arabia.
"There will be no attack on Iran today," Trump told reporters, offering a temporary assurance amid mounting concerns about another round of fighting.
His comments came a day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his claim that Iran had resumed its nuclear program. Netanyahu also released a simulation Sunday depicting a nuclear bomb striking Tel Aviv.
Trump, however, disputed the suggestion that Iran was rebuilding its nuclear facilities, saying American intelligence indicated little activity at sites previously bombed by U.S. forces.
Asked in an interview with Fox News whether Iran was attempting to restore damaged nuclear installations and what satellite imagery showed, Trump said Washington had extensive surveillance capabilities.
"We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space," Trump said. "We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [facilities] are obliterated. They're not moving around there very much."
"We're watching them. We have access to every one of the facilities we bombed. They're covered by thousands of tons of rock," he added.
US commander visits Strait of Hormuz
Meanwhile, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as American forces continued operations aimed at securing the strategically important waterway.
CENTCOM said Cooper toured the area as U.S. military forces marked what it described as a milestone in helping Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
During the visit, Cooper flew aboard a CH-47 Chinook helicopter over the international shipping route to assess the operational environment.
According to CENTCOM, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully passed through the strait with American military support over the past six months.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and is one of the world's most important maritime routes for oil exports.
CENTCOM said commercial shipping through the strait had gained momentum in recent months after U.S. forces cleared naval mines that it said had been deployed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The American military said the mine-clearing operations had allowed vessels to resume using the strait's international shipping lanes.
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," Cooper said.
CENTCOM also claimed that more than 95% of vessels traveling through the strait in recent months had sailed safely despite what it described as unprovoked aggression by the Revolutionary Guard.
The figures, according to the command, demonstrated that the United States and its regional partners maintained control of the international waterway.
US orders embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia
The State Department confirmed Sunday that it had ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government personnel and their family members from the American Embassy in Riyadh amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The confirmation followed reports of diplomatic evacuations from several locations across the Middle East.
"Effective Friday, the Department of State ordered employees to depart Saudi Arabia due to security risks," the department said in a statement.
It cited recent Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes against civilian airports and other critical infrastructure that had caused civilian casualties and significant travel disruptions.
"The Iran-backed Houthis have carried out acts of aggression against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure," the statement said.
The department warned that the violence could escalate rapidly and spread beyond the areas immediately affected by the fighting.
The evacuation order underscored growing American concerns about the security of diplomatic personnel as hostilities involving Iran and its regional allies threatened to expand.
Sri Lanka evacuates 40 Iranian sailors
In a separate development, Sri Lanka's Foreign Ministry said Sunday that the island nation had coordinated the evacuation of 40 Iranian sailors from 19 commercial vessels operating in international waters near the country.
The operation was conducted at Tehran's request after the sailors experienced unspecified medical problems.
Sri Lankan authorities said Iran had submitted its request through established diplomatic channels and that the sailors had since been returned to the Islamic Republic.
The ministry did not explain why the sailors needed to be evacuated or provide further details about their medical conditions.
Local media outlets, along with India's The Hindu newspaper, reported that the sailors had been aboard oil tankers subject to U.S. sanctions imposed as part of Washington's confrontation with Tehran.
A Sri Lankan government source with direct knowledge of the operation told Reuters that the country's navy and coast guard routinely assist with humanitarian missions.
The latest operation followed Sri Lanka's involvement in rescue and repatriation efforts after a U.S. submarine sank the Iranian warship IRIS Dena with a torpedo off the island's coast on March 4, during the first week of the war involving Israel, the United States and Iran.
Dozens of Iranian sailors were killed in that attack, while Sri Lankan authorities helped rescue survivors.
Sri Lanka subsequently assisted in repatriating the bodies of 87 Iranian sailors, as well as 32 survivors from the Dena and 208 crew members from another Iranian vessel.
Iranians stockpile food and medicine amid fears of renewed war
With Israel's elections two days away and the U.S. midterm elections about a week and a half away, fears of renewed fighting are also growing among ordinary Iranians.
As leaders in Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran exchange warnings and threats, residents of the Iranian capital are preparing for the possibility of another military escalation and further economic disruption.
In interviews with The Associated Press, Tehran residents described stockpiling food, medicine and emergency supplies, while some said they were preparing to leave the city if hostilities resumed.
Fereshteh Hajipour, a 35-year-old mother of a toddler, said she had begun accumulating over-the-counter medications and food in anticipation of a possible war involving more powerful bombs.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has contributed to medicine shortages, according to AP, although there have been no indications of widespread shortages of food or other essential goods.
Iran's economic difficulties have intensified as the rial has fallen to record lows and inflation has surged, severely eroding household purchasing power.
A typical monthly salary in Iran is about 400 million rials, equivalent to roughly $150, leaving many families struggling to afford basic necessities.
"Grocery shopping can cost half a month's salary," said Mohammad Mohammadi, 36.
Despite soaring prices, some residents said they felt compelled to purchase additional supplies because of the confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz and the possibility that trade disruptions could worsen.
Mohammad Abdi, 39, said he had stocked up on dried dates, cooking oil and rice for his family.
"I'm worried the situation could get worse," he said.
Others are preparing to leave Tehran altogether.
Hashem Vajdani, a 45-year-old fitness trainer, said he had already packed his belongings and planned to seek refuge in a smaller town in northern Iran if fighting resumed.
"I've already packed my things to go to a safer town in the north of the country," he said. "Today I bought more canned food, crackers and extra blankets."

articles.title: Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
articles.body:
Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
The Financial Times reports, citing sources, that Germany is preparing its first purchase of Ukrainian-developed Bars missiles for its military. If the trials are successful, the order could be expanded to several hundred missiles.
Source: Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sources familiar with the plans indicate that the German government is expected to sign an agreement in the coming weeks to purchase an initial batch of Bars missiles for testing by the Bundeswehr.
The Bars is a jet-powered missile with a flight range of up to 1,000 km and a payload capacity of up to 105 kg, depending on the modification.
Although Ukrainians sometimes refer to it as a drone missile, Germany classifies it as a low-cost cruise missile.
The initial batch will enable the German military to conduct technical trials early next year. If the results are satisfactory, this could potentially pave the way for a larger order of several hundred units.
This initiative is part of Germany's comprehensive efforts to bolster European deterrence against Moscow by expanding its arsenal of long-range strike weapons.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described the Bars as one of the weapons used to strike military bases and energy facilities on Russian territory.
In recent months, Bars missiles have also been manufactured in Germany by a joint Ukrainian-German company whose operations remain shrouded in secrecy.
The first batch of German-made Bars missiles, funded by the German side, was delivered to Ukraine in October.
The joint venture will now also produce goods for Germany, marking the first known procurement of Ukrainian-developed offensive weaponry for the Bundeswehr's own needs.
In addition to the Bars missiles, Germany plans to acquire and test a small batch of Anthem cruise missiles produced by the US startup Covenant. The Anthem costs approximately one-tenth the price of a Tomahawk missile, which ranges from US$4 million to US$6 million.
One source familiar with the details stated that the Bars is even cheaper, but the German side is prepared to purchase both systems.
It was also noted that the potential acquisition of the Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile has been postponed for now.
Currently, the German armed forces only use the air-launched Taurus cruise missile, which has a relatively short range of about 500 km. Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-based launcher system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
Background:
- Media reports indicate that the German government expects to spend nearly €12 billion to create a new arsenal of long-range weapons designed to deter Russia.
- Recently, Denmark also announced a billion-dollar deal to purchase high-precision long-range missiles for the first time in its history, amid intentions to bolster its security.

Under the plan, Germany would spend 1.8 billion euros on low-cost cruise missiles, with three options under consideration: Ukraine’s Bars and Flamingo missiles, and missiles from the American-Israeli startup Covenant Industries.
The agreement would mark the first known instance of the Bundeswehr buying offensive weapons of Ukrainian design for its own use. "On the night of October 26 (from 18:00 on October 25), Russia attacked with one Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, three Kh-59/69 guided air missiles from the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhia and Kherson regions, and 140 Shahed-type strike UAVs (70 of them jet-powered), Gerberas, and 'Parodiya'-type decoy drones from the directions of Orel, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo – Russia, and the TOT of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea – Hvardiyske," the message reads.

articles.title: Iran says US ‘not serious’ about talks, rejects claims over nuclear program
articles.body:
Iran accused the US on Monday of lacking seriousness in negotiations, saying Washington has repeatedly confused diplomacy with imposing demands on Tehran.
“The American side is not serious about negotiations,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said during his weekly news conference, as cited by the state-run IRNA news agency.
He accused Washington of repeatedly making false claims, recalling that US President Donald Trump had expressed support for negotiations shortly before the US military attacks on Iran in June 2025.
“What do you call this? Do you see any goodwill in this approach?” he asked.
Baqaei said Tehran had not received any new European proposal for negotiations beyond a political statement, criticizing Britain, France and Germany for their positions during the conflict.
He accused the three countries of following Washington’s lead on the restoration of UN sanctions and failing to condemn military attacks against Iran.
 
No nuclear weapons
Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed nuclear weapons or sought to acquire them, accusing Washington of using allegations about Tehran’s nuclear program to justify military action.
He said Iran had negotiated in good faith and signed the 2015 nuclear agreement, but the US withdrew from it three years later.
The spokesman accused the US administration of being influenced by Israeli claims about Iran’s nuclear program, describing allegations that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb as a justification for military aggression.
 
Missing Iranian pilots
Baqaei said Iran continued to hold Qatar responsible for clarifying the fate of three Iranian pilots whose aircraft were hit in the Gulf country.
“Until we have evidence of their deaths or receive precise information and documentation, we assume that the country where their aircraft were hit must be held accountable,” he said.
He added that Tehran was pursuing the matter in coordination with its military leadership and through technical delegations and legal discussions.
Baqaei also confirmed that a Qatari delegation recently visited Tehran, saying the trip involved bilateral cooperation and regional mediation efforts.
He described such visits as normal during regional conflicts, noting that Qatar had sought to convey messages and present its positions.
Commenting on Israel’s upcoming elections and threats of military action against Iran, Baqaei accused Israeli politicians of competing over who could commit more crimes.
“It makes no difference to us who takes charge of a regime with a history of violence and killings,” he said.
 
Russia visit
The spokesman confirmed that President Masoud Pezeshkian would travel to Russia on Monday night to attend a summit of gas-exporting countries.
He said the visit would provide opportunities to strengthen energy cooperation with Moscow and hold consultations with other major energy-producing countries.
Baqaei also addressed border-related difficulties with Pakistan and Iraq, saying discussions with Islamabad were progressing positively.
He said Pakistan had described the issue as technical while also raising security concerns, including reports of planned attacks.
Regarding Iraq, he said Iranian diplomatic missions were pursuing the matter, warning that US pressure on Baghdad could harm the Iraqi population and bilateral relations.
Baqaei said Iran summoned the Italian ambassador on Sunday to express concern over the authorities’ handling of protests in European countries.
He accused France, Belgium and Italy of using excessive force and restricting the right to protest, saying such measures were inconsistent with their human rights obligations.
The French ambassador had also been summoned previously, he added.
 
Saudi Arabia and Yemen
On the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said regional security was interconnected and instability in one country could affect others.
He stressed that the dispute should be resolved between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, reiterating Tehran’s readiness to help facilitate a settlement.
“Military approaches make problems more complicated and cause extensive damage,” he said, expressing hope that Saudi Arabia would pursue a negotiated solution.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a regional conflict and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, Trump and Pezeshkian signed a Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding, aimed at ending hostilities, reopening the strategic waterway and paving the way for a broader agreement.
However, disagreements over the implementation of the understanding, including the US naval blockade, sanctions and navigation through the strait, have continued to hinder diplomatic efforts.
Earlier this month, Iran said restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz remained central to negotiations with Washington, insisting that the US must take specific steps to resolve the standoff.

articles.title: Drones keep sinking ships off Romania and Bulgaria—French and US patrol planes are watching
articles.body:
French and US maritime patrol planes are watching the western Black Sea, where drones keep hitting merchant ships, Romanian outlet Curs de Guvernare reported on 19 October, citing flight-tracking data. Romania blames Russia for the attacks, while Bulgaria says it cannot prove who launched them.
Ukraine’s three small Danube ports have kept its grain exports from collapsing further, and Russia has pounded those ports since the summer. The ships serving them are now being hit in the economic zones of two NATO members. Many were anchored near or heading to the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube to the sea. That puts the allied patrols over these waters in the middle of the fight over Ukraine’s grain trade.
Two patrol planes over the western Black Sea
A French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol plane arrived in Constanța, Romania’s main Black Sea port, on the evening of 18 October, Curs de Guvernare said. On 24 October, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said in the Bulgarian port of Varna that a French patrol plane had been operating in the area under NATO for two weeks and had contributed to rescue operations.
Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks
Meanwhile, a US Navy P-8A Poseidon flew into Varna from Sicily on 18 October, AFP reported, citing flight-tracking data. Two days later, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said it had begun reconnaissance patrols after Sofia asked allies for help, and that some allies had responded quickly. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov called the deployment a joint decision of Bulgaria and NATO. He said the plane cannot strike targets and passes its data to NATO, Anadolu Agency reported.
NATO promises more
On 20 October, NATO’s North Atlantic Council met at Romania’s request. Afterward, the alliance said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea. NATO military spokesman Col. Martin O’Donnell added that allies have sent or will send intelligence personnel and explosives-forensics teams. NATO itself has not attributed the attacks to any country.
Romania names Russia, Bulgaria hedges
Romania has been blunter. On 15 October, after four merchant ships were hit within a day, acting Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu wrote on X that “Russia bears full responsibility for these developments.” On 17 October, Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Russian Geran drones near Sulina, Romania’s Defense Ministry said.
On 23 October, a drone sank the cargo ship Khoryv off Constanța, killing a Ukrainian sailor, and President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia too. “It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” Dan said.
Bulgaria is more cautious. Radev told parliament on 14 October that the attacks worked in Russia’s favor but that Sofia could not prove it. Since taking office in May, he has sought a thaw in ties with Moscow.

articles.title: What the US Spends on Patriot Missiles in the Middle East Could Defend Ukraine for Years
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
What the US Spends on Patriot Missiles in the Middle East Could Defend Ukraine for Years
Patriot interceptor missiles expended during US and allied air defense operations in the Middle East could have supported Ukraine’s air defenses for several years, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to RBC-Ukraine on October 26, Ihnat made the assessment during the outlet’s “TSE BAZA” podcast, highlighting differences in how Ukrainian forces and other Patriot operators use the American-made air defense systems.
Ihnat explained that Ukrainian crews have developed tactics to conserve expensive interceptors while maintaining their effectiveness against Russian missiles and aircraft.
One major difference involves the number of missiles launched against individual targets. Ukrainian operators have learned to engage certain threats with a single interceptor, while air defense crews in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at one target.
Patriot systems can operate in automatic, semi-automatic, and manual modes. According to Ihnat, automatic operation can result in multiple interceptors being launched against a single threat, particularly when crews lack extensive combat experience.
He argued that the volume of Patriot missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukrainian Patriot operations for several years, contributing to concerns over interceptor availability.
Ukraine has also adapted how Patriot batteries are deployed. Rather than keeping the systems in fixed defensive positions near military installations, Ukrainian forces have used mobile tactics to intercept Russian aircraft before relocating.
Ihnat cited a May 2023 operation in Russia’s Bryansk region, when Ukrainian Patriot crews reportedly shot down five Russian aircraft—including two fighter jets and three helicopters—in just five minutes. The operation demonstrated Ukraine’s ability to use Patriot systems for mobile air defense ambushes rather than relying exclusively on fixed defensive positions.
The comments come amid growing concerns over Ukraine’s limited access to Patriot interceptors as Russia continues launching ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously stated that Ukraine receives approximately 12 Patriot interceptors per month, roughly four times fewer than during former US President Joe Biden’s administration. Zelenskyy also said that some interceptor shipments already financed by Ukraine’s international partners have yet to receive authorization from Washington.

articles.title: Israeli opposition leaders accuse Netanyahu of spreading ‘terror, panic’ ahead of election
articles.body:
Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Two Israeli opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday of spreading “terror” and “panic” among Israelis ahead of the country’s parliamentary election.
Netanyahu posted an artificial intelligence-generated image early Sunday depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning about the threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons and a call to continue confronting Tehran during the remainder of US President Donald Trump’s term.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief and leader of the Yashar party, accused Netanyahu of hysteria and resorting to the same tactics he used in previous election campaigns: “lies and spreading fear.”
“This time, you are threatening Israeli citizens with total destruction, after failing to achieve the goals of the war in Iran,” Eisenkot wrote on the US social media platform X.
He added that Netanyahu had shifted from promising “absolute victory” to the slogan “We will not surrender.”
“That is the whole story,” he said.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, also criticized Netanyahu in a post on X.
“The prime minister of Israel posted a picture of an atomic bomb over Tel Aviv,” Golan wrote.
He called for the Israeli premier to be barred from social media, saying Netanyahu and those around him had “lost their minds” as pressure mounted.
“On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and rationality to Israel,” Golan added.
The exchanges came two days before Israel’s parliamentary election, scheduled for Oct. 27, amid a tight competition between Netanyahu’s political camp and opposition parties seeking to end his rule.
Netanyahu has focused much of his recent campaign on security threats, particularly Iran’s nuclear program, while opposition figures have accused him of exploiting those concerns for political gains.
On Wednesday, Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s claim that he had destroyed Iranian nuclear bombs and saved Israel was “an outright lie,” adding that “Iran has never possessed nuclear bombs.”
In an interview with Israel’s public broadcaster KAN, Eisenkot also said he did not see an immediate and direct threat that would justify launching a military attack on Iran ahead of the election.
Netanyahu has led a far-right government since late 2022, widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.

articles.title: Ukraine-US-Russia Talks May Resume in November as Trump Eyes Business With Both Sides
articles.body:
Ukraine-US-Russia Talks May Resume in November as Trump Eyes Business With Both Sides
The Kremlin is prepared to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the United States after November 4, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on October 25, as U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington could do business with both Moscow and Kyiv after the war ends.
Ushakov’s remarks followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement on October 23 that another round of trilateral talks was expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi among the possible venues.
“The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, referring to Russia’s National Unity Day.
The Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed ceasefire proposals, insisting that Kyiv surrender the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russian forces have not captured. The territory is strategically important, and handing it over would give Moscow land its military has been unable to take on the battlefield. Ukraine, meanwhile, has accepted several ceasefire proposals put forward by Washington.
Ushakov said he did not anticipate major progress at the first trilateral meeting after the pause, describing it as a “trial run.” He added that a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine “still needs work.”
On October 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg the following day for three hours. Afterward, the Kremlin said it was prepared to restart trilateral negotiations in November. Witkoff said on October 21 that discussions involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives would “continue at the technical level.”
Putin has long avoided direct talks with Zelensky. Instead, the Russian leader is reportedly seeking a meeting with Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace agreement without Ukraine’s participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has criticized Zelensky, announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine without agreement from both sides that ultimately failed, threatened to halt intelligence-sharing with Kyiv and eased restrictions on Russian oil exports. Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to negotiate with Ukraine.
Trump said on October 24 that he expected the United States to resume commercial dealings with both countries once the war was over, despite criticism of efforts to restore business ties with Russia.
The remarks came as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel under a supply agreement announced by Trump on October 9 was heading from the Baltic port of Primorsk to New York. The vessel is due to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel.
Following the announcement of the deal, Moscow partially relaxed restrictions on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 metric tons to be sold.
“Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think,” Trump said. He added that he wanted to “get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both.”
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have obtained greater financial compensation for the billions of dollars in assistance provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden’s presidency.
“I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid,” Trump said.
Plans to import about 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel over the coming months have drawn criticism from European allies, Ukraine and members of Congress. Critics say the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The delivery would be the first shipment of Russian diesel to the United States since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden prohibited imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to the invasion of Ukraine.
The agreement comes as tensions between Washington and Kyiv deepen, with Ukraine facing restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump has intensified his attacks on Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian president of refusing to end the war and calling for him to be replaced.
The resumption of Russian diesel imports also comes as Republicans face a difficult political environment ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polling showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on October 19 found that only 31% of Americans approved of Trump’s performance, the lowest rating of either of his presidential terms. Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would support Democrats if congressional elections were held that day, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead, their largest of the current election cycle.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to hold security talks in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to hold security talks in Iran
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are expected to hold security talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Deputy Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Ali Bagheri Kani, announced that Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin would visit Tehran.
The talks will bring together representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement and Iranian officials, with discussions expected to focus on Israel's expansionist policies, the situation in Lebanon and the ongoing US war against Iran, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei.
Speaking to Iranian state TV, Bagheri Kani said the meeting formed part of efforts to establish a regional security framework led by Middle Eastern countries rather than external powers.
He said it was happening because of Iran's resistance to US-Israeli military attacks and expressed hope that the discussions would contribute to greater regional stability.
He added that the Mecca Defence Agreement countries could draw on Iran's experience in developing its national defence capabilities to establish a regional security system independent of foreign intervention.
Bagheri Kani also accused the United States and Israel of undermining regional stability, saying Israel's actions in the Middle East were a threat to the security of neighbouring countries.
Saudi Arabia says talks aim to reduce tensions
Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Raed Krimly said in a post on X that Khalid bin Salman would lead the kingdom's delegation to the meetings in Tehran.
He said representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement would also meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.
Krimly described the visit as part of continuing diplomatic efforts by the agreement's member states to reduce tensions between the US and Iran.
He added that the discussions would seek to encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions while supporting mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan.
Saudi Arabia also emphasised the role of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries in promoting regional security and stability through cooperation with other states in the Middle East.
Qatar steps up mediation amid fears of renewed war
The planned meeting comes amid growing concerns that the United States and Israel could launch another round of military strikes against Iran, potentially triggering a wider regional confrontation.
Fighting has also intensified between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement, amid continued missile strikes on the kingdom.
A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Sunday evening as part of Doha's efforts to prevent a further escalation between Washington and Tehran, a source familiar with the regional mediation efforts told The New Arab.
The source said the visit was intended to build on ongoing diplomatic contacts aimed at preventing the conflict from worsening.
Iran had already communicated its positions and demands clearly to the mediators, the source added.
Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States throughout the current conflict.
Iran warns against another military confrontation
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday against renewed US military action, saying Tehran would maintain its policies regardless of whether another war broke out.
Araghchi said that although there was growing discussion of another conflict, he was already considering what would happen after it ended.
He argued that previous military confrontations had demonstrated the consequences of attempting to resolve disputes with Iran through force.
The foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's position that lasting regional security could only be achieved through cooperation between neighbouring countries without foreign interference.
He stressed that Iran remained prepared to work with all countries in the region, particularly Gulf states, to establish a more stable security environment.

articles.title: Iraq suspects Israel behind attack on weapons depots and military systems inside Iraq
articles.body:
An attack targeted military facilities in Iraq last week, including Chinese-made air defence systems and ammunition depots reportedly recently delivered from Iran for Shiite militias in the country, Iraqi sources said, with suspicions that Israel was behind the strike.
Saudi media quoted two Iraqi sources as saying that authorities in Baghdad had indications pointing to Israel’s involvement, but had yet to determine how the attack was carried out or whether it involved warplanes or drones.
The attack wounded five people, who sustained minor injuries, according to the sources. Iraqi authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The developments come amid previous reports of possible Israeli military activity inside Iraq. About six months ago, US media reported that Israel had established a secret military base in Iraq, housing special forces and serving as a logistical hub for the Israeli air force, in coordination with the United States, according to sources cited in those reports.

articles.title: The Russia-Africa summit 2026: What you need to know about building a multipolar world without the West
articles.body:
The Russia-Africa summit 2026: What you need to know about building a multipolar world without the West
Trade, sovereignty and peace are on the table as African leaders gather in Moscow this week for the third Russia-Africa summit.
Their participation comes despite what Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has described as Western pressure on African governments to stay away. This prodding prompted Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama to retort that partnerships should deliver investment and fair returns rather than be determined by competition among outside powers.
The October 28–29 meeting will set cooperation priorities for the next three years, alongside an Economic and Humanitarian Forum bringing together officials, businesses and experts. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current African Union (AU) chairman, will co-chair the leaders’ plenary session on the second day.
The gathering follows summits in Sochi in 2019 and St. Petersburg in 2023.
Who is coming to Moscow?
Russia has invited all African heads of state and the leaders of regional organizations. Most African delegations have confirmed their participation, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa arrived in Moscow on Sunday. Writing on X, he said Zimbabwe’s participation would focus on “driving economic diversification, boosting industrial trade, and creating sustainable jobs for our youth,” alongside cooperation in energy, food security and technology.
The presidents of Mali and Mozambique as well as the Senegalese prime minister have also arrived. Delegations from Ghana and Uganda are in Moscow, according to Ruptly footage showing their motorcades in the city center on Monday.
Republic of Congo President Denis Sassou Nguesso left Brazzaville for Moscow on Sunday, according to a Facebook post made by his office.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama arrived in Moscow on Monday after confirming his participation at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London last week. At that event, he defended Ghana’s nonaligned foreign policy, citing friendly relations with Russia, China, the US and the EU.
Mahama also said he would “try to convince President Putin to have a ceasefire if I can,” referring to the Ukraine conflict. His appeal follows earlier African peace efforts, including a seven-country mission led by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to Ukraine and Russia in June 2023.
Kenyan President William Ruto and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni are expected to attend, their ambassadors in Moscow confirmed in June. Kenya’s envoy, Peter Mathuki, said he anticipated “very fruitful talks.”
Burkina Faso President Ibrahim Traore and Niger’s President Abdourahamane Tchiani will also participate, according to Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov.
South Sudanese President Salva Kiir confirmed his attendance in a letter to Putin delivered through diplomatic channels in July, according to Russia’s embassy in Juba. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has also announced the participation of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional leader, Horta N’Tam.
Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah will attend, her office confirmed, announcing her scheduled departure on Monday. It said Namibia would seek partnerships supporting mineral processing, job creation, technology transfer and economic diversification.
Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed al-Menfi is also expected to participate, Sputnik reported, citing a source in the council. Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan will attend, Russian Ambassador to Sudan Andrey Chernovol told RIA Novosti.
Nigerian Vice President Kashim Shettima will lead his country’s delegation, Nigeria’s ambassador to Russia, Joseph Olusola Iji, told TASS.
Ramaphosa will not attend. During talks with Putin in September, he cited local election campaigning, saying he would be “in the middle of a very vigorous campaign.” South Africa’s embassy subsequently confirmed that its delegation would be led by Zane Dangor, director-general of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation.
What is on the agenda?
The topic of sovereignty is central to the forum, which features sessions on development financing, food security and technological independence.
Discussions will cover infrastructure, transport corridors, industrial cooperation and payment mechanisms that reduce reliance on the dollar and euro. Participants will also assess closer links with BRICS and the Eurasian Economic Union, including barriers that continue to restrict trade.
Interdependence regarding agriculture is a foundational sector for Russia-Africa relations, and the forum is expected to address fertilizer supplies, farm machinery, local production and the financial and logistical obstacles facing food trade.
Peaceful nuclear energy is another priority. Rosatom is building four reactors at Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant and has signed roadmaps to advance planned nuclear power projects in Ethiopia and Rwanda. Its cooperation with Rwanda also includes a proposed nuclear science and technology center for research, specialist training and applications in medicine, agriculture and industry.
Digital infrastructure discussions come as Africa’s online economy expands. GSMA’s 2025 assessment put the continent’s mobile internet users at 416 million, projected to reach 576 million by 2030. African companies also bring established financial technology expertise: Kenya’s Safaricom said its M-PESA mobile money service reached 40 million customers in March 2026.Other sessions cover artificial intelligence, healthcare and training African specialists.
Why is the summit important?
African priorities include processing more resources at home, building energy and technological capacity, and diversifying partnerships on their own terms.
Disputes with Western governments have reinforced the emphasis on sovereignty. In September, South Africa’s Foreign Ministry challenged US visa restrictions linked to Washington’s criticism of its domestic policies, declaring: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice.”
The summit builds on sustained diplomatic engagement. Since 2022, Lavrov has visited countries across the continent, including repeated trips to Egypt, Ethiopia and South Africa. His July 2026 tour included Ethiopia, Niger, Mozambique and Burundi.
The summit framework has also developed into regular ministerial consultations. Sochi hosted the first ministerial conference of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum in November 2024, followed by a second in Cairo in December 2025.
The gathering for Russia “is a momentous event – hardly ever before have so many leaders gathered together in the Kremlin,” Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT on Monday. He described relations as undergoing a slow but sustained strengthening, supported by an expanding network of intergovernmental commissions, business councils and other institutions.
Trade between Russia and Africa rose from $16.8 billion in 2019 to $27.1 billion in 2025, according to Nikolay Golovko, a leading expert at HSE’s Center for African Studies. The balance remains heavily tilted toward Russian exports, which accounted for $22.7 billion, compared with $4.4 billion in imports from Africa.
Has the threat of Western sanctions reached Russia-Africa relations?
There still might be concerns about secondary sanctions; however, “they are being removed from the first plan,” Maslov said. A new group of partners has emerged, ready to develop new logistics networks and payment mechanisms. “Sanctions have gone from being a problem to a cost of doing business,” he noted.
Economic cooperation already includes major projects. Russia is building Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant, while Rosatom’s subsidiary Mantra Tanzania opened a pilot uranium processing facility at the Mkuju River project in July 2025.
Russia and the AU also reiterated support in July for greater African representation in the UN Security Council, reflecting their push to reform global institutions.
What was the central theme of Summit 1.0?
The inaugural summit took place in Sochi on October 23–24, 2019, co-chaired by Putin and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, then the AU chair.
Held under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development,” it established a framework for cooperation across politics, security, trade, science, education and culture.
The event provided a foundation for 92 agreements, contracts and signed memorandums of understanding between participants, with publicly disclosed values totaling more than 1 trillion rubles, approximately $12.5 billion at the time. These were signed commitments rather than a measure of completed investment.
What did the second summit deliver?
The second gathering, held in St. Petersburg on July 27–28, 2023, expanded the format to include a humanitarian forum. Official delegations from 48 African countries attended.
Participants adopted a joint declaration and a cooperation action plan for 2023–2026. Separate declarations addressed counterterrorism, international information security and preventing an arms race in outer space. Organizers recorded 161 publicly disclosed agreements, many covering education, science and other humanitarian cooperation.
Food security was a prominent issue and remains a pressing concern. An estimated 309 million people in Africa faced hunger in 2025, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s latest report.
At the 2023 summit, Putin pledged free grain for six African countries. Russia completed the 200,000-metric-ton delivery program in February 2024, according to its Agriculture Ministry. Somalia and the Central African Republic received 50,000 tons each; Burkina Faso, Eritrea, Mali and Zimbabwe received 25,000 tons each.
In August 2026, Russia delivered nearly 556 metric tons of split peas and sunflower oil to Burkina Faso through the UN World Food Program, according to Russian Ambassador Igor Martynov.
What can we expect for Summit 3.0?
A central expected outcome is a new Russia-Africa action plan for 2027–2029, replacing the framework adopted in St. Petersburg. Lavrov has said it will be approved at the Moscow gathering.
Zakharova has also said a substantial package of intergovernmental agreements and commercial contracts is expected. Putin will hold bilateral meetings, while Lavrov will host a working breakfast for African foreign ministers on October 28.
The gathering will also provide an opportunity to review implementation of the 2023–2026 action plan, Golovko writes. Its 181 points cover areas ranging from politics and security to agriculture, energy, transport, education and investment.
What other events are taking place?
The Russia-Africa Media Forum opened in Moscow on Monday, bringing together more than 200 participants from 46 African countries. Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the four-day event focuses on media cooperation and journalism’s role in shaping Africa’s image abroad.
Sebastian Maganga, head of content at Tanzania’s Clouds Media Group, highlighted the value of exchanging stories.
“If you have forums similar to this, that’s when you get the opportunity to share our stories and get stories from Russia and other places respectively and package them,” he said on the sidelines of the event.
The media forum’s published program identifies “strengthening the media sovereignty of African countries” as a priority. Sessions will examine how African newsrooms can develop their own sources, expand the international reach of their reporting and cooperate with Russian outlets through content production, resource sharing and journalist exchanges.
Moscow will also host the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit on October 27. The gathering will address global market developments, energy security and investment opportunities.
The GECF’s members account for 70% of proven global natural gas reserves and 42% of gas exports, according to the organization. Its African members are Algeria, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Nigeria, while Angola, Mauritania, Mozambique and Senegal hold observer status.
Africa exported 39.77 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas in 2025, up 1.8 million tons from the previous year, according to the International Gas Union. Mauritania and Senegal joined the LNG export market that year through their shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project.
Russian companies already have investments in African gas production. Rosneft acquired a 30% stake in the concession containing Egypt’s giant Zohr gas field in 2017 for $1.125 billion, excluding reimbursement for past project costs.

articles.title: Russia promises “favorable conditions” to European firms a month after seizing control of Nestlé and Auchan
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed Russia is trying to create “favorable conditions” for European companies that stayed in the country, The Moscow Times reported. He said it on state TV weeks after his decrees put several of the largest Western businesses in Russia under Kremlin-appointed managers. Meanwhile, Russia’s own government expects investment to fall at the fastest pace in over a decade.
To keep paying for its full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia has drained reserves, borrowed more, and raised taxes. Its war spending will still rise by 27% next year, as the EU moved this month to adopt its largest sanctions package against Russia’s war industry. Fresh foreign money could ease that squeeze, and the Kremlin keeps scaring it away.
Putin: Europe’s companies left Russia in tears
Putin made the claim in an interview with Kremlin propagandist Pavel Zarubin, which Russian state outlet Vesti published on 25 October. He claimed Russia has “many friends in Europe,” but European governments forced their businesses out:
“When some companies were leaving us under pressure from Western European governments, our friends from these countries nearly cried… Some of them, by the way, are working, and we are trying to create appropriate favorable conditions for them.”
He also attacked Western sanctions, calling it stupid to ban “everything that comes from Russia.”
The decrees came first
On 17 September, Putin’s decree handed the Russian assets of Nestlé, Auchan, and the former Leroy Merlin chain to a firm run by an Interior Ministry major general. US packaging maker Aptar and German wholesaler Metro followed. In mid-October, Russia seized French flooring maker Tarkett and four more foreign-owned firms.
“A warning to companies that remain”: Russia takes control of Nestlé and Auchan’s assets – companies that stayed in Russia following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine
The Kremlin claimed their home countries are “actively involved” in fighting Russia, and Putin cited his 2023 decree on retaliating for Western moves against Russian property. Since the full-scale war began, Russia has put 135 foreign-linked firms under such management. Asked which European companies could be next, a senior Russian official said: “Let them be scared.” Metro reportedly asked to be taken over itself, hoping to keep more control over its fate.
“We don’t steal,” Putin said three weeks earlier
In early October, Putin denied that the takeovers amounted to seizures. At the Valdai Discussion Club on 1 October, he claimed: “We take nothing from anyone, we don’t steal, and we don’t nationalize… Yes, we place some enterprises under external management.”
Russia’s investment drop is the worst since 2015
Putin has demanded an urgent new “investment cycle.” Instead, his economy ministry expects investment to shrink by 5.4% this year. Russian authorities have seized assets worth 7.6 trillion rubles (about $95 billion) from their owners during the war, law firm NSP estimates. More than half of large Russian companies ended 2025 with lower profits and cut or froze investment projects.
Two rubles for the army for every one on welfare, schools, and hospitals: Russia’s 2027 wartime budget
Ukrainian long-range strikes add to the risk of building anything in Russia. Overnight on 26 October, drones attacked a Voronezh aircraft plant that makes parts for Russia’s military transport planes. A day earlier, drones reportedly hit a titanium plant in Perm Krai, and Storm Shadow missiles reportedly struck a battery plant in Yelets supplying Russia’s missiles and glide bombs.

articles.title: RFE/RL: 16 more air defense towers spotted near Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing total to about 50 — nearly half the number in Moscow and its outskirts
articles.body:
RFE/RL: 16 more air defense towers spotted near Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing total to about 50 — nearly half the number in Moscow and its outskirts
At least 15 new towers appeared in October within a 50-kilometer radius (31 miles) of Vladimir Putin’s residence in Valdai, likely intended to carry Pantsir or Tor surface-to-air missile systems, RFE/RL’s Russian service reported, citing satellite images it examined.
A ring of towers appeared south of the residence, facing Ukraine, according to the journalists. One tower in the “outer ring” was built as early as March 2026 on the grounds of the Khotilovo military base, which is connected to the residence by a dedicated railway line that allows travel by train.
According to an OSINT analyst who posts on X under the handle @jembobineuse, Russia now has about 177 towers equipped with short-range air defense systems. About 98 are in and around Moscow, and about 50 are near the residence in Valdai.
Russian authorities claimed that more than 90 Ukrainian drones attempted to attack Putin’s residence in Valdai in late December 2025. Ukraine denies attempting such an attack. The CIA concluded that the target of the Ukrainian drone attack in the Novgorod region was an unspecified “military facility” not located near Putin’s residence.
The first air defense system near Putin’s residence in Valdai appeared in January 2023, and a second arrived in July 2024. By April 2026, satellite images examined by RFE/RL’s Russian service showed that at least 27 air defense units already ringed the residence.
