articles.title: Ukraine’s strike capability weakens as Russia hits its military facilities — expert
articles.body:
LUGANSK, October 26. /TASS/. The strike capability of the Ukrainian armed forces declined last week amid attacks by Russian forces on Ukrainian military facilities, including those located in the rear, military expert Andrey Marochko reported.
"Last week, the situation on the line of contact worsened for Ukrainian forces, largely as a result of rear logistics disruption and Russian strikes targeting the military-industrial complex facilities, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure, weapons and military equipment production sites, military-technical equipment warehouses, as well as temporary deployment sites for Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries. "The strike capability of Ukraine’s armed formations has fallen to minimal levels," he wrote on his VKontakte page, after analyzing data released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Marochko noted that amid this decline in strike capability, effective counterattacks by Ukrainian troops in the special operation zone "have become practically impossible."
The military expert added that due to logistical disruptions in several areas in the special military operation zone, Ukrainian troops are not evacuating the wounded and the dead, and are instead "simply finishing off their seriously wounded comrades."
On Friday, the Russian Defense Ministry reported that over the past week, the Russian military had launched three massive and 11 combined strikes on the enemy’s logistics centers, energy and transport sites. Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities were incapacitated.

articles.title: Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
articles.body:
Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
Yemen’s Houthis have struck several targets in Saudi Arabia, including two international airports and energy infrastructure facilities operated by the oil giant Saudi Aramco, the group’s military spokesman said on Saturday.
The conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis, and the Saudi-led coalition escalated last month, when the militant group seized the Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and a key stronghold of anti-Houthi forces.
In a statement posted on X, Yahya Saree said the Houthis had conducted seven operations using ballistic missiles and drones, targeting King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran Airport and Khamis Mushait Air Base, as well as Aramco’s facilities in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and crude oil pumping stations, and a pipeline linking eastern and western Saudi Arabia.
The spokesman said the attacks were carried out in response to what the group described as Saudi “aggression” against Yemen. Saree claimed Saudi forces had launched 100 airstrikes over the previous 24 hours, targeting civilian infrastructure in Sanaa and other areas, leaving dozens dead and wounded. 
He said the Houthis would continue attacking Saudi territory until the “aggression” ends and the Saudi-led coalition lifts its restrictions on the movement of goods and people into and out of Yemen.
The latest attack came as Riyadh’s main air hub prepared to resume operations after more than two weeks of disruption following earlier Houthi strikes. The facility announced a partial reopening from Sunday. In a separate post on X, Saree warned that airlines, airport staff and passengers against using the site, calling it a military target and saying it would remain unsafe.
The spokesman also accused Riyadh of spreading false claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, insisting that the group’s operations were directed solely at Saudi oil facilities and military bases and were announced as they took place.
The accusation came in response to Saudi Civil Defense claims that debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis fell in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday. The debris landed in several locations, including Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh, the agency said on Saturday.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, with Saudi Arabia leading a military intervention the following year to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis. Fighting eased under a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but escalated sharply in September 2026.
The renewed conflict has seen the Houthis launch missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, while the Riyadh-led coalition has intensified airstrikes on Houthi positions, command centers and weapons networks.
The Houthis have claimed the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the latest escalation began has reached 3,123.

articles.title: Ukraine awaits Hegseth's signature for nearly a month on Patriot and NASAMS missiles – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine has been waiting for nearly a month for U.S Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's signature regarding the supply of missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, reported President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy following a conference call, adding that he has instructed relevant officials to hold talks with the American side.
"The Minister of Defense of Ukraine, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs reported on the situation regarding the supply of air defense interceptors to Ukraine, primarily 'Patriots'. We are working in several directions: with the United States, Europe, and other partners who have a reserve of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. In particular, for nearly a month we have been awaiting Mr. Hegseth's signature regarding missiles for 'Patriots' and 'NASAMS'. I instructed to discuss this once again with the American side. Talks are also ongoing with other countries," Zelenskyy wrote in a Telegram channel on Monday.
Also during the conference call, participants discussed preparations for the meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format in November.
"It is important to accelerate the implementation of decisions that have been on the table for some time. Every support package is an opportunity to protect people's lives," Zelenskyy emphasized.
On October 20, it was reported that the administration of U.S President Donald Trump is holding up the transfer of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine from partner countries, which coincides with a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Washington and Kyiv over disagreements regarding strikes on Russian oil refineries.
According to U.S officials, the transfer of weaponry from states friendly to Ukraine requires official approval from U.S Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, as the systems are manufactured in the U.S and are subject to export control rules. Officials note that Hegseth has not yet formally rejected these applications, but has also not taken the necessary steps to approve them. Against this backdrop, Ukrainian representatives previously stated a critical deficit and a remaining stock of "only a few" interceptor missiles in their arsenal.

articles.title: Ukraine Seeks Earlier Russia Talks and EU Role
articles.body:
Ukraine and the United States are seeking to bring planned negotiations with Russia forward by at least a week, while Kyiv is pushing for European involvement, according to a report published Monday, Oct. 26.
Ukrainska Pravda reported the initiative, citing sources close to Ukraine’s negotiating team and President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The outlet placed the tentative start of the Abu Dhabi talks at around Nov. 10, after the US congressional midterm elections. Moscow had not confirmed an earlier date as of the evening of Oct. 25.
A source in Zelensky’s team linked the urgency to approaching winter and the time needed for successive negotiating rounds.
“When you have no electricity, water or heating, every day matters,” the source said.
Kyiv does not expect an immediate breakthrough. Sources suggested that possible delegation changes could make the first meeting introductory, with substantive negotiations and potential decisions coming in later rounds.
Kyiv seeks European involvement
According to the underlying report, Russia opposes European representatives joining the first meeting at the negotiating table.
Ukraine nevertheless plans to bring European officials to Abu Dhabi and brief them as discussions unfold, a source close to the negotiating group said.
The source identified a further obstacle: Europe lacks a single representative authorized to make decisions. Björn Seibert, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s chief of cabinet, has represented the EU at recent meetings, the report noted.
Russia May Seek NATO Rollback to 1997 in Ukraine Talks
Kyiv also wants negotiations to address Ukraine’s long-term protection and Europe’s postwar security arrangements, rather than remain focused on Moscow’s territorial demands. The proposal concerns the direction of future discussions; it does not establish agreement on a settlement or European participation.
Moscow signals readiness after Nov. 4
The reported push for earlier negotiations follows Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov’s statement that Russia would be ready to resume talks after Nov. 4, its National Unity Day holiday.
Speaking Sunday, Oct. 25, Ushakov described the prospective meeting as preliminary and exploratory, playing down expectations of an immediate agreement. He did not announce a definitive date.
His remarks followed renewed shuttle diplomacy involving US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Talks with Ukrainian and European representatives in Oslo on Oct. 20 preceded a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Earlier reporting identified Abu Dhabi or Switzerland as possible venues for working-level negotiations. The contacts have reopened discussion of a trilateral format, while differences over territory and security guarantees remain unresolved.
Ukraine rejects army limits and neutrality
Zelensky has separately ruled out neutrality and restrictions on Ukraine’s armed forces as conditions of a peace agreement.
In an interview broadcast Sunday, Oct. 25, he said Ukraine should be able to maintain an army of 800,000 personnel if sufficient funding is available. He described the force’s size as an internal Ukrainian matter and said the central questions were financing and effective security guarantees.
Zelensky said Ukraine expects guarantees from the United States and Europe that would prevent another Russian attack. He also argued that territorial questions require decisions by leaders, while technical groups can work on other elements of a settlement.
An energy ceasefire, he said, could demonstrate that Moscow is genuinely prepared to move toward peace. He cautioned that Russia’s stated willingness to negotiate must be judged by practical results.
Ukraine remains prepared to participate in technical-level talks, Zelensky said, but such a meeting alone would not deliver a complete resolution of the war. Kyiv wants the renewed process to produce concrete outcomes.

articles.title: Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
articles.body:
Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection on Oct. 25, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term in office, as his opponent, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede defeat and vowed to challenge the election results.
The election ended with Lula receiving 51.79% of votes compared with Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to Brazil's electoral authorities.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election, calling a decision by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting by two hours "unacceptable."
The extension was introduced following transportation disruptions and severe weather that affected voting in parts of the country, according to the Associated Press.
The electoral court has recognized Lula's victory, and Bolsonaro's refusal to concede does not invalidate the result.
Lula had expressed the view in 2024 that Brazil should remain neutral and not interfere in Russia's war against Ukraine, but in the years that followed had been engaging in diplomacy, including efforts to position Brazil as a potential mediator between Kyiv and Moscow.
In June of this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky accepted Lula's offer to assist efforts to negotiate an end to the war, Ukrainian presidential communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said, according to Reuters.
The leaders held a bilateral meeting on during the G7 summit in France on June 17, discussing ways to revive stalled diplomatic negotiations, including potential outreach to permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
While Ukraine maintains close diplomatic ties with three of the five permanent members — France, the United Kingdom and the United States — Brazil has maintained diplomatic relations with Russia and China.
Lula spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone in August, discussing the war in Ukraine and bilateral relations, CNN Brasil reported.
Brazil has maintained diplomatic and economic ties with Russia since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, opting out of Western sanctions and expressing a wish to have a role in a negotiated settlement to the war.
Lula has also rejected suggestions that Brazil supports Russia's invasion, saying in an April interview that his government has never recognized Moscow's right to occupy Ukrainian territory.
The Brazilian president's victory comes after a closely fought campaign against Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a prison sentence for his role in an attempted coup following his 2022 election defeat.
The elder Bolsonaro also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. He was subsequently convicted for his role in a plot to overturn that election.
The victory makes Lula, 80, the first Brazilian president to win four terms and the first candidate since the country's return to democracy to win a presidential runoff after finishing second in the opening round.
While Bolsonaro refused to concede and asked for the vote to be annulled, election officials have expressed "absolute" confidence in the proceedings and the result, as reported by Reuters.

articles.title: Trump uses Michigan rally to attack Democratic Senate candidate El-Sayed
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
US President Donald Trump used a campaign rally Sunday to launch fierce attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed while endorsing his Republican rival Mike Rogers ahead of the November midterm elections.
"I'm here today in Michigan for a very important reason. I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator, and that's the fact. Not going to let that happen," he told the crowd during his 26th rally in 12 days.
Trump claimed that El-Sayed would require a metal detector to enter the chamber, accusing him of wanting to abolish police and federal border enforcement agencies.
The Michigan race pits El-Sayed against Rogers to fill the vacancy left by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, representing a critical battleground for party control in the Senate.
Urging supporters to turn out on Nov. 3, Trump warned that voter participation drops when his name is absent from the ballot.
"Please show up and vote, because essentially we are all on the ballot," he said.
He also targeted Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, alleging that she used an alternate name to assume office and demanding her immediate resignation from Congress while disparaging Somalia. The remarks follow heightened political friction after federal agents executed an early-morning search warrant at Omar's Washington, DC residence on Oct. 12.
Addressing international matters, Trump attributed urban unrest in France, Italy and Spain entirely to immigration.
"I didn't see any students there. These were a lot of large men with very big muscles," he said, recalling how he cautioned French President Emmanuel Macron in 2017 about border policies.
European cities have recently witnessed street demonstrations linked to economic pressures and migration debates.
Trump also voiced frustration toward Norway over the Nobel Peace Prize, arguing that he resolved eight conflicts without receiving recognition after the Nobel Committee awarded the 2025 prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.
"I don't want anybody from Norway," he said, contrasting it with Denmark, which he said was "great,” praising them for cooperating on a security and defense framework regarding Greenland.
Speaking to reporters prior to the rally, Trump said Washington is "getting close to a deal" with Canada, alleging that Ottawa has long profited off the US. Bilateral trade remains strained after both countries imposed tariffs on billions of dollars of goods following the collapse of trade negotiations.
Asked about subterranean uranium in Iran, he dismissed immediate proliferation risks, citing heavy rock coverage at targeted facilities alongside continuous surveillance by the US Space Force.
Strains persist across the Middle East as the Iran war remains unresolved following large-scale American and Israeli military strikes on Iran.
Trump also claimed the US defeated Iran “militarily, financially and otherwise” and said the war will end “quite soon, one way or the other.”

articles.title: Ukrainian intelligence: Russia can probably add 10–15 Su-34 bombers a year, but no new Tu-95s or Tu-22M3s
articles.body:
Russia’s aircraft plants still turn out modern fighter-bombers and fighters, enough to partly cover its losses, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR told Ukrainian news agency UNIAN, which published the reply on 23 October. Its older bombers are a different story. Russia has no serial production of new Tu-95s, Tu-22M3s, or Su-24s and keeps them flying through repairs and upgrades, so each one lost for good leaves a lasting gap, HUR said.
Ukraine’s Navy said its Neptune missiles hit six Su-34M bombers at Borisoglebsk airbase in Russia’s Voronezh Oblast overnight into 15 October. Zelenskyy later said four were destroyed and two damaged. The Su-34 is one of the jets that drop Russia’s glide bombs, heavy bombs fitted with wing-and-guidance kits, on Ukrainian positions and towns.
How fast Russia replaces its jets
Russia can probably deliver 10–15 Su-34s a year now, HUR estimated. Deliveries grew from eight in 2022 to 11 in 2023 and 12–14 in 2024. But the agency said that trend does not confirm the same pace today.
For the Su-35S fighter, HUR pointed to an average of about 11–12 a year in 2021–2025. It called that a rough benchmark, not an established 2026 output. Su-30SM2 and Su-57 production continues, but reliable rates cannot be determined. Su-30 figures also mix new builds with upgrades of older Su-30SMs, HUR noted.
What Russia had, and what it lost or saw badly damaged in 2026
By the end of 2025, Russia had about 125 Su-34 and Su-34M bombers, which HUR counts together. It also had 140–145 Su-30 jets of various versions, 135–140 Su-35S, and about 20 Su-57s, HUR estimated. These are only fleet estimates, not a guaranteed number of jets Russia can send on combat missions at the same time, the agency cautioned. Some are under repair or upgrade, and HUR is not disclosing the current fleet size.
HUR also named specific 2026 cases of Russian aircraft destroyed or critically damaged. A Tu-22M3 crashed in Irkutsk Oblast on 15 June. Strikes on Engels airbase on 17 July and 28 August hit two Tu-95MS. The first suffered critical damage to its tail section, and HUR treats the second as a probable irrecoverable loss.
The list also includes a Su-35 that Ukraine’s military says it shot down on 8 July, a claim backed by published materials showing debris. It adds a Su-57 crash in Moscow Oblast on 23 July and a collision of two Su-35S over Kursk Oblast on 7 September. Full official details on those two incidents are still missing, HUR noted. Strikes on several Su-57s and a Su-34 at Shagol airbase on 25 April, and on a Su-24 in Crimea on 7 September, were also reported, but the state of those jets is unknown, so counting them as destroyed would be premature, HUR said. The list, as published, leaves out the Su-34s at Borisoglebsk and the Tu-95MS that Russia’s defense ministry said crashed on takeoff in Amur Oblast in late September.

articles.title: For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
articles.body:
For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
What A7 is and how it became the largest player in the shadow payments market
Sanctions against Russian banks and payment systems, along with their disconnection from SWIFT after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, gave rise to shadow intermediaries offering Russians cross-border money transfers. Many have offices in the capital’s Moscow City business district, the investigative outlet Proekt reported in spring 2026.
The largest is A7, a company owned by Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, who was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in Moldova. Shor owns a controlling stake; the remaining 49% belongs to Russia’s state-owned Promsvyazbank (PSB). In late 2019, PSB officially became the designated bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry and defense industry.
The state development corporation VEB.RF, headed by Igor Shuvalov, “provides support” to A7. Proekt’s journalists suggest that Roman Abramovich may play “an important but secret role in the company.” A source in the cross-border payments business described Abramovich to Proekt as A7’s “protector and sponsor.” In the source’s view, Abramovich began working with Shor because he valued Shor’s ability to “devise financial schemes.” Abramovich’s representatives deny that he is involved in A7.
How Abramovich is connected to A7
According to Proekt, Shor’s first flight to Russia after a Moldovan court ordered his arrest in absentia was aboard Abramovich’s plane, suggesting that the two knew each other well.
Igor Shuvalov, the head of VEB.RF, the state corporation that “provides support” to A7, is a longtime acquaintance of Abramovich’s.
In 2024, A7 rented offices in Abramovich’s Belye Sady and Skolkovo Park business centers. Two A7 subsidiaries still occupy offices owned by Abramovich.
“Another indication of the oligarch’s involvement is the enormous financial support A7 receives from businessman Viktor Kharitonin, whom the press has long called ‘Abramovich’s protégé,’” Proekt reported.
A business partner of Abramovich’s, who spoke to Proekt on condition of anonymity, estimated that A7 handles about 15% of all cross-border transfers in Russia. The company puts its share even higher, at 19%. “No one else even comes close to A7,” a source working in the market told Proekt. The outlet’s other sources agreed that A7 is the largest player in the industry.
Proekt obtained a list of all of A7’s clients. They included at least 25 Russian companies already under U.S. and EU sanctions. Five manufacture or supply combat drones used by the Russian army in its war against Ukraine.
Other A7 clients include Arkady Rotenberg’s tour operator Biblioglobus, the online marketplace Wildberries, cigarette manufacturer International Tobacco Group, the Sunlight jewelry chain, and industrial companies including Leonid Mikhelson’s natural gas producer Arctic LNG 2, AAEM Turbine Technologies, and S7 Engineering.
In late October, journalists from the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) expanded on Proekt’s investigation. After reviewing internal company documents and speaking with sources, they found that most payments entering A7’s network are funded by hundreds of metric tons of rubles in cash collected from individuals and companies at several Moscow wholesale and retail markets, including the largest, Sadovod.
Sadovod is known as a market where most transactions are conducted in cash, and many of its shop employees and owners are migrant workers from countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. “Sadovod is simply a big client base,” a source familiar with the situation told ICIJ, explaining A7’s choice of location.
How the scheme works
Before 2022, intermediaries at Sadovod were already converting cash into ordinary bank transfers or into cryptocurrency, which most often went to China. Western sanctions later disrupted this system by cutting Russian companies off from SWIFT.
A7’s improved system allowed a group of brokers at Sadovod to keep operating. They now accept bags of cash brought in by vendors and count the money, according to the documents. A7’s records refer to these initial cash collection points as “departments”; there are at least eight.
The brokers then pack the rubles into numbered bags. The bags are loaded into vans along with customers’ payment orders and sent to an A7 payment processing center elsewhere in Moscow. About 50 cashiers work there, recording the cash in A7’s counting system. The cash is then delivered to Promsvyazbank, which places it in a vault and credits A7’s accounts.
A7 then uses its shell companies registered abroad. Intermediary companies in Kyrgyzstan buy cryptocurrency through Grinex, a crypto exchange linked to A7. By this point, the money is no longer identified as originating in Russia, thanks to Kyrgyzstan’s permissive policies on cryptocurrency transactions.
PSB provides the banking infrastructure for transferring money to Kyrgyzstan, along with loans and guarantees when needed. From Kyrgyzstan, the money goes to intermediary companies linked to A7 in third countries, most often in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. They convert the cryptocurrency into local currencies and send the money to the end recipient.
“By the time [an A7 payment] is received, nobody in the chain, from the U.S. clearing bank to the Chinese supplier, knows where it came from,” said illicit finance expert Zachary Tvarozna, who co-authored an investigation into A7 conducted with the British nonprofit Open Source Centre. “Washington essentially created a market for A7 [by restricting legitimate transactions] and then did nothing about it,” he concluded.
The risks this scheme poses to the global financial system
From November 2024 to July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 metric tons of rubles in cash worth more than $14 billion, ICIJ and Proekt reported. The journalists were unable to trace the cash’s origins, but it is clear that most of it went to China, as before.
A registry of A7 promissory notes that leaked online and was reviewed by ICIJ shows that A7’s cash deposits at PSB rose in 2025, reaching 195 billion rubles ($2.3 billion) a month by April and 250 billion rubles ($3.1 billion) in June. At its peak, A7 processed at least 58 metric tons of cash a month.
On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 a “significant transnational criminal organization.” This means U.S. financial institutions will no longer be able to process transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents” — foreign shell companies through which the network routes payments for clients in Russia.
A7 “uses a modern, multilayered system of controls” and “was established to ensure uninterrupted payments in the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures,” the company said in a press release issued after the Treasury Department’s announcement. “All clients are screened to identify risks and prevent us from serving individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” the company insisted.
Just two years earlier, when it launched, A7 presented itself as a “sanctions-proof payment system.”
George Voloshin, a financial crime expert at the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists, told ICIJ that A7 “not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls” but “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime.”
International intermediary banks and beneficiaries effectively become complicit in these activities even though they do not know where the money comes from. The reason lies in the cash itself, Voloshin added:
Cash is considered one of the highest-risk payment methods because it is anonymous, can move across borders, and is not tied to a specific person or company.
The entire scheme “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” said Ilya Shumanov, managing partner of TriTrace Investigations, a Russian company specializing in financial market due diligence. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
According to documents reviewed by ICIJ, A7 received 314 payment requests totaling $76 million from brokers working at Sadovod in late 2024. All of the money was intended for the Hong Kong export company Yiton Trading Ltd.
A7 representatives did not respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Ukraine has waited nearly a month for US to sign off on Patriot missiles, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has been waiting for almost a month for the US defense secretary to sign off on critical missile supplies, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
"In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again," Zelensky said on X/Twitter.
The Ukrainian leader has repeatedly called on the US, which supplies missiles purchased by NATO allies under a program known as PURL, to speed up deliveries ahead of winter.
Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that a batch of interceptors may not have been delivered, but said that the delay was not for political reasons.
Delayed missile deliveries are adding to Ukraine's tensions with the US after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticized Zelensky for Ukraine's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine struggles with limited intelligence sharing, Starlink issues
In recent weeks, Ukraine said that at some point it experienced gaps in getting intelligence from the US on Russian missile attacks. It also reported that Starlink's military version has been throttled for days, disrupting military operations and air defenses.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Both SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and US officials have said publicly that any decisions on Starlink and Starshield limitations could only have been taken by the other.

articles.title: Baltic defence conference opens in Vilnius to discuss regional security
articles.body:
Politicians, military officials and industry leaders are gathering in Vilnius for a two-day conference on Baltic defence strategies and lessons from Russia's war in Ukraine, starting on Monday.
Held at the National Gallery of Art, the event will focus on strengthening European air defence, addressing gaps in NATO's military capabilities and exploring the role of artificial intelligence and drone technology on the battlefield.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas will open the conference, while European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius will speak about a unified European defence shield.
"Ukraine teaches us that to defend the Baltic region and the whole of Europe, we must be able to produce a lot, be fast, innovative, and resilient," Kubilius said.
The programme includes presentations by practitioners from Ukraine's Defence Ministry and armed forces.
Discussions will also cover societal resilience, the European defence industry's production capacity, nuclear deterrence, and military intelligence.
Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said insights from Ukrainian specialists would help improve understanding of what constitutes effective preparedness and what practical solutions are needed before a crisis begins.
The event will be attended by top-ranking Lithuanian military officers, as well as international experts from the Institute for the Study of War, the Royal United Services Institute, the European Space Agency and other institutions.

articles.title: US ready to strike Iran 'within 96 hours' of Trump's order, Israel pushes for joint attack - report
articles.body:
US forces are prepared to launch a major attack against Iran "within 96 hours" of receiving the order from US President Donald Trump, two US officials told CNN on Sunday.
While Trump has not made a final decision on whether to commit to major military action after the US midterms, officials said any attack that would be conducted would "be a big effort," going beyond prior US strikes against Iranian assets that can be quickly rebuilt, such as missile launchers and radars.
One source briefed on the matter told CNN that Israel had been preparing for possibly striking Iran, as well as lobbying the US to participate in the strikes.
However, US officials, including Trump, told Israel to hold off on attacking, likely until after the midterm elections.
“The plans are ready, waiting for Trump’s approval, could be after the midterms,” the source said.
Iran, Houthis unlikely to preemptively strike, but ready for retaliation
Two other sources told CNN that both Iran and the Houthis were taking the possibility of renewed US attacks very seriously, according to US intelligence.
Any attack launched by the US - or Israel - would trigger immediate retaliation against US personnel and facilities in the Middle East, the sources added, which is one of the reasons the US is expected to withdraw more personnel from its embassies in the region.
However, one source familiar with US intelligence assessments said that officials believe that both Iran and the Houthis were unlikely to preemptively strike US or Israeli infrastructure at this stage.
The White House declined to comment, while a senior Pentagon official told CNN that “The Department is a planning organization, and its job is to develop and execute military options ordered by the President.”

articles.title: Not just Iran: Netanyahu defies IDF chief over continuing Hebron operation
articles.body:
The military operation in Hebron, launched after a deadly shooting attack near the West Bank city killed two IDF soldiers, has become another point of contention between the military leadership and Israel's political leadership, just a day before Tuesday's election. While troops from the IDF's 98th Division continue intensive operations involving searches for weapons, arrests of suspects, the evacuation of Palestinian residents and the demolition of unauthorized structures, military officials believe that the limited operational results so far warrant reassessing whether the operation should continue in its current form.
According to sources familiar with the discussions, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir presented his position during a meeting with the political leadership, attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, arguing that the time had come to end the operation. Netanyahu and Katz, however, rejected that assessment and instructed the military to continue. Ultimately, the chief of staff's recommendation was not accepted, and the decision was made to keep the operation underway.
The IDF has pointed, among other concerns, to the legal difficulties involved in keeping Palestinian residents away from their homes for extended periods, particularly when the operation is not producing significant military gains. So far, troops have made arrests and located a limited number of weapons, but have not uncovered unusual weaponry or large weapons stockpiles.
The political leadership, however, presents a different assessment. Officials argue that the two terrorists who carried out the deadly attack were armed with automatic weapons and substantial quantities of ammunition, making it necessary for the IDF to continue searching for additional weapons in the area. They also maintain that prolonging the operation will strengthen deterrence. Security officials explain that the very presence of large IDF forces operating inside Hebron creates a psychological impact among Palestinians, particularly because the troops have entered a major Palestinian city rather than refugee camps, as they did during previous operations in Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem.
The current disagreement recalls an IDF operation in the Qalandiya refugee camp in August. At the time, the military defined its objectives as targeting terrorist operatives and infrastructure. Katz also pushed for a large-scale operation and again raised the possibility of taking control of another refugee camp, similar to the operations carried out in Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams.
IDF officials said the military had operational plans for every refugee camp but had not mobilized forces to carry them out because there was no operational necessity. There was also tension over contingency planning for a scenario known in the military as a "turning of the guns," involving a possible armed escalation in which Palestinian security forces turn their weapons against Israel. Katz presented the IDF's extensive and aggressive plan for such a scenario, although intelligence assessments at the time did not indicate that an escalation of that kind was imminent in the West Bank.
It is important to note that the prolonged military operations in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, which Katz was among those pushing for and which were conducted under Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, led to a significant decline in terrorist activity in the area, according to Israeli security assessments. 
However, the Qalandiya operation ended after just two days and, based on the information available so far, did not produce significant operational results. Now, in Hebron, the question is once again whether continuing the operation is likely to yield further results or whether it has already achieved its main objectives.
But the debate over the Hebron operation is unfolding against a broader and more complicated security backdrop. The IDF is currently also focused on preventing the next attack, particularly attacks carried out by lone assailants inspired by previous incidents. Security officials are concerned about copycat attacks that could develop following exposure to incitement on social media and military activity on the ground. Central Command is therefore concentrating its efforts on identifying threats early, thwarting potential attackers and preventing an escalation that could emerge from several directions.
The IDF stresses that such conditions require precise, targeted counterterrorism operations, accompanied by constant assessments of their operational value and their consequences on the ground. The concern is that an escalation could develop rapidly, making it necessary to consider not only existing threats but also the reactions military operations themselves could provoke.
Against this backdrop, the Hebron operation illustrates the tension between the political leadership's demand to continue military activity in pursuit of deterrence and additional weapons discoveries, and the IDF's position that the operational benefits must be weighed against the consequences of prolonging the operation for the local Palestinian population.

articles.title: Ukraine confirms strike on Russia's sole manufacturer of power batteries for aerial bomb modules
articles.body:
Ukraine confirms strike on Russia's sole manufacturer of power batteries for aerial bomb modules
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has confirmed a successful strike on the power supply element production workshop for Russian weaponry at the Energiya plant in the Russian city of Yelets in Lipetsk Oblast, which was carried out on 25 October or in the early hours of 26 October.
Source: Ukraine's General Staff
Quote: "A fire broke out on the premises of the plant. The strike complicates the Russian army's manufacturing of power sources for missiles, guided aerial bombs and other armaments."
Details: The General Staff added that the plant is the sole manufacturer of power batteries for glide and correction modules used in aerial bombs, whilst also producing batteries for Iskander-M operational-tactical missile systems and sea-launched cruise missiles.
OSINT analysts previously reported that on 25 October, the Energiya plant in Yelets was attacked, likely using Storm Shadow cruise missiles.
The General Staff later detailed the results of a strike conducted on 23 October against the Proton-Electrotex company in Oryol in Russia's Oryol Oblast.
Quote: "The main microchip production workshop was destroyed and the building alongside servers of the Proton-Electrotex in the city of Oryol in Oryol Oblast was damaged."
Details: The General Staff noted that this complicates the Russian military's production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles.
Damage was also confirmed to three buildings used for the preparation and fitting of strike UAVs and one launch rail following a 23 October strike on a drone storage, preparation and launch site near Donetsk.
Another targeted facility was the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Tolyatti, Samara Oblast. As a result of a 24 October strike, a process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units and one fractionation column were damaged.
Quote: "This deals a blow to the supply chain for solid rocket propellant used in tactical and ballistic missiles."
Background: On 23 October and on the night of 23-24 October, Ukraine's defence forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, and Proton-Electrotex in the city of Oryol.

articles.title: Ukraine’s air defenses down 112 Russian drones, three missiles overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses down 112 Russian drones, three missiles overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
According to the military, overnight on October 26, beginning at 18:00 on October 25, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with one Kh-31P missile, three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles launched from temporarily occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and 140 Shahed-type attack drones, including 70 jet-powered ones, as well as Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoy drones. The attacks came from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo and Millerovo in Russia, as well as Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on October 26, air defenses had shot down or suppressed three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles and 112 enemy drones, including Shahed-type drones (56 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and other types of unmanned aerial vehicles.
Russian aerial weapons were recorded hitting 15 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at four locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, over the past week Russia launched about 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky: Hegseth’s approval for Patriot missiles has been pending for nearly a month
articles.body:
Zelensky: Hegseth’s approval for Patriot missiles has been pending for nearly a month
The President said this on Facebook following a meeting on weapons supplies from Ukraine’s partners and efforts to restore the energy system after Russian strikes, Ukrinform reports.
“The Minister of Defense of Ukraine, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs reported on the supply of air defense interceptors to Ukraine, first and foremost Patriot missiles. We are working on several tracks – with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again. Conversations with other countries are also ongoing,” Zelensky said following the meeting.
According to Zelensky, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi reported on the work underway in the regions.
“I thank every repair crew and all energy companies that are fully carrying out their assigned tasks. The work is continuing virtually nonstop, and we are using the equipment reserves we have built up,” the President said.
He added that preparations for the November Ramstein meeting were also discussed. According to Zelensky, it is important to speed up the implementation of decisions that have been on the table for some time.
“Every support package is an opportunity to protect people's lives. Thank you to everyone who is providing real support and, in particular, helping speed up these critically important deliveries,” the President said.
As reported earlier, in an interview with TSN Tyzhden, Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been progress on the issue of providing Ukraine with missiles for Patriot systems, but the process was moving very slowly.

articles.title: France Deploys Maritime Patrol Aircraft to Protect Black Sea Shipping
articles.body:
France has deployed an Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft for operations in the Black Sea following a series of drone attacks on merchant vessels near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
The Romanian media outlet Curs de Guvernare reported this, citing flight-tracking data for military aircraft.
According to the publication, a French Navy Atlantique 2 (ATL2) maritime patrol aircraft arrived in Constanța, Romania, on October 18.
On October 24, France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said during a visit to Varna, Bulgaria, that the Atlantique 2 had been operating in the region for two weeks as part of NATO missions.
According to the minister, the French aircraft had also taken part in rescue operations following recent attacks on merchant vessels. Barrot recalled that three vessels had been attacked, one of which sank within minutes about 100 kilometers from Varna.
Meanwhile, a U.S. Navy Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and anti-submarine warfare aircraft, which arrived from Naval Air Station Sigonella in Sicily, patrolled the western Black Sea near the Bulgarian coast.
Militarnyi previously reported on the deployment of a U.S. P-8A Poseidon to patrol Bulgarian waters on October 19.
The deployment of additional patrol aircraft comes amid a deteriorating security situation in the western Black Sea.
On October 17, two Romanian Air Force F-16 fighters shot down two Geran-family strike drones that had violated Romanian airspace over the country’s territorial waters.
Following the series of attacks, Romania initiated a meeting of the North Atlantic Council, which took place in Brussels on October 20.
Following the meeting, NATO decided to strengthen surveillance of the Black Sea, including through additional patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and reconnaissance units.

articles.title: Zelensky undermines Trump more than Iran and Cuba do – Medvedev
articles.body:
Zelensky undermines Trump more than Iran and Cuba do – Medvedev
Vladimir Zelensky’s disregard for Donald Trump is doing more damage to the US president’s interests than Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela do combined, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev said on Sunday.
Ukraine’s leader has publicly backed Trump’s predecessor and former political rival, Joe Biden, rejected US proposals to settle the Ukraine conflict and worked to turn European leaders against Trump, Medvedev alleged.
“The Kiev scumbag regularly spits straight in the face of the US president, ignoring his demands and turning influential Americans (and not-so-influential Europeans) against him,” Medvedev, who currently serves as deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said in a Telegram post.
He said that Zelensky “shamelessly lined his own pockets with American taxpayer money” under Biden, who Trump says provided Ukraine with some $350 billion in US aid. “And he kept dipping into the pot under Trump, too, taking whatever was left,” Medvedev added.
The Ukrainian “cozied up to Mexican drug cartels” by providing drone warfare training in exchange for proceeds from drug sales in the US, he alleged.
Zelensky has also “given the American president the finger” by refusing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries despite Trump’s repeated warnings.
There is a growing rift between Trump and Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop, accusing it of exacerbating the global fuel crisis and raising prices for Americans – a sensitive issue ahead of the November 3 US midterms. Kiev has thus far refused.
Zelensky has also accused Washington of temporarily restricting intelligence sharing and access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone operations.
To ease the fuel crisis, Trump temporarily waived sanctions on Russian fuel exports as part of a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Under the agreement, Moscow agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tons in November and further shipments thereafter. The first three tankers carrying Russian diesel are already heading across the Atlantic, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.

articles.title: I saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’
articles.body:
It was mid-April and after a month of deadly airstrikes across Lebanon, Israel agreed to a ceasefire. Much of the bombing had focused on southern Lebanon, where entire villages had been demolished. But with the truce, people were hopeful of being able to return to their homes or to see what remained.
Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old photojournalist, decided to join Amal Khalil, 42, a newspaper reporter in Lebanon, on a trip to an area in the south of the country to document the aftermath of war. The two had worked together on a number of assignments after Khalil had seen Faraj’s work on social media and contacted her.
“I expected it to be like every other time. Amal and I would go out, take some footage and then leave. I had absolutely no sense of fear. We could hear some gunfire and artillery, but as a videographer, you find those things important to document and capture,” says Faraj, who was freelancing alongside finishing her degree in radio and TV.
By the time they reached the village of al-Tiri on the afternoon of 22 April, Faraj began to look out the window and reminisce. She was born and grew up in the nearby city of Bint Jbeil. “My whole life revolved around this area. As we say, a fish suffocates when it’s taken out of water. That’s how we feel whenever we leave Bint Jbeil.”
Ahead of them was a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, 27, a municipal official in Bint Jbeil, and Mohammed Hourani, 37, a friend of the mayor. They had met them by chance earlier in the day at Tebnine governmental hospital, which had become a gathering point because people considered it relatively safe and would base their movements from there. Bazzi was due to sign a marriage contract that evening, but was still keen to join the trip.
Faraj says she did not hear the missile coming, just the sound of Khalil screaming and then the sight of the car in front of them on fire. The two women got out of their car.
“I do not know how I managed to stay so calm. The only thing I could think was: if I come closer, I will be able to see Ali. Maybe I will be able to pull him out.”
Khalil kept repeating: “Oh God, they’re gone.” Slowly, Faraj began to understand what was going on. “I could see their bodies torn apart.”
Then the drones appeared.
“When the drones came, my heart started pounding in a terrifying way. The drone started coming very close to my face. I tried to cover my face, but whenever I did, it would fly back up. That was when I really felt the real danger.”
The drones flew low and close as Khalil and Faraj frantically made phone calls to emergency services who repeatedly assured them that help was on its way. Faraj says the assurances were “like an anaesthetic”, something that briefly numbed the reality that no one was rescuing them.
One of the paramedics on a call told them to get into their car and try to drive back up the road, as ambulances were being preventing from driving to where they were. But as they tried to get into the car, it was struck by a missile.
Both of them were thrown backwards, with Khalil wrapping her arms around Faraj. As the drone continued to circle overhead, Khalil said she hoped it would “think we were dead”.
With the nearby car engulfed in flames, they decided to take shelter in a nearby house. Khalil had visible injuries, with blood on her face, hand and leg. Faraj says she sent her sister a last message before her phone died: “There’s no hope left. Forgive me.”
Inside, they sat on a bathroom floor. Khalil was unable to move, so Faraj says she crawled to a position from where she could watch the road. Suddenly a drone descended towards her.
“It had been high up and suddenly it came down. The way it descended was terrifying. My heart stopped.” Soon after this, Faraj says she came back inside and began to feel tired and detached from what was happening. “I felt alone.”
Then came the sound of a missile falling. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life. I’ve heard so many strikes and drones, but this was completely different. It was terrifying and Amal was screaming,” she says.
She does not remember what happened next, but when she opened her eyes an enormous weight was pressing down on her body. Everything was black and she could barely breathe. She was trapped underneath rubble. “I couldn’t bear the weight. It felt like something was pushing me down, crushing me. All I cared about was being able to breathe.”
Faraj says she then heard a voice and thought it was her father, but it was a paramedic who had managed to reach the scene of the attack. As he held her by the shoulders, Faraj says she instinctively clung to him and refused to let go. “I told him: ‘Don’t leave me. I’m afraid to stay alone.’” He stayed beside her while a second paramedic cleared the rubble.
As the sound of drones returned once more, the paramedics quickly pulled Faraj free as she screamed from the pain. At about the same time, Faraj says she heard a stun grenade dropped by the drone. As they drove away in the ambulance, she repeatedly mistook the sound of the vehicle for a drone. “They’re going to hit us. We’re not going to make it,” she says she kept repeating.
After they got to a hospital, Faraj says she started to ask about Khalil. At first the nurses tried to reassure her. But eventually, she says, they fell silent. “That’s when I knew she was gone.” Khalil is believed to have died about an hour before the paramedics had been allowed to return to the area again after rescuing Faraj.
The Israeli military justified their attack saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. However, human rights groups called it a war crime. As Khalil and Faraj took refuge in the building the Israeli military received repeated messages urging them to allow a rescue operation. A week before the attack, an Israeli military spokesperson shared a video of Khalil published by her newspaper and described it as “terrorist media”. Khalil had also received death threats from Israeli numbers.
Today, as Faraj prepares to return to university, she still struggles to walk properly and has visible injuries to a hand. An injury to her face has affected the movement of one eyebrow; others are hidden by her clothes and hijab. Her limp is especially hard to bear. “I was always on the move. I lost that. Even climbing stairs can be hard,” she says.
At first she was in shock, she says, but now more symptoms are starting to appear. She wakes at night screaming and buries herself in the pillows as if a missile is going to strike. The sound of drones and warplanes put her on edge.
Returning to frontline journalism feels uncertain and she says she is repeatedly haunted by the image of Hourani lying on the ground after the first missile attack. “His head was turned towards me. His eyes open and looking at me. That is something I will never get out of my head.”

articles.title: Trump rules out Sunday strike on Iran as Netanyahu warns Israel faces imminent existential threat
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch a military strike against Iran today.
Asked by a reporter whether a US attack on Iran could take place as soon as today, Trump replied: “Would I tell you that? The answer is no. There will not be a strike today.”
The president did not rule out military action at a later date.
Earlier on Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has yet to make a decision on whether or not to renew strikes against Iran.
“Should I finish the job - which would be very easy to do - or should I reach an agreement? That is the whole decision," he said.
Trump says 'not much going on' at Iranian nuclear sites, Netanyahu claims Israel facing existential threat
Trump added that the US is actively monitoring activity at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site as well as three other sites that were allegedly destroyed in previous strikes.
“There isn’t much activity going on there,” he clarified.
Trump’s comments came after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a post on X/Twitter that Israel is currently facing “real and tangible existential danger” coming from Iran.
Netanyahu claimed that only a small window of time remains for Israel and the US to act and completely defeat Iran.
Netanyahu also shared a video from one of the IDF's anti-missile batteries where he said: "The IDF is prepared on both defense and in offense. I warn our enemies – you will absorb strikes out of proportion, stronger than you can even imagine."
Trump said on Friday that Washington is weighing another military operation against Iran, saying that the US “may do another little Epic Fury” during a pre-midterm election rally in Florida.
US-Israeli strike on Iran: Not if, when
Additionally, US officials believe that a joint US-Israeli strike on Iran is not a question of “if,” but “when.”
“It appears that Trump has decided he wants to carry out a significant strike against Iran. The only question is when to do it,” one official told The Jerusalem Post.
Another official said the president was “very close” to escalating US action against Iran.
The prevailing assessment in Washington is that Trump will hold off on making a final decision on military action against Iran until after the November 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told Fox News in an interview: “I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's the decision.”

articles.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
articles.body:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

articles.title: Germany’s elite special forces unit is preparing for a possible war with Russia - media
articles.body:
Germany’s elite special forces unit is preparing for a possible war with Russia - media
Kyiv • UNN
Germany’s KSK special forces unit has changed its training due to a possible conflict with Russia. The soldiers are training to operate against tanks, artillery and drones.
The German Special Operations Command (KSK) is reviewing its training program in light of a possible military conflict with Moscow. BILD reports, according to UNN.
Details
"We are very specifically orienting ourselves toward an adversary represented by Russia," KSK commander Andreas Kühne said in an interview with BILD.
According to him, operations used to be planned for approximately three days, but now the soldiers are preparing to remain in the field for much longer. In addition, the special forces are once again training to face an adversary equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare capabilities. They are also practicing operations in extreme cold: the KSK is preparing for conditions typical of the eastern flank.
The unit is based at the Zeppelin Barracks in Calw, near Stuttgart. Approximately 1,500 personnel serve in the KSK. However, only one-third of them are special forces operators; the rest are administrative staff. The selection process is extremely rigorous: only about 15% of candidates pass it.
Just a few years ago, the future of the most elite unit hung by a thread. Incidents involving far-right extremists, a Nazi salute and pig heads at a farewell party, missing ammunition, and the discovery of a weapons and explosives cache at a KSK soldier's home shook the unit. In 2020, one of the special forces unit's companies was disbanded.
We remind you
The President of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Martin Jäger, considers the threat of an armed confrontation between Germany and Russia to be real.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis say they targeted Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
articles.body:
Muhammed Emin Canik and Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Yemen's Houthi group said early Monday that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh and launched attacks on pumping stations along the East-West crude oil pipeline.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on the US social media platform X that the group targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.
Saree also said the Houthis carried out drone attacks targeting crude oil pumping stations along the East-West Pipeline.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense Directorate earlier announced that the early warning system had issued a danger alert for Riyadh.
Major General Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh had been intercepted.
Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since September 2014, when the Houthis seized control of the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces.
The East-West Pipeline is one of Saudi Arabia's most important crude oil transportation routes.
Operated by the state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, the pipeline stretches approximately 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from the Abqaiq area in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Located entirely within Saudi Arabia, it transports crude oil from production and processing facilities in the east to refineries and export terminals along the Red Sea.
The pipeline provides Saudi Arabia with an overland alternative for transporting oil to the Red Sea without relying on maritime shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's internationally recognized government since March 2015.
Clashes between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis have intensified in recent months. The group has targeted Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones, accusing the kingdom of being responsible for attacks against it.

articles.title: Ukraine is stalling EU-required reform of bureau that can raid any official, risking European money it badly needs
articles.body:
Whoever controls Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation wields enormous influence over law enforcement, judges, and government officials. The EU wants Ukraine to reform it, and Ukraine’s government is likely to pass changes that satisfy monitoring requirements on paper while leaving the body effectively under the President’s Office’s control, the investigative outlet Texty reports.
The stakes are money and power at once. The State Bureau of Investigation, known by its Ukrainian initials DBR, investigates officials, judges, prosecutors, and soldiers. So choosing an independent director is one of the rule-of-law conditions the EU has tied to Ukraine’s 2026 and 2027 budget aid.
Yet the version the government may pass would change how the director is chosen only for the one after next, in 2032. Brussels wants the model used at the anti-corruption bureau NABU, where the chief cannot be confirmed without the votes of independent foreign experts.
Who picks the watchdog
Today a nine-member commission selects the director:
- three named by the president
- three by a parliament his party dominates
- three proposed by the government on international partners’ suggestion.
That leaves the foreign experts without a decisive vote and the President’s Office effectively choosing the winner. Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy promised in January that a reform bill would reach parliament within a month.
It is now October, and there is none.
Director Oleksii Sukhachov’s term ends this year, so his successor will be picked under the old rules.
Sukhachov has publicly argued that overhauling the bureau during the war would threaten the state.
The deadline to adopt the reform was October. To carry it out, the end of 2026. Miss it, and Ukraine risks reputational damage and the European funding it needs amid a budget deficit, money the EU has frozen before when anti-corruption guarantees slipped.
A factory of “procedural nightmaring”
What makes the fight so bitter is that the bureau’s searches, seizures, and summonses are levers over individuals and whole institutions.
For example, NABU’s Operation Midas tapes, from the $100 million kickback case at the state nuclear company Energoatom, mention the bureau’s entire leadership. In March 2025, its investigators searched the commission that vets and appoints Ukraine’s judges, itself reformed with international experts, in what the commission called pressure that could stall the courts.
Cases against the bureau’s own officials, meanwhile, are handled by a unit inside the bureau. And its director sits under his own cloud: the outlet Slidstvo.Info reported that his brother bought 143 apartments cheaply from a developer.
