articles.title: Israeli media highlights Egypt’s Rafale deployment as part of broader regional deterrence strategy
articles.body:
Israeli media have highlighted the deployment of Egyptian Rafale fighter jets on the eastern front, describing the move as part of a broader military strategy aimed at strengthening Egypt’s deterrence capabilities and maintaining operational readiness across multiple regional fronts.
The Israeli platform Ntziv.net reported that Egypt possesses an advanced network of modern airbases, challenging the assumption that its most sophisticated fighter aircraft are positioned toward Israel because of insufficient infrastructure elsewhere in the country.
According to the platform, Egypt’s deployment of modern combat aircraft, particularly the French-made Dassault Rafale, reflects a strategy of multi-front deterrence, strategic independence and regional power projection extending beyond its eastern border.
The report identified Gabal al-Basur Air Base, northwest of Cairo, as the principal operating base for Egypt’s Rafale fleet, noting that it is located well inside Egyptian territory, away from the Sinai Peninsula and the Israeli border.
It emphasised that the Rafale is a multirole fighter aircraft with an operational radius of approximately 2,000 kilometres, allowing it to conduct missions across several strategically important areas without requiring permanent deployment at forward bases.
These areas include Libya to the west, the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Sinai Peninsula.
The platform also pointed to Egypt’s extensive network of operational airbases, including facilities in Mersa Matruh and Sidi Barrani near the Libyan border, as well as Aswan in southern Egypt.
It noted that Cairo has invested billions of dollars in modernizing its air force infrastructure, including the development of Berenice Airbase on the Red Sea coast, a strategic facility designed to accommodate advanced combat aircraft.
The report argued that Egypt’s air force modernization should not be viewed exclusively through the lens of its military relationship with Israel, but rather as part of a wider doctrine of active deterrence and strategic autonomy.
It further suggested that Egypt has sought to diversify its military suppliers to reduce dependence on the United States, particularly given Washington’s restrictions on certain advanced weapons exports intended to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge.
According to the Israeli platform, Egypt’s acquisition of Rafale fighters from France has enabled Cairo to obtain advanced radar and missile capabilities outside the framework of US arms export restrictions.
The report concluded that Egypt’s Rafale fleet and expanding military infrastructure reflect a broader effort to maintain operational flexibility across several regional theaters while strengthening the country’s independent defense capabilities.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it downed 2 missiles fired by Houthis
articles.body:
(Reuters) -- Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.
It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery.
Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases."
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognized government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilization there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

According to relatives and officials the agency cites, many of the men had gone to Russia for work, only to be tricked or forced into its army.
Russia fills its ranks partly with foreigners. In April, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said the Russian Defense Ministry plans to enlist at least 18,500 of them in 2026. Foreign recruits let the Kremlin put off hard choices about another mobilization at home, the Atlantic Council argued in May. Home governments have pushed back before, among them Ghana in August. Kyrgyz minister: contracts are forced in enlistment offices and jails
Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev addressed the problem at a parliamentary committee on 13 October, answering lawmakers’ questions. Kenya wants five men held by Ukraine treated as possible trafficking victims
Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, who also handles foreign affairs, gave lawmakers a count on 8 October. “The Ministry has records of 354 Kenyan nationals involved in the Russian-Ukraine crisis,” he told them. Kenya says Russia agreed to stop recruiting its citizens – families of the missing are still waiting
Ukraine holds five Kenyans captured while fighting for Russia, and Nairobi has already appealed to Kyiv over them. The government told Parliament it wants them treated as people who may have been trafficked abroad.

articles.title: Could Syria help Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis without troops?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria denied plans to send troops to Yemen – but how could it still help Saudi Arabia?
Reports have continued to circulate about a possible deployment of Syrian fighters to Yemen despite Damascus' denials.
But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said such a move was unlikely given Syria’s own domestic security challenges, and suggested that any military support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis could take other forms, without involving troops on Yemeni territory.
Citing unnamed Yemeni intelligence sources, Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Riyadh and Damascus had held talks on transferring up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to Yemen.
It said a Syrian military delegation had recently visited the Saudi capital and the kingdom’s southern regions to assess the proposed deployment.
According to the newspaper, Brigadier General Khaled Khattab, formerly leader of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and now commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army, spent four days in the southern Saudi regions of Asir and Najran, accompanied by Saudi officers. The delegation reportedly visited sites being prepared to receive Syrian fighters.
Meanwhile, Brigadier General Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army’s Third Corps and a former Hayat Tahrir al-Sham commander, was said to have met Saudi officers at the defence ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, benefits and their expected military role. Al-Akhbar said the delegation had finalised logistical preparations for the transfer.
The New Arab could not independently verify Al-Akhbar’s claims.
Could Syria support Riyadh without entering Yemen?
Muaz al-Abdallah, a Syria analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), told The New Arab that any Syrian military support to Saudi Arabia would not necessarily involve deploying troops inside Yemen.
He said one possibility was that Syrian forces could be sent to help protect Saudi Arabia’s southern border, rather than take part directly in the fighting against the Houthis on Yemeni territory. Al-Abdallah said this statement left open the possibility of military cooperation with Riyadh, even if Damascus maintained that it had not deployed forces inside Yemen.
"Damascus has said it has not sent forces to Yemen, while also expressing support for Saudi security and saying military cooperation would take place through official channels and bilateral agreements," Al-Abdallah said.
He added that deploying Syrian personnel to the Saudi side of the border would not necessarily contradict the government’s denial that it had sent forces to Yemen, but could instead represent another way of supporting Riyadh.
Al-Abdallah suggested that Saudi Arabia could increase its financial assistance and investments in Syria’s reconstruction in return for military support.
Syrian drone expertise could help Saudi Arabia
Al-Abdallah also pointed to the potential for Syria to offer expertise in drone operations, particularly given its forces' experience operating drones during the war against Bashar Al-Assad’s regime. He said drones had played an important role in the lightning rebel offensive that toppled Assad, giving Syrian forces considerable experience in their use.
That expertise could prove useful to Saudi Arabia amid its confrontation with the Houthis, particularly if cooperation were to involve training or the use of smaller attack drones.
Al-Akhbar also reported that Syrian drone specialists were already involved in training forces in Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and that Syrian operators had helped establish drone units within Saudi emergency forces. However, these claims have not been independently verified.
Despite the reports, Al-Abdallah said ACLED had not documented evidence of Syrian fighters currently operating in Yemen. The organisation had found no reports of Syrian casualties, captured fighters or funerals linked to a deployment there, he said, noting that such evidence had helped establish the presence of Syrian fighters in other conflict zones, including Libya.
Al-Abdallah also questioned reports, including those published by Axios, that Syria could send its 84th Division to Yemen. He said the division was deployed around Suweida, in southern Syria, which remains largely outside the central government’s control after last year's sectarian clashes.
"Given the situation there, and reports of heavy Israeli arming of the National Guard and a possible escalation with the Syrian government, I don’t see how this division would leave Suweida," he said.
Syria's unresolved issues make deployment unlikely
The prospect of Syria deploying fighters to Yemen remains unlikely given the transitional government’s security challenges at home, according to Benjamin Schmida, a Middle East researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Schmida told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia likely requested that Syria send forces to Yemen, but Damascus appears to have declined.
"It does not seem like these discussions proceeded very far beyond consulting CENTCOM," he said, adding that the Syrian government’s public rejection of the request suggested the talks had not continued.
Schmida said it remained unclear what forces Syria could realistically deploy, given the security challenges facing the country, including Kurdish areas in the northeast, Druze militia control over Suweida, sporadic Islamic State group attacks, and repeated Israeli incursions in the southwest.
He also cautioned against assuming that foreign fighters integrated into Syria’s military would be available for deployment abroad.
"Foreign fighters, such as Uyghur Turkistan Islamic Party fighters that are integrated into the Syrian Defence Ministry, represent some of Syria’s most elite units," he said.
"The Syrian government likely views integrated foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, as vital assets for Syria's defence and internal security that must remain in Syria in the event of a future crisis."
Would Syrian fighters change the balance in Yemen?
The possibility of transferring foreign fighters to Yemen was also raised in Al-Akhbar's report, which suggested that Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks, Afghans, and Chechens who joined Syrian opposition factions before Assad’s fall could be among those considered for deployment.
However, Schmida said the potential impact of any Syrian deployment would depend on the number of fighters sent and where they were integrated into the conflict.
Axios recently reported that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 fighters. Schmida said this would represent a sizeable proportion of Syria’s total army manpower and could meaningfully bolster forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose forces he estimated at around 100,000.
But he noted that the Houthis are a much larger force, while government-aligned fighters remain spread across several frontlines, including Taiz, Marib, and Jawf.
More importantly, he said, sending additional fighters would not necessarily address the divisions undermining the Yemeni government’s war effort.
"Merely sending more fighters - though they may be experienced - is unlikely to solve one of the primary challenges for the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis: its own internal disunity," Schmida said.
He pointed to the political fragmentation and poor military coordination among government-aligned forces, warning that they could struggle to integrate Syrian fighters effectively, limiting their ability to change conditions on the battlefield.
Ultimately, Schmida said a meaningful Syrian deployment was unlikely "at this time or in the foreseeable future," as the government’s focus on domestic stability took precedence over Saudi requests.
While Riyadh could potentially use aid and investment to encourage Damascus to provide military support, he warned that doing so "could risk souring the Syrian-Saudi relationship and pushing Syria closer to Turkey or Saudi rivals like the UAE".
Louay Faour is a journalist at The New Arab focusing largely on the Levant, with a particular interest in Lebanese affairs

articles.title: Koretsky: government must deliver new mobilization social contract by Dec 1
articles.body:
Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky predicts that following changes to the reservation system, over 90-95% of employees in the fuel-energy and defense-industrial complexes will be re-reserved.
"We are separating the concept of criticality from economic reservation criteria. This is very important. Why? Because salary and the absence of tax debt are not the same as an enterprise's criticality. This is important, it indeed brings transparency, cleanup, and additional revenues, but it does not equal criticality. Critical means energy, the defense-industrial complex, communications, housing and communal services, pharmacies, groceries, logistics, and so on. But there are enterprises, a large number already, that got there largely due to salaries and a lack of tax debts. Therefore, we are separating criticality from the economy," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He emphasized that workers currently in the energy sector or the defense-industrial complex have nothing to worry about, as over 90-95% will be re-reserved.
"However, creating a large number of enterprises, whether IT or conditionally defense industry, where three drones are made and hundreds of people are reserved – I am conditionally simplifying, hyperbolizing in a certain sense, but that is how it is. And there are very many such cases. Contracting organizations. And it grows, grows, grows," he added.
According to the Prime Minister, changing the rules is designed, on the one hand, to cut down on unfair reservations without letting the economy collapse, and on the other hand, to give active military personnel a clear understanding regarding rotations.
"To say that these mobilization and reservation rules will produce a super-effect – no, there is no such thing, but we are at least stopping the endless growth of sometimes unfairly reserved individuals. And now, most importantly, what I am appealing to enterprises, business, and the economic sector about: we need to jointly come up with a new social model where, even if everyone is reserved, enterprises provide predictable mobilization of people into the army. This is an idealistic model. If such a solution could be found, the need to search for people on the streets would disappear. And if a business, entrepreneur, manager, or head takes on such a commitment – then nothing else is needed at all, this is a new social contract. But not thinking about it, not preparing for it, is a super-strategic mistake," Koretsky stated.
He stressed that failing to prepare in advance for a potential tightening of mobilization in Russia, which could reach 300,000–500,000 troops, would mean being forced to make unpopular decisions in manual mode once again.
"Then it won't be about reservations, or percentages. The issue is the survival of the state, and therefore this must be taken into account. Seeking to increase accountability for those who hide is also on the agenda – this is all a comprehensive story. By December 1, we must deliver a new social contract," he added, announcing a meeting with businesses on this issue.
As reported, on October 23, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky stated that the Cabinet of Ministers had finalized changes to the reservation system – an enterprise's criticality is being separated from its economic indicators, sectoral and regional criticality criteria will be updated, and enterprises will be checked for abuses.
The second change is that the maximum reservation level, particularly for the energy sector and defense industry, will no longer be 100% (dropping to 95%). The government will not weaken the work of those manufacturing weapons or maintaining critical infrastructure, and if uninterrupted operation requires reserving more, the enterprise can submit a justified appeal to a special Coordination Center.
The third change involves the Ministry of Defense strengthening liability for draft evasion. The fourth is the preparation of a mechanism for 100% reservation provided mobilization obligations are fulfilled: an enterprise will be able to fully reserve employees if it regularly and voluntarily recruits a portion of them for military service.
The Cabinet has also initiated a review of sectoral and regional criticality criteria, taking into account new requirements within 10 days.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: What is known about FSB’s thwarted attack on Moscow air defense site
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained two men from the South Caucasus who, acting on orders from the Ukrainian State Security Service (SBU), were preparing an attack using FPV drones against one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility, the FSB press office reported.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Thwarting of terrorist attack
- The FSB thwarted the sabotage and terrorist activities of two men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, the press office reported.
- According to the Federal Security Service, the men were going to prepare attack drones obtained from hidden stashes, transport them to the Moscow Region for launch, and activate them before takeoff.
- It was specified that the drones were to be controlled remotely from Ukrainian territory.
- While preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electric power facility and one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system, the suspects were detained by FSB officers, the press office said.
- The FSB released a video showing the FPV drones that the two detainees, natives of the South Caucasus, were using, on orders from the SBU, to prepare an attack on one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility.
- A video provided by the FSB press office shows the suspects assembling the drones and getting them ready for use according to instructions from their handler.
- The video shows two drones, both disassembled and assembled, as well as the communication devices used by the agents and instructions for assembling the drones.
Recruitment
- According to the FSB, one of the detainees was recruited by an SBU officer. Acting on his orders and in exchange for a promised monetary reward, the detainee traveled to Russia to plan a terrorist attack.
- To this end, he enlisted the help of a close acquaintance. Together, they retrieved FPV drones and components for homemade explosive devices from hiding places in the Smolensk and Kaluga Regions.
- The FSB had prior intelligence indicating that individuals from the South Caucasus were preparing an FPV drone attack on air defense and energy facilities in Moscow on behalf of the SBU. These individuals were agents of the Ukrainian special services, just like their handler, an FSB officer reported.
- The operation involving the handlers is ongoing, he noted.
Investigation
- A criminal case has been initiated against the detainees under Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code (Participation in a Terrorist Organization).
- The court remanded them into custody.
- The Federal Security Service is conducting the necessary investigative and operational measures to establish all the circumstances of the suspects’ illegal activities and their possible connections, the press office noted.

Palestine, Iran and world leaders celebrate Brazil's Lula election win
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian have joined world leaders in congratulating Brazil's Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his historic re-election, with Abbas praising the Brazilian leader's support for Palestinian rights and Tehran calling for closer bilateral ties.
The messages came on Monday after Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential run-off, securing a fourth, non-consecutive term with 51.76% of the vote against his rival's 48.24%.
In a congratulatory telegram, Abbas praised Brazil's longstanding support for the Palestinian people and their national rights, as well as its condemnation of crimes committed against Palestinians.
He expressed appreciation for Brazil's solidarity with Palestine and confidence that Lula would maintain these positions during his new term.
Abbas also described the election result as a reflection of the Brazilian people's confidence in Lula's domestic and international policies, praising what he called the president's courageous and responsible positions.
Brazil has emerged under Lula as an important international voice in support of Palestinian rights, with his re-election expected to ensure continuity in the country's foreign policy towards the Middle East.
Iran calls for stronger ties and multilateral cooperation
Iranian President Pezeshkian also congratulated Lula, expressing hope that relations between Tehran and Brasilia would expand during the Brazilian leader's new term.
According to Iran's IRNA news agency, Pezeshkian called for greater cooperation in areas of mutual interest and efforts to strengthen multilateralism and international peace.
Iran and Brazil maintain friendly diplomatic relations and are both members of BRICS, the grouping of emerging economies that has sought to strengthen cooperation among countries outside traditional Western-led institutions.
The congratulations follow diplomatic contacts between the two countries, including a telephone conversation between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Brazilian counterpart Mauro Vieira on 19 October, ahead of the presidential run-off.
Lula's victory is also expected to reinforce Brazil's role in the Global South and its engagement with international organisations such as BRICS, at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions and strained relations with Washington.
China and Russia hail Lula's re-election
China and Russia were among the major international powers to welcome Lula's victory, highlighting Brazil's growing importance in international diplomacy.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun congratulated the Brazilian president and said Beijing was ready to continue developing its relationship with Brasilia.
China hoped to advance the two countries' shared strategic vision and strengthen cooperation during Lula's new term, he said.
The Kremlin also welcomed the result, with spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praising Lula's contribution to relations between Russia and Brazil and his role in developing BRICS.
Peskov expressed hope that Lula would continue pursuing closer cooperation with Moscow and other members of the grouping.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Lula, describing the result as a victory for democracy and multilateralism.
She pledged to continue working with Brazil on trade, climate action and the international rules-based order.
French President Emmanuel Macron called for stronger strategic cooperation between Paris and Brasilia, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed Lula's victory as part of what he described as a broader progressive resurgence.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also celebrated the result, declaring that democracy and the Brazilian people had prevailed.
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel praised Lula's victory as a continuation of policies centred on sovereignty, peace and social justice.
Leaders from Canada, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay and Ecuador were also among those to congratulate the Brazilian president.
Divided reactions in the United States
The election prompted contrasting reactions from political figures in the United States, where relations with Brazil have been strained.
Donald Trump Jr, the son of US President Donald Trump, criticised the decision to extend voting hours by two hours during Sunday's run-off, accusing the American mainstream media of applying double standards in its coverage of the controversy.
The extension had been ordered by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin following procedural irregularities that disrupted the transportation of voters to polling stations in several Brazilian states.
Both candidates had requested additional voting time, but Bolsonaro subsequently called for the election to be annulled, describing the extension as unacceptable.
Progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders, meanwhile, congratulated Lula on his re-election, praising his record on workers' rights and democracy.
Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna welcomed the result as a rejection of extremism and urged Trump to respect Brazil's election outcome.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also celebrated Lula's victory, while California Governor Gavin Newsom's office welcomed continued cooperation with Brazil on democratic institutions, environmental protection and workers' rights.

Yemen's Houthi group on Monday claimed responsibility for two missile attacks targeting Saudi forces and weapons depots in the southern provinces of Aden and Lahij, according to a group spokesman.
In a statement posted on US social media platform X, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the attacks targeted military positions in the Salah al-Din area of Aden and the Al-Wahat area of Lahij.
Saree claimed that the group fired several ballistic missiles that accurately struck their targets, “resulting in dozens of dead and wounded … the destruction and incineration of a number of vehicles and weapons depots.”
He also said the targeted positions and military assets were under the supervision of Saudi officer Badr al-Harbi.
His remarks came hours after the Houthis launched a ballistic missile toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, which the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed.

Putin’s Valdai Residence Now Has 50+ Air Defense Positions—Half as Many as All of Moscow
Russia has built another 16 air-defense towers around Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing the number of identified air-defense positions in the surrounding area to more than 50, according to a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) investigation published October 25.
The new sites were identified through satellite imagery analyzed jointly with OSINT researcher jembob.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators found that the 16 towers were constructed in October within roughly 50 kilometers south of the residence—the direction facing Ukraine.
The new structures appear to form an additional outer air-defense ring and are expected to host Pantsir gun-and-missile systems, Tor surface-to-air missile systems, or similar equipment.
No corresponding new positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the outer ring, although investigators said additional construction could follow.
The new defensive belt passes through Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
Khotilovo is used for Putin’s travel, and a dedicated railway line connects the airfield area with his Valdai residence. One air-defense tower at the base had already been constructed by March 2026.
Several additional positions have appeared around the reservoir, including near Lisiy Island. Russian forces have built a laboratory complex there that, according to an earlier RFE/RL investigation, may be connected to Russia’s biological weapons research program.
Construction of two air-defense towers near that facility began in early September, roughly when the investigation into the laboratory became public.
The latest expansion pushes the number of known air-defense positions around Valdai above 50.
That figure is particularly striking when compared with Moscow. Russia has built roughly twice as many air-defense positions to protect Moscow and the surrounding region since the beginning of the full-scale invasion—but Moscow and its suburbs are home to more than 20 million people.
Fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, the surrounding district, and nearby territory within roughly 50 kilometers.
Previously, Russian leader Vladimir Putin signed an order to expand the core personnel of the Federal Protective Service, marking the fourth increase since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
articles.body:
Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous waters for commercial shipping, the Financial Times reported. At least 40 sailors have died there since the start of 2026, compared with 24 who died in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war the United States and Israel are waging against Iran has complicated shipping.
More than 570 ships have come under attack in the Black Sea since the start of the year, according to the maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization. Some ships were hit by accident, while others were deliberately targeted. Both Russia and Ukraine try to disrupt each other’s maritime shipping to reduce export revenues.
War-risk insurance for the Black Sea now costs as much as 15% of a ship’s hull value, almost twice the rate for ships in the Persian Gulf. Nearly the entire Black Sea is now classified in the highest war-risk category, except for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey.
Shipping oil from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz is now cheaper and safer by comparison. As a result, shipping companies increasingly refuse to operate in the Black Sea or use older vessels that are cheaper to insure.
Crews are recruited from Syria, Egypt, and Azerbaijan. The FT found that Syrian sailors earn about $800 a month working in the Black Sea. They are promised double pay for each day spent in the combat zone, and their families are to receive $25,000 to $50,000 in compensation if a sailor is killed.
Ukrainian forces struck more than 300 Russian vessels over an 11-week period, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said in September. The targets included sanctioned tankers as well as cargo ships carrying grain.
Russia has responded by stepping up strikes on ships entering Ukrainian ports. Russian attacks accounted for about 90% of strikes on commercial vessels over the past 45 days, according to Ambrey’s estimates.
The strikes are affecting global fuel and food supplies. Russian wheat exports fell 52% in September compared with a year earlier, while Ukraine is exporting only half its projected volume of agricultural products. Russian diesel exports fell by 467,000 barrels a day in September compared with a year earlier, according to Kpler.
The global effects of the war in the Black Sea are difficult to separate from those of the conflict in the Persian Gulf, Bloomberg reported. High global wheat stocks have kept disruptions in grain supplies from significantly affecting prices, while diesel fuel grew more expensive even before Russian–Ukrainian attacks escalated, because of the war the United States is waging against Iran.
The war in photographs
A family from Oleshky starts a new life in the Kyiv region
Vitaliy and Iryna fled the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in September with their 13-year-old son, Vlad, and their cat, Marsik. By then, residents had been left in complete isolation, without food, water, electricity, or medical care.
A drone damaged Vitaliy and Iryna’s home, prompting them to leave Oleshky and walk more than 20 kilometers (12 miles) along a mined road. The family traveled through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory and is now rebuilding its life in the Kyiv region.
Russia and Ukraine agreed last week to a ceasefire in Oleshky for the evacuation of residents. It is set to take effect at 4 a.m. on October 27.

articles.title: Ukraine changes tactics for using Patriot systems, Ihnat says
articles.body:
Ukraine changes tactics for using Patriot systems, Ihnat says
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command, made this statement on the RBC-Ukraine podcast, according to Ukrinform.
Ihnat explained that during the full-scale war, the Ukrainian military has changed its approach to using the American systems. In particular, they have learned to use the Patriot in various tactical situations and to use the expensive interceptor missiles more efficiently.
One example is the ability to deploy the system not only from fixed positions but also for ambushes followed by a change of location.
“For example, you can use the Patriot not as a stationary system—the way the Americans keep it at airfields or bases—but make it, so to speak, ‘mobile’: set up an ambush, shoot down five aircraft, and return unscathed,” explained the Air Force spokesperson.
Another difference concerns ammunition consumption. According to Ihnat, Ukrainian crews have learned to use one missile against a single target, whereas in the Middle East, in some cases, up to eight interceptors could be launched simultaneously.
He explained that the Patriot has three operating modes: automatic, semi-automatic, and manual. In automatic mode, the system can launch a significant number of interceptors, and in the absence of relevant combat experience, the entire salvo of missiles could be fired from the launcher at a single target.
“Due to a lack of such experience, they could have fired the entire salvo of interceptors from a single launcher at a single Shahed or a single ballistic missile,” Ihnat noted.
According to his estimate, the number of missiles used in the Middle East would have been enough for Ukraine to operate these systems for several years.
“That is why we now find ourselves in the crisis we are in—because what was spent in the Middle East would have been enough for us to operate the Patriot systems for several more years,” Ihnat concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, Volodymyr Zelensky stated that progress is being made on the issue of providing Ukraine with missiles for the Patriot systems, but the process is moving very slowly.

articles.title: Mecca pact members to meet Iranian leaders in Tehran
articles.body:
Senior officials from the Mecca pact countries, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Oct. 26 in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities have announced.
Türkiye’s intelligence chief İbrahim Kalın will travel to the Iranian capital for the meeting.
“As agreed, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting,” said Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The visiting delegation will also meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, according to Saudi Arabian officials.
The meeting follows eight months of war in the Middle East and recent U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran.
Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran.
Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement on Aug. 7. Under the agreement, a threat to the territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognized borders of any signatory would require the parties to use all necessary means to eliminate the threat or danger.
The talks will mark the first high-level contact between Iran and the three-country bloc since Saudi Arabia became more deeply involved in the conflict.
“The Tehran meeting could serve as a starting point for shaping regional security,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei sai during a press briefing on Oct. 26.
Baghaei added that countries in the region were seeking to establish regional security mechanisms to safeguard their own security and promote peace.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom’s defense minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Oct. 26.
“The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis,” Krimly said in a post on X.
It is aimed at “promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan,” he added.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal which laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.

articles.title: Algeria to Deploy Troops Abroad for First Time Since 1973, Sending Forces to Niger
articles.body:
Algeria’s two parliamentary chambers approved on October 25 the deployment of the country’s armed forces to Niger to protect Algeria’s energy interests and honor bilateral agreements.
Algeria’s Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, made the announcement.
The decision was approved in closed-door sessions after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune submitted a request on October 22.
The lower house of parliament, the National People’s Assembly, also approved the troop deployment by an overwhelming majority.
According to an official statement by the Council of the Nation, the decision aims to protect Algeria’s energy interests and fulfill the terms of a bilateral agreement with Niger.
Algerian authorities have not yet disclosed the size of the military contingent, the exact deployment date, or the duration of the planned mission.
According to Reuters, one possible deployment site for Algerian troops is the Madama area in northern Niger, near the border with Libya.
Algeria has significant economic interests in Niger, particularly in oil production and the development of transcontinental energy projects.
The state-owned company Sonatrach is developing the Kafra oil project in northern Niger. In August 2026, its subsidiary ENAFOR was preparing to drill the Kafra Sud-Est 1 exploration well, approximately 85 km from the Algerian border.
Algeria, Niger, and Nigeria are also pursuing the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project, which aims to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria.
In June 2026, Sonatrach announced the start of construction on the pipeline’s Algerian section.
In August, Militarnyi reported that Algeria had deployed four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger following an attempted military coup in the country’s capital, Niamey.

articles.title: More than a US briefing: Brussels security talks on Ukraine planned for 27 or 28 October, Kyiv says
articles.body:
Ukraine, the US, the EU, and NATO plan to meet in Brussels this week to discuss security for Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Ukrainian TV. The meeting would follow last week’s talks in Oslo and a US envoy’s visit to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Guarantees are what would oblige Ukraine’s allies to act if Russia attacks again. The Paris Declaration laid plans for that commitment in January. Kyiv had a briefing from the Americans, and now the partners want a broad discussion of security and guarantees, Zelenskyy said. Brussels comes ahead of three-way talks with Russia, which the Kremlin says Putin is ready in principle to resume in mid-November.
Zelenskyy: meeting planned for Tuesday or Wednesday
The meeting is planned for Tuesday or Wednesday, 27 or 28 October, Zelenskyy said in the interview, aired on 25 October. The EU would take part at the presidential level and NATO at the level of its secretary general. He did not know whether anyone else would join. He also said Ukraine’s neutrality and limits on its army are not up for discussion.
After Oslo, Witkoff briefed Putin in St. Petersburg
Earlier, on 20 October, Zelenskyy met US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre present. According to Zelenskyy, a wider round there included national security advisers from Germany, the UK, France, and Italy, the chief of staff of the European Commission president, and NATO representatives.
A day later, Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg and said he had brought papers setting out possible paths to a settlement. He told Putin the Oslo talks had been productive. However, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov claimed the new ideas from the Europeans and Kyiv that Witkoff relayed held little of use for a settlement.
